W,Ottnl• FAREWELL TO SUMMER. Summer is fading; the broad leaves that grew So freshly green when June was young are falling, And all the whisper-haanted forest through The restlesa birds in saddened tones are calling From rastling hazel-cope and tangled dell, "Farewel', sweet Summer, Fragrant, fruity Summer, Sweet farewell!" Upon the windy hills, in many a field, The honey-bees hum slow above the clover, Gleaning the latest sweets its blooms may yield, Aid knowing that their harvest-time is over, Sing, half a lullaby and half a knell, " Farewell, sw et Summer, Honey-laden Summer, Sweet farewell!" The little broak that babbled 'mil the ferns, O'er twisted TOOta and sandy shallows playing, Seems fain to linger in its eddied turns, And with a plaintive, purling voice is saying, Sadder and sweeter than my song can tell: "Farewell, sweet Summer, Warm and dreamy Stammer, Sweet farewell!"

The fitful breeze sweeps down the winding lane, With gold and crimson leaves before it flying; Its gusty laughter has no sign of pain, But in the lulls it sinks to gentle sighing, And mourns the Summer's early broken spell,— "Farewell, sweet Summer, Rosy, blooming Summer, Sweet farewell !" So, bird, and bee, and 'brook, and breeze make moan, With melancholy song their loss proclaiming, I, too, must join them, as I walk alone Among the sights and sounds of Summer waning; I, too, have loved the season passing well,— "So farewell, Summer, Fair but faded Summer, Sweet farewell !"
...Young England.

A gentleman made a rockery in front of his hbuse, in which he planted some beautiful ferns, and having put up the following notice, found it more efficient and less expen- sive than spring-guns and man-trapa. The fear-inspiring inscription was—" Beggars,:beware! Scolopendriums and Polydiams are set here." A clergyman sends a couple of University anecdotes. Pro- fessor Sheepshanks, of Jesus College, Cambridge, was one of the examiners for the previous EMataillStioll. By mistake, one of the questions WAS printed thus—" Describe the satyrs of Horace.' A young wag thus answered The satyrs of Horace are satyrs of note. With the bead of a man and the legs of a goat; But the satyrs of ....iverus" all satyrs surpass. With the shanks of a sheep, and the he‘el ot an ass. Here's the other story. In one of the previous Examina- tions a question ran thus—" Describe the common pump."

This was the answer : Let X be the handle. And Y bathe spout, Move X upland doers,. And the water oomes out. How TO BECOME THETOTAL.—Mr. Walter, M.P., con- cluded a temperance speech the other day by giving a piece of advice to those who might be unable to withstand the temptation to drink, and that was to follow the highly com- mendable example of a gentleman who, in 1795, was so overcome with the temptation that he published the follow- ing advertisement in the Bahama Gazette :—" Whereas the subscriber, through the pernicious habit of drinking, has greatly hurt himself in purse and person and rendered him- self odious to all his acquaintances; and finding there is no possibility of breaking off from the said practice but through the impossibility to find the liquor; he therefore begs and prays that no persons will sell him, for money or on trust, any sort of spirituous liquors, as he will not in future pay for it, but will prosecute any one for an action of damage against the temporal and eternal interests of the public's humble, serious, and sober servant, JearEs eller: NERS.—Witnesa, William Andrews.—Nasaau, June 26, 1795." Two VIEWS OF NIAGARA.—A correspondent writes : Comparisons may be odious, but one cannot help making them sometimes. For instance :—" The Falls of Niagara did not give one that feeling of awe and sublimity which the guide books stated could be got without any extra ex- pense. If one wanted really to appreciate Niagara it was necessary to go beneath the Falls and wear the most un- becoming texture ever invented, viz. yellow oilskin, almost as bad as macintosh, which he hoped none of them ever wore."—Oscar Wilde. "I was in a manner stunned, and unable to comprehend the vastness of the scene. When I came on Table Rock and looked—great Heaven, on what a fall of bright-green water—it came upon me in its full might and majesty. Then, when I felt how near to my Creator I was standing, the first effect, and the enduring one, instant and lasting, of the tremendous spectacle was peace. Pelee of mind, tranquillity, calm recollections of the dead, great thoughts of eternal rest and happiness; nothing of gloom or terror. Niagara was at once stamped noon my heart, an image of beauty, to remain there change- less and indelible, until its pulses cease to beat for ever."— Charles Dickens. THE READING OF TILE PARIS OuVRIER.—To judge from Oak way the ouvriers gather round bookstalls, and the aridity with which the young among them may be seen de- vouring a book while waiting for the tram, reading must be a real enjoyinent for the more intelligent. I have seen a young fellow in a blouse reading a book as he sat astride on the back of a heavy cart horse. A friend, a lady who has made friends with an (Merl er family at Belleville, finds them not only to possess a good library, but to be well acquainted with French literature. When a workman is a reader his taste will be good. He will despise novels, especially of the vicious order; his favourite books are histories of the Re- volution, such as Lamartine's " Girondins " ; Louis Blanc's " Dix "; " Histoire de Deux-Decembre," Ac.; and for cliseics, Voltaire, Rosseau, and perhaps Corneille. If in the present adnit population many may be found with literary and artistic tastes, the ouvriers of the next generation will be educated men, in the vulgar sense of the word; for it would be difficult to give adequate expression to the fury with which the instruction of the people is pressed forward. All classes combine; the Republicans because they sincerely believe that popular instruction is the great panacea for all the ills of the world; Conservatives, because they hope that it will make the people reasonable; Catholics, because they fear to lose even those who still hold to the church.— R. Breath, in "Good Words." How To GET Ali ArDIENCE.—I venture to tell a little story about a lecturing experience of Mr. StanleyWhe African explorer. When he had returned to England from that wonderful journey of his across the continent of Africa, and while he was writing his book, I suggested to a theatri- cal manager th A he should propose to Mr. Stanley to make a lecturing tour through England and tell the people of that country of his wonderful adventures. Stanley consented and sallied forth. The tour was fairly successful. After some weeks' absence from London, Mr. Stanley returned for a few days,_and his manager went to see him and ask him how the lecturing flourished. "Very well," said Stanley, "in a financial sense. The halls are always crowded when I begin, but as I go on, the people go trickling out, till at the end, I am left with only half an audience, and I don't like it. It seems to me that they come to stare at me as if I were a gorilla, and when they have stared their fill, they rise and go, not pretending to take any interest in what I am telling them." The manager suggested that, perhaps, he was too monotonous, that he ought to diversify his serious parts with some play of humour. But Stanley objected that there was no humour in his composition, which was quite true. "I am not like Mark Twain or Artemus Ward,' said he. "There is no fun in me, but only dead earnest." (This puts me in mind of the remark a Scotch ex-editor once made about the man who had succeeded him. "Aye," said he, candidly, "the new man is a much better man than me. It is true I can joke, but I joke with difficulty, whereas he jokes just spontaneous." Well, Stanley can't joke, either spontaneously or with difficulty.) Just then the managerheard a hideous howling, proceeding from the lower regions of the house. "What, in the name of Cmsar, is that noise?" asked the manager. "Oh," said Stanley, "it's only my black boy Kalulu, that I brought from the interior of Africa, you know. He's singing one of his confounded war-songs while he polishes my boots." A bright thought occurred to the manager. "Have him up," he explained, "and let us hear him." Kaluln was summoned, and nothing loth, gave llia war-song and its accompanying wild dance, in their native blood-curdling horror. In fact, he wanted to go on wax-dancing and war-singing all day, and was with dif- ficulty suppressed, after breaking most of the furniture, and was sent back to his boots. "Now," said the man 'ger, with the acumen of a showman, "here is your chance for the introduction of a diversion. About the middle of your lecture lead up to and introduce one of Kalulu's war-dances and songs, and say that the lecture will conclude with another exhibition !" Stanley agreed, and the necessary in- timation was duly given in the advertisements. Some weeks later, Stanley returned again to London, and the *manager went to see him. "Oh, yes," said Stanley, "the audiences stop right through to the end. By the way, you'd better alter that advertisement. It runs now Lecture by Mr. Stanley on South Africa, with War-dance and Song by his Native Boy, Kalulu, in the middle and again at the conclusion.' You had better have it changed to this, I think 'A South African Concert by Kalulu, Mr. H. M. Stanley's Black Boy, accompanied by War-dances, with an Introduction and some Explanations, by Mr. Stanley.' You see," continued Stanley, moodily," the crowd keeps on encoring Kalala's first performance till the time comes for the second; when I try to get a little show, tney won't have me, but put me down with wild shouts for "Kalulu ! Kalulu!'" which evidence of bad taste hurt Stanley's sense of self-esteem, and he felt quite jealou3 of pooqalutu, who, however, soon died, partly of over zeal for his war dancing and singing, and partly becausehe was too fond of rum.—Mr. Forbes in the Century. self." HEAVY LOSSES OF ATRICULTURIsTs.-The agricultural depression so long existing in some parts of the country has been attended with disastrous consequences to a number of farmers in Warwickshire. One agriculturist living near Coventry sowed a 10-acre field with wheat, and the entire crop, which has just been disposed of, brought only £5, not- withstanding that the coat of erowing it was more than ten times that amount. THE FARMERS' ALLIANCE.-A spec,al general meeting of the Hampshire branch of the Farmers' Alname will be held at the George Hotel, Winchester, on Thursday, the 10th inst., at half-past three o'clock, to consider the present representation of the county, and the advisability of starting a candidate or candidates at the next election who will be sdecially pledged to support the programme of the Alliance. Several other counties are stated to be contemplating a simi- lar coupe of action. FROG Paps.-Mr. Colin C. Baird, veterinary surgeon, Dick's Veterinary College, Edinburgh,has invented an India- rubber freg pad for fitting into the heels of the shoes of car- riage and saddle horses, with a view of preventing the ani- mals from slipping and falling on the causeway. A small steel plate protrudes from the centre of each end of the rubber, and can easily be slipped into apertures made inside the heels of the shoe. The pad can readily be removed in the evening, and replaced in the morning. The invention is said to have already given much satisfaction. A set of pads is expected to wear out two sets of shoes. SMITILFIELD Cram -A meeting of the Council of the Smithfield Club was held at the Agricultural Hall on Friday. The Council proceeded to consider the state of foot-and- mouth disease throughout the country. It was resolved that the following special regulations be in force for the forthcoming show:-1. That no animal (cattle, sheep, or pigs) exhibited at any other show after the let November, 1883, be allowed to be exhibited at the Smithfield Club's show this year. 2. That each exhibitor be required to certify that any animal to be sent by him for exhibition at the Smithfield Club's show this year, has not been, and will not be, shown at any other exhibition after the let Novem- ber, 1833.-A number of new members were elected. EDUCATION.-Last winter an experiment in teaching agricultural science was tried at South Kensington. While it was not directly associated with any Government depart- ment, its utility was recognised in the permission given to one or two prominent men in the Science and Art Depart- ment to assist in the organisation of the classes, and also in the gratuitous loan of lecture rooms and apparatus. This winter the Institute of Agriculture, as the new undertaking is called, will be carried on upon a somewhat more ambi- tious scale than last year, though still without a great amount of ostentatidn. A staff of experienced professors is engaged; and the curriculum will cover all the sciences bearing upon agriculture. The opening lectures in the vari- ous classes will be given at the end of the present month. FAIRY RINGS.-In a paper on fairy rings, we have estab- lished on tolerably good evidence that the fungus destroys large amounts of the organic matter in the soil, and appro- priates to itself the nitrogen contained. Its action is more like that of an animal than a plant, in burning off large quantities of carbon to obtain the nitrogen it requires. By removing the fungi as fast as they were formed, I satisfied myself that the growth of the grass was not due to the de- cay of the above ground growth of the fungus alone, for I found that the removal made little, if any, difference in the luxuriance of the grass. It is to the underground action of the fungus, therefore, that we must attribute its beneficial effects upon the pasture. By its action the total amount of organic matter in the soil is reduced, but at the same time portions have been rendered as food for the grass. LANCASTER ANNUAL STORE SHEEP SALE.-MeSSYS. Hay- thornthwaite and Son held their second great annual sale fir keeping sheep, lambs, rams, &c., on Monday, at their sale yard, Scotforth, near the Old Station, when there was for sale upwards of four thousand sheep and lambs, includ- ing 133 rams of all breeds and ages, selected from some of the best flocks in the district. The sheep comprised half and three-ports bred ewes, Shropshire down ewes, cheviot ewes, horned ewes, and lonk ewes. The lambs comprised half and three-parts bred gimmers and wethers, lonk wethers, horned wethers, and a few horned ram lambs. Farmers and buyers of stock assembled in large numbers from all parts of the count-y. Biddings were spirited, and sheep were sold in exceedingly large numbers, coming into the ring as many as 200 at a time, and one lot especially, of which there yea% 239 all in the ring at once, and all sold in the course of a very few minutes, before even one left the ring. In many cases exceedingly high prices were realised. The following are a few of the prices :-Rey. C. T. NATIONAL APPLE CostottEss.-A. typical show of apples in connection with an informal conference on the culture of this fruit was opened last week in the beautifully vine. adorned conservatory of the Royal Horticultural Society's Gardens at Chiswick. The objects of the society, carrying Out suggestions made at a meeting of fruit growers recently held at South Kensington under the auspices of the Fruit Committee of the society, is to take advantage of the ex- ceptionally good and abundant yield of the apple orchards this year throughout the kingdom, with a view to the cor- rection of nomenclature, to the comp arson of the merits of varieties, to the determination of their suitableness for cultivation in different localities and in different soils, and I generally to the dissemination of the fullest information ' obtainable with respect to the growing of apples. The re- sults of the experiment have been highly satisfactory, and the remarkable collections of county exhibits, of home and foreign stocks and varieties, may be instructively compared with the widely representative series of specimens grown in the societiy's grounds under the management of Mr. Barron. There are no prizes or certificates offered, but exhibitors, while contributing their quota of particulars may find a reward for their pains in the increased value every addition made to the data will give to the generalisations it may be possible to record as to the outcome of the conference. Altogether about 8,000 plates of apples, with four to six specimens on each plate, are ranged on the tables of several houses in the Horticultural Society's grounds, and of this number of exhibits over 1,000 have been sent from Scotland. With the exception of Northumberland, Cumberland, Rut- land, Suffolk, and Cornwall, every county in England con- tributes. The finest display, which, as might be expected, is from the home counties, will be found set out in the great vine-houses, with specimenesof 200 sorts of apples grown in the society's gardens. Kent is the largest contributor, followed closely, however, by Surrey, Sussex, and Hertford- shire. Next in variety to the society's collection, perhaps, is that from the Queen's gardens' at IFrogmoro1 whence Mr. T, Jones hat forwarded absut oosorts for purposes of mi.. parison. Contributors have been asked, and most have com- plied with the request, to give, together with the name by which each kind of apple is known in their locality, the habits and character of the tree and the nature of the soil on which it grows. Among exhibits specially interesting may be noted a little bough on which the well-grown apples (Lane's Prince Albert) appear in two close rows from end to end. The Tweedside and the Lothians make the best show from the north. Cheshire and Hereford are fairly well re- presented, the latter county sending some particularly good specimens of an apple we owe to an Irish grower, the Eclin- ville seedling, which was raised near Belfast. A fine show of apples, with some good pears, &c., grown under glass in Sweden, has been sent from Ofveras, Gothenburg, by Mr. J. Loney, gardener to Mr. Oscar Dickson. The exhibition will remain open for the inspection of those interested in fruit- growing until the 18th inst. PROFESSOR TANNER'S TOUR IN CANADA.- Professor Tanner, in a report to the Councit of the Institute of Agri- culture, refers to the confusion in the public mind as to the real state of Canada. The reports of the delegates of the British farmers who had visited Canada showed very clearly that emigration, prudently carried out, gave unbounded facilities for securing a comfortable support, and for the accumulation of profits. But many correspondents to the public press had given heartrending accounts of failure by those trusting to favourable statements as to the capacity of Canada. He tried to localise these failures, but neither in England nor Canada could he obtain one single instance, from any of the writers of the discouraging letters, which he could. examine on the spot. He says :-" I, therefore, proceeded on my tour through Canada, and by personal ob- servation I have been able to form a very definite opinion upon the facts of the cage. Australasia. It is estimated that the value of gold mining plant in use at the present time in Victoria is fully two• millions sterling. The mention of such a figure is a proof that the conditions of mining are now such as to necessitate the recourse to a considerable amount of capital for working expenses. The cost of deep sinking and extensive under- ground works, together with the machinery that will yield the best payable r esults from crushing and washing, is sufficient to deter the individual speculator, and most of the mining enterprises of the colony are now carried on by companies whose scrip in the market varies in value with every chaaging yield from the claim and upon the pros- pects of holders having to pay calls or res,eive handsome dividends. So far as a new-comer is able to observe there is no want of spirit displayed by mining investors in Vic- toria. In some parts of the country where there is gravel believed to be auriferous, but not being tried, complaints , may be heard that if capitalists would come forward splen- did results would eventually follow. There may be founda- tion in these complaints, but generally speaking where there , is a likelihood of gold being got in any remunerative quan- tity there the prospector has been succeeded by the inves- tor in the shape of a Company with the best appliances from the Melbourne machine shops. If it be true, as stated, that one-third of the total area of Victoria is occupied by gold bearing rocks, then there is much country yet to be oc- cupied by the miner. To help in the realisation of this desirable result the Government of the Colony is continu- ally being urged to enter upon a systematic plan of pros- pecting. It is urged that the expenditure of forty or fifty thousand pounds on this official preliminary would be omoney well spent, and on the principle of looking to Parlia- ment for everything, it is not easy to see how the appeal can be resisted. Meanwhile, by the provision of diamond drills, which are let out on cheap terms to prospecting comp iniee, much good is being done. Everything taken into the account, gold mining in Victoria at the present time is in a highly prosperous state. The last yearly re- turn exhibited a yield of 858,850 ounces, valued at 0,435,400. There is good warrant for believing that with the vigorous working of the claims now opened and the extension of the producing area the yield annually will rise much higher. Quartz mining is the most in favour now. Owing to the improvements which have been effected in the stamping machinery and saving processes the yield of a few penny weights of gold to the ton of stone can now be made remunerative. The average yield is about 10dwts. Several quartz mine shafts are over 2,000 feet deep. Rapid borings through dense basalt by the diamond drill machines, and the information disclosed by the cores of rock obtained, have given a great lift to alluvial mining of late, and have enabled the companies to determine the downward courses of the "leads" at distant points, and to sink shafts with pre- cision either upon or in close proximity thereto. There are other metals and minerals found in the Colony, such as silver, antimony, and tin. The latter is got in the Upper Murray district, but there are no indications of Vic- toria turning out such quantities as does the neighbouring island colony of Tasmania. Of building stones there are fair supplies, and there is also plenty of clay from which good bricks and excellent pottery ware are made. Coal also there is, but as yet it has not been come across in such thickness as to pay for the trouble of getting and hawling. Three or four companies are conducting operations' and their shareholders believe that eventually the black dia- monds may be met with in measure to compensate for their patience and faith. The geological surveyor of the colony likewise strongly holds to the theory. It may be that these hopes will some day be realised. For the nonce Victoria must be classed as a non-coal bearing country, and she is therefore so far behind her principal rivals—New South Wales and New Zealand. • Spite of this great drawback, Victoria—or one should perhaps rather say with this connection Melbourne—is the principal manufacturing centre of Australia. Machinery, carriages, manufactured jewelry, boots and shoes, confec- tionery, and many other things made altogether or prepared in the colony are exported largely to the adjoining colonies. Whether those colonies now taking Victoria made or Vic- toria prepared goods in large quantities will continue to do so for any long time has to be seen. They may not be con- tent that Victoria shall be the workshop for the group as Victoria would fondly be. It is highly probable that, as they are even now already doing, the other colonies will continually strive to manufacture as much as they can for themselves, and Victorian firms may experience keener and keener competition every day. Already they feel the pinch, and are now among the warmest advocates for a kind of free trade by which the colonies would admit each other's goods without a duty but impose a tax on articles manufactured by the foreigner. These same men, it should be observed, after being established in or encouraged to enter on the business with which they are engaged by high protective duties on all goods likely to compete with "native" indus- try are leading advocates for State-assisted immigration as a relief to the labour market. .This is no doubt highly con- sistent. Finding that the public has been content to tax itself largely to build up local factories, these traders now ask that they should be coddled still further, and coddled among others by neighbouring colonies they have hitherto sought to shackle. The extent and variety of the manufacturing industries Victoria are undoubtedly calculated to profoundly astonish anyone unaware of the handicapping which the fiscal policy of the colony has imposed on their behalf. Their success is pointed to as a proof of the wisdom of adopting Protec- tion for their nurture; but however that may be, it is unde- niable that a large share of tin progress whish has been made in manufactnres is to be credited to the intelligence and energy of those who have entered into the several busi- nesses established in the colony. It is probably capable of proof that some of the zeal infused into these channels might have been for the colony more profitably directed into other classes of production, but that must pass. The Legislature has, with the concurrence of the working men and of those having money to put into these enterprises, done its beat to beat out anything which would compete, and the result is that, either for good 91 evil, there are close 'Tort 3,000 hnhnfacturing establishments of one sort or another in this small community, and employing about 40,000 hands! The imports into the country amount to 15 millions sterling. These consist chiefly of soft goods (dra- peries which are scarcely attempted to be made in Victoria yet), iron and steel, foreign wine and spirits glaesware, books, and chemicals. It is manifest from thedgures which are available, and which indicate that the exports (£16,000,000) are made up of the products of the soil (agri- cultural and pastoral), and from the gold mines, leaving short of one million sterling as the extent of exportation of manufactures, that the manufacturing industry will prove a little overdone unless the inward wants of Victoria should largely increase, or the import trade in those articles now competing with the colonial articles greatly diminish. Meanwhile the manufacturers and their employOs are a powerful section of the community. According to the evi- dence which has been given before a Royal Commission on the existing Tariff arrangements, there are several trades now quite capable of holding their own on equal terms with the imported products, though, as a matter of fact, they are all agreed about maintaining duties which tend to make dear that which competes with them from Great Britain, America, or the European Continent. Visits made by the same Commission to the principal factories have disclosed what I have before suggested, viz., that in several of the branches a highly creditable state of excellence is shown. The making of soap and candles, boots and shoes, the plainer kinds of earthenware, glass-making, hat-making, jewelling, paper-making and stationery, biscuits and con- fectionery, agricultural and mining machinery, carriages, &c., are each of them trades which may be mentioned as in a particularly efficient state. But withal, as the reader will have supposed, I prefer to place the real producing interests of the colony, the agricultural, the pastoral, and mining, as being the more important. There remain many other topics upon which one could have touched, but I must close, as my aim has been com- pression rather than expansion. If I have succeeded in creating a deeper interest in one of the most interesting and vigorous of the British Colonies, I shall have been re- warded for the little trouble I have taken. As those who have followed me closely will have noticed, I do not held nut Victoria as the most promising of the fields for the

emigrant, but I certainly regard it as one in which any man of small capital and a knowledge of husbandry, or any smart man with a good trade in his hands, is bound to do well. There are, I firmly believe, great things in store for these southern colonies, and I fancy that in the long run Victoria will not be far from the front in the race.

EXPRESS FROM BLACKBURN TO ~o_,.„i ~,—....,.. .„ BLACKPOOL. 3,„ .::T. - rvvo,4 • BY GEORGE JONES. Blackpool! How differently that talismanic name affects one as the years get on. lA hat an almost incredible differ- ence is experienced between the first time of going, in the flush of early youth, and the same journey in maturer years. Though people may tell us that it is ourselves and not Blackpool that has changed, yet we cling a little to the consoling idea that Blackpool is not what it used to be. gut whatever may lee said to the contrary, if anyone will have the temerity to venture on an early Whit-Monday trip thither, ocular demo-nstration may be had that the youth of to-day enjoys the outing quite as boisterously and keenly as the youth of twenty-five years ago did. And there is no doubt that for certain temperaments, and certain purposes Blackpeol, with all its monotony, is a very enjoyable place; and being made by the railway companies so very easy of accese great numbers of people take advantage of the oppor- tunities to inhale its salubrious breezPs. I can hardly say that it was for the sole purpose of breath- ing its ozone that I decided, the other Thursday, to avail myself of the chance to go there, "on the cheap," by the tradesmen's one-and-niaepenny excursion. No! I think it was more for the change, and to aces if the place had altered any; or perhaps it was as old Ned Hodson once said, "1" wife axed too to tek her, un aw dossent deny her." lot whatever the reason, half-past two of that particular afternoon found myself, Mrs. J., a sister, and a fair sized crowd waiting on the platform for the express to take us. I know it was an express because the stationmaster told us so, and I was very glad he did, otherwise we should perhaps never have found it out. A few minatei and this firey, un'am al, unbridled, express came dashing in with an ear-eplitting yell; and then ensued the usual unnecesea7 scramble for seats, and in five seconds there was no one on the platform but the officials, and every- body was telling everybody else that " Ther wer no 'casion to feight sooa to ged in; ther wer plenty o' room to spare." Punctually, as is, of coarse, usual with the "L. & Y ," this unrestrainable express gave another yell—a bit jerky this time—and rushed madly into the open country, at the rate of five miles an hour, and nearly everybody in the compartment uttered the customary exclamation, " Wer off maw." We had in our compartment five motherly-looking females, and their conversation certainly helped to relieve the ennui of that impetuous express journey. Their talk was ofttimes nonsensically complimentary to each other, but they gave utterance te some hard facts occasionally. It ran something like the following— " Wey, Mary, whoa'd a thowt o' seem n thee here? Wod is id as is tekkin thee to Blackpool ?" "Ay, tha mud wed lax thad! Its o through Nancy tin Jane here! They sed ther fellas hed gin urn two shillin a piece to gooa, un aw tout as weel gooa wi' urn; sooa aw put mi bakin off, un aw up an geet ready, we here aw am." "Well, tha jest dad reight. Tha'r as fit to gooa as eny- body else. Heaw's Mrs. Pilkitonj geddin on neaw ? 800 lives i' yo'r street, doesn't hoc ?" ' Will ta howd thi noise abeawt Mrs. Pilkiton ! Hoo'd be reight enuf if id wornd for yon gred hulkin lazy fella of hors. 800 werks like a he3s to keep him, an hoo hesu'd hofe enuf to heyt." " Wey, is he eawt o' werk'ogeon ?" . "He's never into werk, un he doesn't want to be. When he's abeawt hooam he's up un deawn i' hoe middins, un o sooarts o' places, wi' an owd salmon tin un a spade catchin worums, an when he's getten as mony as he wants off he pops, an he's happen nod sin ogeon for three or four days." "Wey, weds he want wi' t' worums ?" "He gooas a fishin mon ; he never does nowt else!" "Un wadever does he do wi' his fish? Does he sell um !" "Sell urn! wey he does'nt catch as mony in a week as he con sell for threepence. Un if he does catch one owt like t' size of a herrrin, he's up and deawn t' street wi' his thumbs in his wes-cote, swaggerin abeawt as if he'd catched t' seea ser- pent as they keep botherha abeawt i' t' peppers. He's woe then thad chap as used to live deawn Wensley Fowd. Thad mon once catched a fish—aw think he co'd id a peeark—un he wer showin id everybody. Fishermen wer comm n fro o perts ot' teawn to look at this peeark. He wrooat off to sorewheer to ax if ther wer ever one as big catched afoor." "War id such a size as o thad ? " "Size! aw'll tell tha. Aw thowt as ther wer sich a lot a fooak gooin to see this peeark aw'd hey a look at id too. Well, aw went, un wods ta think? Id actily wornd th' hate size of a gradely herrin !" " Well aw never ! " "Ids true aw tell tha ; tin he bed id laid eawt like a corpse on a white cloth an he kept throwin watther on id. Owd Mary Berm went wi' mo to look at id an we booath laughed sooa tell he ordered us eawt o' th' heawse." As I said before, this conversation somewhat mitigated the wearisomeness of that terrific express journey. If we . had'nt been express I don't think we should have got to Blackpool in time to catch the return train home. As it was, in the unprecedented time of forty five minutes from starting we began to see the chimneys and steeples of the distant town of Preston, and by the impetuosity of that in- tractable express, we just managed to get into Blackpool in time for tea I always think that a good tea is about as enjoyable as anything in Blackpool provided you can watch the promena- ders at the time you are having it, and I am not quite sure that a good meal is not the most enjoyable thing whether you can watch the promenaders or not. After tea we must of course have a stroll round and see the sights, which said sights are indelibly imprinted on my mind; not by virtue of this visit, but on account of previous experiences. There was the ever-present diminutive specimen of hu- manity with the useless nether limbs and expressionless eyes; sitting on ,his chair lof locomotion, with hie small donations-thankfully-received can prominently before him las usual. There was the stall with the prawns, •which the vendor will persist in calling shrimps. And there was as there always is the oyster stall next to him, the owner of which told me that, if I would try a few they would "make my blooming neck swell." As I didn't want to have a swelled neck, I didn't have any. Then a little farther on we came to a blind man with a voice like a sea trumpet, accompanying himself on a harmonium, and singing a song about a sailor who was swallowed by a whale, and who them put his hand ' out and siezed the whale by the tail and turned him inside out. So we went on for fear there might be more of it. ' We have a few relations and friends in Blackpool and my companions now proposed calling upon them. Knowing that this meant wasting what little time we had I objected ' strongly and got quite eloquent, thinking to carry my point. • It ended as usual in my having to do as I was told. This . performance lasted so long that we had no time after for ' anything but a walk on the promenade, which, lighted up by electricity, prcsented a very lively appearance. We had'nd proceeded far, in fact we'd hardly proceeded at all, when we came upon another blind man and a girl, with a harmonium, singing in a very mild treble one of Moody and Sankey's hymns, in which a few individuals in the small audience that had collected round them were making spasmodic attempts to join. As this was'nt exactly what we'd come to see, and there being a crowd about forty yards further on we went to see what it was. Here was a girl of about thirteen, with a very existence-out-of-doors look on her face, singing with another blind man who played another harmonium. They were singing "The sweet bye and bye," and oh, the mouth of that blind man when he came to the "bye and bye !" It may be very bad taste to dwell en the subject, but that face I am afraid will ever haunt me. I ceuldnt describe it, nor would I try, but it re- minded me of some small stone faces that I used, when a boy, to see ornamenting the singer's gallery surrounding the Blackburn Parish Church own.. A little further on was another blind man, a girl and a harmonium, and further on it was repeated, until we got to the North Pier. There seems to me to be a superabundance of blind man and har- monium ; in fact, I consider it the prevailing feature at Blackpool. Well, we promenaded, and we sometimes stopped to listen to the groups of singers. We enjoyed the breeze and ad- mired the electric light, which I consider has a very striking resemblance to bright moonlight, but less soft and more weird. In this manner, as thousands before us have done, ave Idled the time away till within a few minutes of the hour for returning, and then we proceeded to the Central Station. When we got on the platform of the station we found that nearly all the passengers had taken their seats, though it wanted ten minutes of the time for starting. By going to the fore part of the train we managed to get seats in a compartment in which were three elderly men and their wives. They seemed to be enjoying themselves, and were laughing heartily because one of their number—a rather innocent sort of man—had lost his ticket. " Tha'll get locked up certain," said one. "Nay, they surely cornd lock too up for loysin mi ticket?" " Nowe, id'll nod be for loysin the ticket, id'll be for travellin beawt ticket." " Well, if he geds locked up through id, aw'll be locked up too," said his wife. . " Well, yo see, its this way," said another "if a chap has a good appearance abeawt him, sometimes t' railway fooak 'II let him off; but as soon as ever they clap their een on Wardle here, they'll do him certain; for wi' wearin his whiskers t' shape as he does they'll tek him for, a heawse- breaker in a crack." " Abbut, aw'll tell yo wod aw'll do!' Aw'lL noather be locked up nor catched, awll ged under t' seeat, and if yo'n sense to be quate aw's never be sin." "Ay, thad's t' best thing as tha con do, Wardle," said a man with a red beard," aw never heerd of onybody bein catched under t' seeat, nobbut one, an he geet four year for defraudin t' company; but if tha gets catched we can happen ged tha off." " Un dud he rayly ged four year?" asked Wardle. "He dud; but tha does'n need to be freet'nt abeawt thad. They may nod gi' thee aboon three yer." "By gum, chaps, yo mun be quate when aw'm under t' seeat, or else aw'm done certain. Aw say, Mester, wed dun yo think abeawt Id? Dun yo reply think they con put Imo i' prison for this job?" This was addressed to me, and ins: as I was about to reply, the man with the red beard winked at me, so I said— " Well, I must say that it is a very serious case indeed. I happened to be in court at the trial of that man your friend spoke about just now, and it was the most affecting scene that ever I saw. I remember that the melee wife and seven

John Whitehead, the drayman who set fire to his horse's taa by lighting an armful of straw beneith it, has been

sent to gaol. Mr. Buncombe, of Consbe Florey, has lost two horses, which died through eating a quantity of new wheat. Four others were for some time in a critical condition. At Salford, a dairyman, named Hunt, has been fined £2O for selling milk adulterated with 40 per cent. of water. He had previously been fined £lO for a similar offence. At Middlesex Sheriff's Court, the Earl of Craven, as landlord of a farm in Berk, obtained £lOO as damages from Mr. R. B. Horner, owner of a traction engine, sparks from which, when it was being driven along the high road near the homestead, set fire to a barn and destroyed it. EXPERIMENTAL PRYSICS.—A Texas paper tells this cheer- ful tale of the experimental school of medicine :—A woman came to a prominent physician, and asked for a remedy for \her husband's rheumatism. The doctor gave her a pre./crip- lion, and said, "Get that prepared at the drug store, and rub it well over your husband's back. If it does any good, come and let me now. I've got a touch of rheumatism my-

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

Buoccom—ln localities where this does not stand or- dinary winters, it is advisable at this time to lay them on their side, with their heads to the north. This has a ten- dency to check exuberant growth, and hardens the already formed tissues. Consequently, it is wise to lay some por- tion of the crop down every season, and more especially in mild autumns, when plants continue growing beyond their usual period. It must be acknowledged that smaller heads are produced by the operation, but this is better than no heads at all, which frequently occurs after a prolonged severe winter. The layering of the plants is a simple pro- cess. A spadeful or so of soil is dken from the north side of the plant and near to it, and the spade thrust into the ground east and west, and drawn out, and on the south, after the spade is pushed in, it is used as a lever to place the plant in a recumbent position. The soil removed from the north side of the plant is utilised round it where most re- quired—treading the whole firmly down, and the work is completed. A VALUABLE APPLE.—Those engaged in horticultural pursuits are often as much at a loss what to grow as they are how to grow it. The most valuable fruit in our gardens is the apple, but the varieties that adapt themselves to our northern clime are not numerous. One of them is the Golden Spire, to which our attention is drawn in The Garden by the Rev. C. H. Wood, of this town, who is a good authority in several matters connected with horticul- ture. The experience of individuals residing at a distance if ever so practical is often worthless compared with that of one who has had 20 years' experience in a locality. The season for planting apple trees is now at hand, and those who contemplate doing this should make a note of the Golden Spire apple, respecting which we quote what the rev, gentleman says :—" I send you a few fruits of an apple bearing this name. Whether it is a local name or net Ido not know, but I suspect it is. However, it is one of the very best apples I know. It is a most excellent baker, for as soon as the fruits are large enough to pan they bake as well as when full grown, a great desideratum, as the tree is a very heavy cropper, and the fruits can be gradually thinned, leaving a good crop to finish. I have had a very heavy crop, a fine sight—in short, the feature in my garden. I have pulled hundreds off, besides what fell off. I have treated the trees liberally, or they never could have produced such a crop as they have had on them. I have picked some of the best for you, and I do not call them a bad sample for our north country. I planted my trees about 18 years ago. I think you will agree with me that the fruits are good. They will keep as a rule until Decem- ber. I believe I had some into January the year before last." The Editor of The Garden says :—" It is a capital cooking apple; we have, indeed, rarely tasted one with a more de- licious flavour when baked." THE FRONT GARDEN.—Cuttings of Calceolaria should be put in now. They do best if they have the protection of a frame, though this is not absolutely necessary, as they have frequently been kept over the winter where inserted against a wall or fence having a west aspect. They should be screened from the sun, and in frosty weather they may be protected considerably by placing a board over them, which should rest on the wall or fence. They should also have the same care bestowed on them when there are signs of snow falling. The cuttings should be selected from those shoots that have no flower buds on, and not more than 4in. in length. The two lowest leaves should be neatly cut off, and a neat cut should be made just below the point from which the leaves have been moved. The soil should be moderately sandy, and half an inch of sand should be placed on the surface of the soil, so that when each cutting is inserted the sand will trickle into the hole ; thus the rootless shoot is surrounded with a substance that is likely to prevent decay. The distance between the cuttings is best regulated by the amount of foliage. They will do very well so long as the leaves do not touch each other. THE WINDOW.—The crowded state of the window, on account of the various subjects that have been taken in- doors, will demand some attention. The plants should be so arranged that each receives its share of light and sun. Fuchsias and geraniums of the bedding-out type that have flowered may be placed in a window not favoured with the sun's ray's reserving the best aspect for such that look fresh and flowering, as well as for the pelargoniums that have been cut back and potted, which should by this have shoots an inch long and will require all the light and air possible, and whenever it is convenient the window should be opened or the plants may be stood outside and taken in when it rains. We must here warn the cottager against giving these too much water. We do not mean that their watering should be in driblets, but that after so much is given as shall pass through at the hot tom, the saucer should be emptied and no more given until the surface soil shall become so dry that when a pinch is taken up the particles will not adhere when pressed between the thumb and finger. Examine the plants carefully for green fly, which soon cripples the growth. The remedy is fumigating with to- bacco, first covering the plant with a paper hood and in- serting the bowl end of the pipe underneath and blow down the pipe. The covering may remain on for half an hour.

BERTITON BOATS.—An invention of the greatest import- ance is that known as the Berthon "Folding Boats." The Berthon boats were invented some years since by the Rev. E. L. Berthon, a clergyman residing at Romsey, in Ramp- I shire. They may be roughly compared to an ordinary leather hand-bag turned inside out, so that the folding frame closes backwards, the bottom being strengthened with longi- tudinal ribs and the framework kept open by stretchers. When folded up they resemble a very long narrow cheese- cutter in shape, while when open they are of the form of a very long pointed oval, with beautiful lines. The vans and stretchers are laid lengthways along each side of the folded boat and secured by straps, a handle being provided for con- venience of carriage. The longitudinal ribs and keel, exclu- sive pf the folding framework, which forms the gunwale of the boat, are front fire to seven or more in number, accord- ing to size, and are made of the finest Canadian elm—an almost indestructible wood, which has in addition the two necessary qualities of lightness and strength—covered with a double casing of specially prepared long flax canvas, which has been made perfectly waterproof. The canvas covering being both inside and outside the open boat with the ribs between, the act of expanding it fills the space between the outer and inner coverings with air, rendering it perfectly buoyant. When required for use, it is simply opened as far as the framework will allow—that is to say, until the two halves form one plane, the boat being kept open by the necessary thwarts and stretchers. The canvas forming the double lining of the Berthon boats has been tested by suspending weights from a strip one inch wide. When cut off longitudinally, they have borne a weight of 5701b5., while the strips cut transversely bore a strain of 7301b5. When collapsed, these boats shut up into a space one-fifth of their width. It will thus be seen that the con- struction of the Berthon boat is so simple that no instruc- tions are necessary. Even in the case of the stupidest ser- vant or follower the boat can be opened and fixed ready for use in a few minutes. From the construction of the boat, as above described, it will be seen that it is provided with six or more air cells, perfectly independent of each other, so that if one is accidentally pierced or cut the buoyancy of the boat is only slightly diminished. Ordinarily speaking, the Berthon boats are propelled by a pair of light sculls, but they cam be easily fitted with a mast and sail. Under sail, even in bad weather, they are almost without rivals in speed. In an ocean trip made last year by Capt. Harvey, RN., one of the 28-foot boats made ten miles an hour. In beating to windward in a heavy sea they beat ordinary wooden boats, as was proved on many occasions in Algoa Bay in December, 1881. A 22-foot boat, which was carried by the Union Company's SS. Spartan to the Cape, and which made splendid sea trips, is to be seen in the Exhibi- tion, and is here depicted. Enough has been said of the lightness, portability, safety, convenience, speed, and sailing 'qualities of the Berthon boats to show that they are most admirably adapted for lake, river, and sea angling.—" The Fisheries of the World," for October.

"Jenny, you're my sweetheart," said a seven-year-old to a girl of thirteen. "How can Ibe your sweetheart, when lam thirteen, and you only seven ?" "Are you thirteen ?" he asked. "Of course I am." "Well," re- plied the juvenile beau, after a moment's reflection "I'd be thirteen too, if I had not been sick so much when I was little." ALLEGED ADVERTISEMENT SWINDLE.—TWO RIM named Pollard and Lee, the former being a clerk he the Bradford borough surveyor's office, were remanded at Bradford, on Saturday, on a charge of stealing postage stamps. It was stated that the defendants advertised in the local papers for a clerk, asking the applicants to send a atatnp for reply, and had received 250 answers from various parts of the country. The defence was that the advertisement was inserted as a joke. "Did you ever hear me preach ?" said Coleridge to Lamb, seizing him in Bloomsbury, as his own Ancient Mariner did the wedding-guest. "I never he-heard you d-do anything else l" was the reply, as, drawing a knife from his pocket, he cut off the button by which he was de- tained, and marched away. Coming back, hours after, Lamb found his friend standing on the same spot, twirling between thumb and forefinger the button he had removed by a surgical operation, and still preaching to an imaginary audience. When asked why he was always so bright and cheerful, Sydney Smith replied—" The secret is I take short views of things." Somehow this is'the Scriptural idea. "Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof." A good story was told of an old man who had endured many of the ills of life in his long journey. His friends upon one occasion, more try- ing than usual, condoled with him, saying that he really had more troubles than other men. "Yes, my friends, that is too true; I have been surrounded by troubles all my life long; but there is a curious thing about them—nine-tenths of them never happened." A GOOD UNDERSTANDING."—The following story is told by the Bieester Herald. The landlord referred to is a clergyman, who lives less than a hundred miles from Bices- ter :—About two years since a farmer took a certain Glebe Farm, which was in a bad state of cultivation, at the rate of £2 per acre, besides paying rates and taxes, which would come to something like another 103. per acre. He told his landlord that he ought to have it the first year for nothing. The landlord said he could not afford that; but, if the ten- ant would get it into a good state of cultivation, he would never move him. The tenant, on the faith of the promise, employed labour and purchased manure. The farmer asked for a lease, and the owner said he would be willing to grant a lease for seven, 14, or 21 years, on condition that the oc- cupier paid the cost of the lease. To that the tenant as- sented. The lease, it was understood, was to be drawn up at once. In 14 days after the owner gave the tenant notice to leave. Upon inquiring into the reason of this the land- lord said he could make more money of the land by letting it out in portions. The tenant then asked him to let him have the grass field on the farm. The owner said he had promised it to another man who attended and took more in- tereQt in church matters than the tenant did. On the 28th of September this year the tenant received a letter from his landlord asking him to pay the rent of the farm due at Michaelmaa, to a person mentioned, and that party would give a receipt for the money. In answer to this letter the farmer wrote asking his landlord to appoint a valuer, as he had arranged with a firm on his behalf to value the acts of husbandry, and the balance should be forthwith paid. On the Ist of October a bailiff went and asked the tenant for _ _ _ _ _

„. the half-year's rent. He was informed of the letter sent to the landlord. About four o'clock the same day, without any warning, a distraint was left at the tenant's house while he was away from homeotnd the man was put in possession of the rickyard. The rent, with £3 Is., the costs for a dis- traint, was paid the next morning. The tenant's claim was not recognised. A MARVELLOUS ESCAPE.—A fatiguing day's ride, which, with the exception of the unavoidable mid-day siesta, had been continued since soon after sunrise, was brought to a close by our finding ourselves somewhere in high latitudes upon that everlasting range of Asiatic snow- peaks of which the Bop-Dagh forms the culminating point. There was no disguising the fact—the compass had failed us; and, with night closing in with Eastern rapidity, we found ourselves utterly and hopelessly lost. Our horses, too, were thoroughly jaded, and had in several cases to be led by those who, tired as themselves, could scarcely put one leg before the other. Then, again, we were in a neigh- bourhood known to be infested by brigands, and since we had lost the beaten track we might, for all we knew, come upon their haunts at any moment. . . . Thus it was that even the luxury of pipes was denied, lest the tell-tale spark should betray us. So we crept noiselessly along till we were almost enveloped in long, dank grass and lost in brushwooi, each man carefully leading his horse with one hand, while in his other he held his six-shooter ready for emergencies. Half an hour had probably been thus occu- pied and still no convenient place had been found, when Johannes, the driver of my araba, utterly exhausted, fell by the way. This, accompanied with the distant sound of trickling water, which promised well for the morning, decided beyond argument our course. To go on now became impos- sible, and though it was at first thought wise to ascertain the whereabouts of the watercourse, this was overruled by the majority, so we prepared to camp. While tethering our horses one slipped, but soon recovered himself, on the rough edge of what we supposed, in the darkness, to be a ditch. This trifling circumstance would not have attracted attention had not my dragoman again called my attention to the sound of rippling waters. We were both inclined to move our camp on a little nearer to the inviting allurement, but finding that several of our party had picketed their horses meanwhile, and were already rolled up in their huge cloaks, prepared to snatch what sleep they could before day- light, we abandoned the idea. In a very few minutes all re- membrance of that dreary night-ride was steeped in sweet forgetfulness. And now comes the denouement. At the first streak of dawn we were astir untethering our horses and preparing for our onward journey. A dense vapour made all as imperceptible around us as if we had still been en- veloped in the shades of night; this, however, was not long in lifting, and then it was we realised the terrible death which we hid so narrowly escaped. We had encamped on the very edge of a frightful precipice, so close, in fact, that my dragoman, the correspondent of the Manchester Guar- dian, myself, and several others, had literally slept upon its very brink, and the rippling water, which had so nearly tempted us to advise camping yet a little further on, was now to be seen like a silver thread winding its way hun- dreds of feet below.—” Adventures of a War Correspondent," in Good Words. The Mersey Dock Estate accounts for the year ending Ist July show a total income of £1,273,752. A movement is on foot among the Jewish community for commemorating the event of Sir Moses Montefiore complet- ing his 100th year, upon which he enters on the 24th inst. Leicester had the lowest and Preston the highest rate of mortality last week, the figures being respcetively 11•7 and 323 per 1,000 per annum. In Liverpool the rate was 23 6 Per 1,001 BANKRUPTCY OF A CONSERVATIVE M.P.—lt is stated that the bankruptcy of a prominent member of the Con- servative party in the House of Commons will shortly be announced. A MILL DESTROYED.—A weaving mill at Bolton, worked 1;7 Mr. S. Entwistle, was destroyed by tire on Monday morn- ing. The damage, estimated at £6,000, is largely covered by insurance. ATTEMPTING TO MURDER A WIFE. The Rochdale magistrates on Monday committed for trial at the assizes an elderly man mined Barker, accused of having attempted to Murder his wife by cutting her throat with a razor. CHARGE AGAINST A. CHEMICAL MANUFACTCRER.—James Ormered, chemical manufacturer, was on Monday committed for trial by the bury magistrates for fraudulently inie• aPPropriating £3OO, which he held as trustee for his half aister,‘Mrs. Ann Aspin. BURIED ALlVE.—Stephen Hodson, a pit-sinker, was en- tombed in an old shaft at Momley, near Wednesbury, on Monday morning, the fallen brickwork pinning him against the side. Ile was still alive at noon on TuPsday. Food w.as lowered to him from the surface. Royal, VISIT TO YußKsHlßE.—Before leaving Hudders- field for London, on Monday, at the termination of his week's visit to Yorkshire, the Duke of Albany was presented With an address by the Freemaeons of the town, who held a Grand Ledge at the Town Hall. A heavy south-easterly gab o prevailed on Tuesday over a great part of the kingdom. Several shipwrecks are ffe- Ported, with some slight loss of life. Great damage has been done to grain and fruit crops, and there have been extensive floods owing to the heavy rain. A NEWSPAPER OFFICE DESTROYED. A fire broke out about three o'clock on Sunday morning at the offices of the Stratford and South Essex Advertiser. The building was completely gutted, and the whole of the printing machinery and contents of the premises were destroyed. A LONG FIRM SWINDLE—At the Durham Quarter Ses- sions, on Tuesday, a an named Ridgway, a member of a Liverpool long firm gang, was sentencedlo ten years' penal servitude for fraudulently obtaining money by means of flash advertisements in Durham newspapers, offering gold- finches for sale. RIVAL " ARmins."—There was an alarming breach of the Peace at Gravesend, on Monday. A large number of mem- bers of the Salvation Army arrived in the town in the after- noon, and as they marched through the streets they were assailed by roughs of the "Skeleton Army" and many of them badly used. • MINERS' CONFERENCE 10:7 WIGAN.—A conference of dele- gates, represmting more than 30,000 miners in Lancashire and Cheshire, was held on Tuesday afternoon at Wigan. The men were represente-d as unanimously in favour of an increase of wagee, as reco mead i by the recent conference in Manchester ; andft was reeoived to address a circular to all employers asking for a 15 per cent. advance at once. Snometo Mrreeema OF a. BROTHER.—At Dudley, about dhe‘o'clock, on Sunday morning, a chain-striker named James Groarke, aged 24, murdered his brother William 'in their father's house, Chapel-street. William, who was the 'elder of the two, returned home late on Saturday night and quarrelled with his hrother, whom he strack. The latter thereupon -stabbed him with a butcher's knife, and he fell dead. The prisoner had been regarded as a conEdential-servant up to the moment of his being found to be, as Lord Truro pt it, "a thorough adept in hypocrisy." ACCIDENT TO THE EARL OF DAEHT-CSIE. While his Lordship was driving over his estate near Carnoustie, along with Mr. Cows, hi sub-factor, the vehicle in which they were seated was over turned and both were thrown to Ll= ground with consithrr- able violence. Mr.'Cawe was verreeverely hurt. MORE BANK Fueurs.—At Newcastle-on-Tyne, on Mon- day, the late meager of the Northern Counties Bank, Alex- ander Ogilvie was charged with falsiication of bainnce sheets and other irregularities, corimitted with an intent to defraud. George Hutchinson. oil merchant, Newcastle; and George Bell, contractrr, Gatechead, were charged, with Ogilvie, with having-zonspired to defralrd the bank thare- holders and ci-editerc,,and the one was adjourned. The Tr:soner went home drunk,Tavagely seized the girl, and threw her up to the •ceiling. She fell with a crash upon the floor, and was ricked wpnnoonsciaqs. His excuse was that he was very drunk.

- THE SALVATION ARMY NIIISLNCE.—At Truro on &ant- day the magistrates fined Edwin Gay, captain of the Salvation ArLIIV, two guineas and costs, with the alternelye of two months'. imprisonment, for playing a concertina in the public streets, contrary to the bye-law. Notice of appeal was given.-4t Birkenhead on Saturday 18 persons, three of whom were women, were committed for tritai for being concerned in the Salvation Army Riots on the pre- vious Sunday. The defendants were the ringleaders of the Party who attacked the army whil=t on their march. The stipendiary magistrate most strongly Cbndemned the con- duct of the leaders of the army for marching through quarter of the town inhabited chiefly by Roman Catholics. LIE UNITED KINCZOIt ALLIANCE.—The report ef tlac Executive Committee, after referring to the improved posi- tion of the question in the Rouse of Commons, as shown by the divisions last session, treats of the different bills intro- duced into the House more or less affecting the drink traffic: The committee wish it to he distinctly understood that in, submitting the local option resolution-for the Permissive, Bill there was no compromise of princ,i,ple as erroneously supposed in many quarters, as the new resolution gave the temperance movement precisely the same aid as was in- volved in the old preatnhle.of the rertuimiefe Bill. Dealing With Mr. John Bright's addross at Birminghatn in August, 'the committee say hie proposal to transfer the licensing authority from borough magistrates to town councillors is -not a proposal for the abolition, either locally or nationally', Of the great scourge of the •British people, an they express satisfaction that there is little prospect of ...Mr. Bright's • scheme being adopted by any Government. Ths committee conclude by saying they will continue to demaiat: and agitate for an efficient measure of local apticn. •

The Cork Exhibition came to a close on Saturday. It was I open three months' and was visited by 300,000 people. , AN ELECTION AGENT FlNED—Frank Webb, election agent, for tampering with voting-papers in Marylebone, was fined 20 at the Old Bailey, London, on Thursday. A LIFEBOAT IN THE MANCHESTER ,CANAL.—A new life- boat, which has baen presented to the Lifeboat Institution by a Manchester lady, was launched in the canal at Man- chester on Tuesday. The boat is intended for use at Car- narvon. STABBING.—At the Central Criminal Court, London, on Wednesday, William Sullivan (43), indicted for feloniously wounding Elizabeth Scamtnell, at West Ham, on August 7th, by stabbing her with a knife, was sentenced to 10 years' penal servitude. An influential deputation on Wednesday waited on the *Mayor of Birkenhead to urge the acquisition of Bidston Hill and Oxton Common as public recreation grounds. His Worship gave a favourable reply, and promised to lay tt.e memorial before a meeting of the General Purposes Com- mittee. Two LADIES DROWNED.—A. deplorable bathing accident occurred at Westward Ho, North Devon, on Tuesday even- ing. Miss Vidal, daughter of Mr. E. W. Vidal, of Corn- borough. Abbotsham, near Appledore, and a lady friend were drowned whilst bathing. The bodies have not yet been recovered. FALL OVER A CLIFF.—A distressing accident occurred on Wednesday afternoon at Torquay. A gentleman nan-mcl Rolph, well known in the town and highly respected, was walking on the top of the Daddy Hole Cliffs, when his hat blew off, and in endeavouring to recover it he fell a distance of 2,000 feet, and was killed. FATAL ACCIDENT TO A DOCK LABOURER.—Patrick Ban- non, a dock labourer, who resided at 7, Darwin-street, kirk- dale, died at the Stanley Hospital on Wednesday evening from injuries received by him on the Bth inst. while work- ing down the hold of the Spaniel steamer Alava, then lying in No. 2 Branch Huskisson Dock.

-•-• FATAL GIG ACCIDENT.—WhiIt Mr. Kerr, farmer, Burn- side, Kirktn the, Wai returning home in a gig from Dumfries on Wednesday night, the horse which be was driving bolted when near Locharbriggs. The vehicle was overturned, and Mr. Kerr sustained such injuries that he died silo; tly after. Three other occupants of the gig were also seriously hurt. At the Central Criminal Court, on Wednesday, William Scully, who was indicted for murdering George Thomas Neale, in S. Luke's, on the 2nd of September, by stabbing him during a quarrel respecting a girl with whom both were on terms of intimacy, was found guilty of mantlaughter, and was sentenced to ten years' penal servitudes How BASE SOVEREIGNS ARE MADE.—At Birmingham, on Wednesday, Ingram Belborough, 66 years of age, of Popple- ton, Yorkshire, was remanded, charged with having in his possession two dies used in the manufacture of sovereigns. He had ordered them, it is stated, from local firms, who communicated with the palice, and the prisoner was arrested. IRE BLUE RIBBON MOVEMENT.—"BIue Ribbonism," it is stated, has taken a firm hold in several Devonshire towns. In one of them &Dartmouth) it has been resolved by the Town Council to decrease the police force of the borough on the ground that the work Of the constabulary and the police-court fees had fallen off gradually, so that now there was not enough work for the men to do. SUICIDE AT A WIEE'E GRAVE. A Sheffield grinder, named Thomas Hail (ft) has taken his life under peculiarly distressing circumstances. A few months ago he lost his wife, to uhom he was very much attached, ,and at whose grave he has spent much time. He went there on Sunday afternoon, stretched himself on the grave, and cut his throat. He was found before life was extinct, but qied before medical assistance was obtained. TERRIBLE LE&V.—A woman named Francis Hirst has been admitted iuto the Queen's Hospital, Birmingham, suffering from shocking injuries sustained through juinping through a bedroom window into the; street. Becoming alarmed in the course of a domestic quarrel, she:leaped fran- tically tbrcirgh the window, carrying the sash with her, and falling a distance of over 30 feet. She was picked up , unconscious. FOUNT`ERING or A LARGE SA-ve.—lnteltigence received from Lloyds on Thursday states that the 'fine iron ship Iquique, 899 tons register. which was on a voyage from the Tyneto Peru with a valuable cargo, is missing and is sup- pcseli' to have been lost off Cape Horn with the whole of her crew. She sailed on the 17th 'Februarr last and was seen 'oEetape Horn on the let Jane, but nothing further has been heard of either the vessel or irer crew. At the East Riding Quarter Sessions, Beverley, on Wed- ,resday, Francis Randall, aged 48,-schoolmaster, of Naffer- ;ten,near Drifileld, was charged with counselling a fisher- man, named John Smith-, to infiiSt rievsus bodily harm eapon Sarah Jane Bell, aged 1. 'Evidence was given that the prisoner, who is a married man, gave Smith money to strike and render the girl unconscious, so that the prisoner might criminally assault her. He was found guilty, and sentenced to 12 months' imprisonment. A man named M‘Carthy pleaded guilty at the East Kent Quarter Sessions, on Tuesday, to obtaining several sums of money from residents ,of P.iree and Ewell, near Dover, by falsely reoresenting that he had parcels to deliver Which had come by the parcels post, and that until money due on them was paid they could not be delivered. The prisoner was an extra postman for the Dover district. He was further indicted for detaining a number of letters, and to this charge also he pleaded guilty. 'Lord Brabourne sentenced him to 12 months' bard tabour.

SCENE AT Ag ENTEPETAINMENT.—An unusual scene occurred on Monday evening at Maidenhead Town Hall, where an entertaiment was announced to be given "under distinguished patronage." When the time arrived for com- mencing the performance a lady and gentleman appeared, and proceeded to go through some extemporised scenes and dialogues without the aid of scenery, music, or dramatic costume. The indignation of the audience found vent in hisseq, yells, and showers of cirrots and cauliflowers, and eventually the peeformers made their exit from the hall with some difficulty. SINGULAR Snacrr AeIDENT. A singular accident ic reported from Wednesbury: Two brothers named Hudson were at work cn Monday dismantling an old pit shaft, when a portion of the, sides caved iv, and one of the men wre; partially buried. Assistance was obtained, and efforts .made to release him, but fresh falls of earth took place, and for many hours Hudaon was in danger of suffocation. Eventually a new shaft was sunk -in the immediate vicinity of the eld one, a heading was driven between the two, and the impri- soned mar. was released early on Wednesday morning, having been in his most perilous situation for nearly forty hours.

, - A-v Potacce:iete SHOT-.—Shortly after midnight on Wed- nesday a serious affair occurred in East India Bock-road, ' ti Poplar. Police-eonstabie,George Phillips (160 K), stationed 1 at Limehouse, caw a man and woman quarrelling onteide Ithe Stanley Arms Tavern, and on going up to them the , woman ran away, but the man, or. being questioned, made some indictinct reply, •and drawing a revolver from hie pocket shot thee-constable, the bullet penetrating his right 1 side and causing him to stegger and fall. Lord Edmond Fitzmaurice is reported to be eerious!y un- well. The Queen has approved D:e appointment of General Sir Henry W. Norman, K CU., to be Governor nf Jamaica. A new Town Hall was opened at Brechin, on Tuesday-, and the freedom of the city conferred upon Lord Dalhousie. Count Miinster, the German Ambassador,left the German Embassy, London, on Friday eveßing for Scotland, to shoat. Mr. Goschen has promised to deliver a political address at the Edinburgh Rosebery Club on the Ist November. Lord Elgin will nreside, The Lon7lon Gazette announces that her Majesty has been pleased to confer a baronetcy on Mr. Thomas Henry Farrer, of Abinger Hall, Surrey, Permanent Secretary to the cQM- mittee of Privy Council for Trade. THE PREMIER.—Mr. Gladstone accompanied by Mrs. Gladstone and Miss Mary Gladstom, attended divine service at the Parish Cnurch, Harwarden, on Wednesday morning. In the afternoon Mrs. Gladstone left for Eaton Hall, on a visit to the Duke and Duchess of Westminster. SIR ARCIIIBALD:ALISOIL - Sir Archibald Alison, Batt, was, on Thursday, presented with a sword of honour by the citizens of Glasgow, in recognition of his services to the country. The Honourable the Lord Provost made the pre- sentation, and Bailie Wilson afterwards presented Lady Alison with a tiara of diamonds.

A model of the statue of John Brown was last week placed in position on the pedestal. It is of stucco, painted bronze colour. The permanent bronze statue is not to be erected till the spring. The site of the memorial has been changed, and, instead of being seen fi mit the windows of the Castle, it is now viiVe only from the top of the toWef. The death ot the Earl of Mounteashell rerrioveB the only nonagenarian member of the House of Lords, the decetsed nobleman having attained his 91st year on August 20 last. The oldest peer now is the Earl of Buckinghamshire, who was born on November 1, 1793 ; while the distinction of being the " Father " of the House of Lords must be claimed for the Earl of Chichester, aged 79, who succeeded to the title anti his seat as far beck as July, 1826, having therefore been a member of that assembly for upwards of 57 years.

SIR STAFFORD NORTHCOTE. Sir Stafford Northcote landed at Larne on Saturday afternoon, and was presented with an address from the " constitutional inhabitants," to which he replied. The right honourable gentleman was entertained at luncheon by Mr. Chains, M.P.' and after- wards proceeded to the 6eit of Sir 3. M'Garel Hogg. Mr. Acland, M.P., at a Liberal meeting en Monday night at Saltasb, defended the Government, as regards its home, foreign, and financial policy, against the recent attacks of Mr. Edward Clarke. He declared that Europa would not have sanctioned our work in Egypt except that a Liberal Government had been in power, ani that our iscreased ex- penditure was due to Tory extravag ince and to inherited Tory debt. MR. SEELY, M.P., .AND PARLIAMENTARY REFORM.—Mr. I Charles Seeley, M.P., for Nottingham, proposes, as a n measure of parliamentary reform, that 600 members of the Houma of Commons shall be intrusted with the power of electing the remainder, so that etninent men who, by reason of personal infirmity, are net able to appeal to the consti- tuencies, shall have an ocpartusity of serving the country in Parliament, the selection to be made in proportion to the strength of the parties in the House. Mr. John Bright, who has been communicated with in regard to the scheme, altogether discourager it, on the ground that it is wholly opposed to the spirit and principles of the Constitution, and offers no compenseing advantage. Mr. Henderaon, M P., addressing his constituents at Dun- dee, on Monday, said the Conservatives had been making prodigious oratorical efforts during the past week or two to convince the country it had arrived at a tremendous political crisis; that the nation had suffered degradation abroad, • society wasthreatened with destruction at home, and the members of the Government had shown themselves utterly lincompetent. So far as he could judge, however, the country 'obstinately refused to see any such crisis exist, or the Government would suffer by comparison with its critics in respect Of honesty, capacity, or wisdom. He expressed the hope that the. count,y franchise would not ba passed nest session, as it would involve a dissolution, and they already had sufficient work before them to oceupy all mit session— work which the present Parliament was able and willing to perform.

Mr. Wm. Daley, agent to Lord Dunstable, was attacked ty a party of men when returning from Tuam on Wednesday night. His servant was also injured. Mr. PARNELL has written to one of his constituents irlti- mating his intention to pay a public visit to Cork at an early date, and asking that a hall be provided in which to [-address his constituents.

ORANGE DEMONSTRATION.—the Government have de- cided to perthit the Nationalist and Orange dernonstrati .tns to,be held at Rosslea, in connection with which rather ex- citing placards have been issued on both sides. Mr. Davitt, Mr. Healy, am! Mr. Sullivan have intimated their intention of attenling the Nationalist meeting. Detachments of ! cavalry, infantry, and police moved into Rosslea on Monday night.

A writ in an action for libel has been served on behalf of County Inspector French, of the Dublin Detective Depart- ment, on the publisher of United Ireland te recover dam- ages for slander in alleging that he had absconded, carry- ing with secret service moneys belonging to the Govern- ment. United Ireland hopes the action will be proceeded rith, and promises such exposures as will asteniet the public. -An alarming accident.occurred during a performance in Powell and Clark's Circus. Londonderry, at which over 1.500 eoplo were present. The cries of women and children caused great consternation, but i•mo one was seriously injured. . _

On his death, however, a bitter dispute occurred between the brother and sister as to the possession of the second bolding.
