NATIoNAL LIBERAL CONFEP.EN(II, AT LEEDS. The National Reform Conference was ofr`ened at Leeds Wednesday, and was attended by ;tlidat 2,000 delegates from 500 Liberal organisations. Among the members of Parliament who were present were Mr. John Morley (who presided), Sir Andrew Fairbairn, Mr. H. Broadhurst, Mr. E. C trbutt, Mr. 11. H. Fowler, Me. H. Shield, Mr. J. Barran, Sir R. Cunliffe, Mr. Mappin, Mr. Holden, Mr. Illingworth, Mr. Heneoge, and Mr. Firth.—.ln his opening address Mr. Moter.EY said he believed that the present Government was as popular now al it Niraff three years ago, and were bound soon to remove the ts..lctoral anomalies which now made a juggle and mockery of so much of our representation. All present were agreed in principle on the measures which would be under their discussion, and they had simply to discuss points of detail and procedure upon which there might well be differences of opinion. He doubted whether it was wise to defer to the eleventh hour of an expiring Parliament, what was in their own view and by their own admission the most important of all the objects for which this Parliament was elected. His own opinion was that the Government would do best to brino in their County Franchise Bill at the beginning of next session. If they could carry another bill, so much the better. Letters were read from Mr. G. 0. Trevelyan, M.P., and others who were unable to be present; and Mr. Kitson, the President of the Leeds Liberal Association, stated that in a private letter which he had received from Mr. John Bright the right hon. gentleman said :—" If I were to advise the conference it would be to say that the session of 188.1 must deal with the County Suffrage and the London Govern- ment Bill."—Dr. It. W. DALE (Birmingham) moved the first resolution, which was " Tnat this Conference, believing that the extension of the franchise is a matter of paramount and urgent importance, that it is the duty of Her Majesty'S Government to introduce a bill dealing with the question in the next session of Parliamentr. JOHN Ems. chairman of the orth Nottinghamshire Liberal Associatioo. i€C mded the motion.—Mr. J. F. B. FIRTH, :IP., moved the following amend- ment, viz, t—" That this conference regards the extension of the flanchise as a matter of paramount importance which should be dealt with during the present Parliament, hut is of opinion that the first legislation of next session should deal with the reform of the government of London and of the counties." He said this amendment was brought forward at the unanimous instance of the London and Counties Liberal Union, which represented all that there was of Liberal organisation among six millions and a half of people. If that important union were represented at the present meeting on the basis allotted to delegates to the con- ference, it would have 1,300 representatives, of whom 1,200 would vote for the amendment. The metropolis was simply asking what provincial towns had gained in 1835. If the conference voted, on the contrary, for i resolution denying the rights of the people of London (cries of " No, no ") they would take a course both supremely selfish and supremely unjust. A long debate followed, and in the end the amendment wee rejected by a very large majority.—Mr. W. L. BRIGHT moved a further amendment by which the conference, whilst recogelsing the importance of the County Franchise and other bills which had been referred to, was asked to ex- press entire confidence in time discretion of the existing Liberal Government as to the order in which these various measures should be submitted to the consideration of Par- liament.—This ametalenent was seconded by Mr. J. DENT DENT, but the resolution as moved by Mr. Dale was ulti- mately carried.—A resolution in favour of household suf- frage in the counties, together with a rider (moved by the Rev. Br. eitOSSEEY, of Birmingham) recognising the chime al women to the suffrage was also carried, and the conference then adjourned.— Mr. BRIGHT, speaking at a .tonversazione in connection with the conference the same evening, dwelt on the fact that no more fitting lace than Leeds could have been chosen to the conference, the West Riding of Yorkshire having al- ways been true to Liberal principles, even when Lancashire fell behind. He hoped the result of the proceedings would be to give more streneth to an already strong Government, and enable them to p-roceed in the next and ensuing session, and in the succeeding Parliament, with a policy that was wise and just, enabling people in years to come to point to that day as one when true patriotism, wisdom, and modera- tion directed their counsels and acts. The Conference was resumed at Leeds on Thursday. Mr. John Morley again presided. A resolution was moved by Mr. J. Kitson, Juno President of the Leeds Liberal Associ- ation, declaring it to be the opinion of-the Conference that a measure for the redistribution of seats ought to follow the passing of one for the extension of the franchise and the completion of the register of the new electorate. The reso- lution was seconded by Mr. Southall, of Leominster, and a lengthened debate followed, in which the desire for equal electoral districts was given expression to by -several delegates, and an amendment favouring such a phase of reform was moved and seconded. , Mr. Kitson, in reply, urged the Conference to have confidence in the Government; and the amendment having been put to the meeting and negatived, the resolu- tion was passed unanimously. A resolution was then moved by Mr. E. R. Russell, of Liverpool, and seconded by Mr. Isaac Hoyle, of Manchester, declaring that in the opinion of the Conference " the attempt to secure the re- presentatiou of minorities by special legislative enactments Is a violation of the principle of popular representative go- vernment." Mr. Seebahen and Mr. H. G. Fordham, both from Hertfordshire, respectively moved and seconded an amendment which stated that the question of the representation of minorities were too important to be disposed of by that Conference. The Con- ference however, would not accept the amend- meet, and Mr. Russell's resolution was carried by a large majority. The case of Mr. Bradlaugh neait occu- pied the attention of the Conference, and in a resolution moved by Mr. Alderman Gripper, of Nottingham, and seconded by Mr. Manfield, of Northampton, the action of the House of Commons in refusing to allow the thrice duly elected member for Northampton to take his set was strongly condemned; and the Conference declared its opinion that the Parliamentary oath ought to be abolished. A resolution in favoue of a simplifica- tion of the wessnt system ot registration ant other minor reforms, including an amendment of the Ballot Act, was posed ; and provision having been male for bringing the decisions of the Conference under the notice of the Prime Minister, the meeting adjourkied. A vote of thanks having been given to Mr. John Morley for presiding, the Conference broke up. On Thursday night, Mr. Bright presided at a great meeting of Liberals, at the Town Hill. He spoke of his undimmishol interest in the gut ?stion of parliamentary re-• form, and said that every evil prophecy which had been made of it in the past had retnaineil unfulfilled. Great measures had always followed reforms in the representation of the people. Sir Stafford Northcote hid spoken of the supremacy of numbers, and he admitted it, his desire being •to see them more extensively represented. A large number of the smaller boroughs must be disfranchised, and these whieh now had the vote wou,cl hive to give it in the coun- ties, so that it would he no less an extension of the franchise. That was comparatively easy, but redistribution was (IV- ficult and complex, and he, therefore, urged the Government to deal with the two questions separately, taking the Fran- chise Bill next session, together wt 'l the Loden Municipal Bill, and leaving redistribution to the followino year. The minority clause ought to be abolished, as it was An anomaly ; and he urged the Liberals to support an honest Covetn•nent and a pat-iotic Prime Minister, and not to split noon small points. Referring to the House of Lords, Mr. Bright said : Now, I have only one or two more sentences to utter. There are no doubt other questions which wiil come on for discus- sion and for settlement. There is one which I think is not very remote. It is a great question which will have to be faced. It does not comeexactiv within the object of tins conference, according to its announced proceedings, nor yet this meeting, but I m ke nevertheless take this opportunity of referring to it. The question is, and will be, how to deal with the constaat conflict between the Lords and Commons. (Hear, hear ) It is in my mind a conflict which is full of peril to coo of them—(cheers)—and full of humiliation to both of them. (Hear, hear.) It bas been a common opinion, supported by many writers on the conetitutien, that the two Houses are necessary, and that no steady Govern- ment can succeed in any country whose policy and .whose legislation is determined by the vote of a single representative chamber. I recollect myself when I was a boy writing an essay in defence of that very opinion. (Laughter.) But I think the conduct of the majority of the Peers is fast dispelling that opinion and that delusion. How do we stand with regard to the Crown? The ,Crown cannot now reject any bills sent up for its accept- ance. Not one of you ever heard that the cateen or the kings who preceded her have rejected any ineasare which has passed both Houses of Parliament. If the Crown be limited in this way, now not the Peers. (Hear, hear.) Whv not enact that if the Peers have rejected a bill one o and it has been considered in a subsequent session by the Com- mons acd after due deliberation has been again sent up to the Peere,, then the Peers should have the power to pass it on •to receive the Royal assent and become law. Some years ago I said., and the statement caused a good deal of discussion at the time, that a house of legislation hereditary or:3 irresponsible cannot be e. permanent Znstitution in a 'free country." (Laud cheer- lug.) Bear in enind that I said hereditary and irresponsible. By4otne method the two House& if they are to continue to exist, mast be racenciled, and made.equally and sufficiently resf.xemsive to the national wants. (Hear, hear.) The task is porhaps ditlicuta, but it is not imposeible. This is not the time ,tossay more a:nut it, but I recommend the observa- tions [leave made open it to the calm consideration of the people ct thia.countay. As for me I in*V.Zee, which is very Uwe, in the future>ony political career dr.e.vs very near its close—(cries of" No, co ")—but I will cherish the hope and the faith that my cowl:vine:l, whatever the form of their Government, will, in the changes which are deefore us, ex- hibit the wisdom and moeeration which become an mutellm- eut and a Chr4tian p?opie. (Lend cheering.)

Cetewayo has surrendered to Mr. Osbirne, and is now in Natal. - On Sunday night the magazine in the cen•re of the town of Nantes was destroyed by lire, together with goods of con- siderable value.

The traffic receipts of the Suez Canal, on Thursaav amounted to 200,000 f., against 250,000 f. on the correspond- ing day of last year. Cholera broke out on Thursday in the Arab village of -'" ;,Ist outside Alexandria. Four of the inhabitants have died from the disease.

It is rei»rted that in the recent earthquake in Asia Miner, which convulsed the whole peninsula from Smyrna to Chesme, 1,000 people perished. A despatch from Montreal states that Sir John M•Donald, Premier of the Dominion, has been unseated for the con- stituency of Lennox owing to bribery by agents. At INliava, in Upper Hungary, there has been a serious encounter between the Slav and Magrar factions. Ibe mili- tary fired upon the rioters, but with what result is not stated.

Sir Henry James, Mr. A. Cohen, and Mr. Cooks repre- sented the English Bar at the opening, on Tuesday, of the new Palace of Justice at Brussels by the King of the Belgians. THE COREAN AMBISSADORS.—Tne Corean Ambassadors paid their farewell visit to President Arthur on Friday, and will leave San Francisco on the 24th inst. on their home- ward journey. The Chinese autthoriries are making all necessary pre- parations for closing the port of Canton. The Chinese troops recently embarked at Lungmunt near Tonquin fron- C‘lc, have been landed at Whauipoa. The CLir has sent a confidential officer to Sofia to ascer- tain the intentions of the National Assembly with regard to the Bulgarial military forces. The news is published by the official organ of the German Foreign Office. ARREST OF A SocrAusT.—lnteligence from St. Peters- buro announces the arrest at Reval of a Socialist who ar- rived there a few days ago by a steamer from abroad with a forged passport. The prisoner was conveyed to St. Peters- burgh. _ _ _ _

THE HAYTI REVOLT.—The revolt In Hayti has resulted in the destruction of half the wooden city of Port-au-Prince by incendiarism and bombardment, the pil- lage of the capital and the slaughter of a large number of the inhabitants.

THE SII4W DIFFICULTY.—The Paris Teleyraphe states that the Shaw difficulty has been arranged, that Mr. Shaw will receive an indemnity of 60,000 francs, and that a letter of regret will be sent to our Foreign Odice by M. Challeuael Lacour.

PANIC IN A SYNAG3GUE.—An unfounded alar,n of fire which was raised in a synagogue at Ziwonka, Podolia, dur- ing divine service, led to a terrible cal unity, The congre- gation was se:zed with panic, and during the rush to the door 40 women were killed and 30 injured. THE HUNGARIAN BuDozr sub,nitted to the Diet, on Siturday, shows a total expenditure of 329.000,000 florins and total receipts of 308,000,000 florins, showing a defi- ciency of nearly 21,000,000 florins, a large proportion of which will be prJvided for by means of credits. FINANCIAL AGITATION IN CANAPA.—The financial un- easiness which has prevailed in Montreal for some time past has culminated in something very like a panic. Large ad- vances have this season been made by financers to the cotton mills proprietors, and these have been called in. MUTINY OF Cofsviers.—At Voula, Conder Island, belong- ing to French Cochin China, 150 Annemite convicts em- ployed in erecting a lighthouse, mutinied. M. Datong was murdered ; also a native•warder. M. Pridault was maltreated and left for dead. They had no protection except that of six natives, who laid down their arms. PRUSSIA AND THE VATlCAN.—Negotiations are proceed- ing between Prussia and the Vatican for the conclusion of a convention by which the present relations would be im- proved without the necessity of a new ecclesiastical law in Prussia. It would also settle the questions concerning the Prussian bishops still excluded from their dioceses. THE GREAT EARTHQUAKE.—A Central News telegrant dated Constantinople, Thursday, states: Further particulars from Smyrna show that the Katopanaya, Reis Dere, and Lidja were entirely destroyed by the recent earthquake. The Porte is considering the advisability of appealing to England for subscriptions on behalf of the 20,000 homeless survivors.

THE NEW SPANISH MINISTRY.--A new Spanish Ministry has been constituted, with Senor rosida Herrera as Presi- dent of the Council and Sewn. Moret with an important portfolio. The views of the Free-traders will be well repre- sented in the ne,v Ath&nistration, and the hopes of British merchanth who are anxiously waiting for a treaty of com- merce will be revived.

PANIC IN A SCHOOL.—A school, containing 600 children, at Waterbury, Connecticut, caught fire on Monday. The children rushed out to escape, wildly trampling on each other in the stairways, with the result that six were badly hurt, three being expected to die. The teachers finally quelled the panic and prevented further injury being done by marching the children out in an orderly fashion. RAILWAY COLLISION IN ITALY.—A serious collision Oc- curred on Saturday between an express and a passenger train at Savignano Station. Six. carriages and the Post Office vau attachei to the express were smashed, and the per- manent way was 60 bully damaged that the traffic was stoppei for several hours. No persons were killed, but a number of plstal and railway officials were injurel, some of them serionAy.

A MORMON CONSPIRACS.—The Governor of the State of Utah has made a report to the Department of the Interior on the Mormon question, in which he asserts the existence of a conspiracy to nullify the national laws, and warns the country of the dangers this may result in. The Governor recommends that the military forces of the Uuited States should be available to zecure the proper observance of the will of Congress.

A ghastly story is reported from Mscheno, in B )hemia. A mai, who was apparently dead, had just been lowered into the grave when the mourners were horrified to sea the coffin-lid bin to move and the linen shroud gradually appear, ontil the corpse at last sat up. The man said that he had throughout his illness beau] all that had been said. He wac aware they thought him dead, but he was unable to make any sign. From the graveyard the man was taken home' and there is now every prospect of his recovery. M. JULES FERR.Y.—M. Jules Ferry, accompanied by the Minister of Works, pooceeded on Sunday to Havre, and was present at a " reception " at which all the foreign consuls were present. The French Premier warmly shook hands with the Spanish Consul, who, it is said, had been specially instructed to pay his respects to the ministers. At a banquet in the evening M. Ferry urged the importance of pursuing with greater vigour than ever the policy of Republican union, which was that followed by the Cabinet, and which offered the best solution of the Parliatnentary problems now pending._

• WES—r Coast' OF AFRICA.—The t-ial of the English lieu- tenant, George Patterson, at Freetown, has te-minated. The prisoner was found guilty by the jury of stealing the letter from the post-office, and he was sentenc,al to a month's im- prisonment in the common jail.-1 Greek sailor was sen- tenced to death at Sierra Leone on the 10th September for the wilful murder of a negro, named Trial. A comrade of the Greek, both of whom belonged to a sailing vessel, was wrestling with Trial, whom the Greek stabbed. He made off in his Lost, but before he could reach his own vessel, which was lying in the bay, he was overtaken and arrested by some native 'Alice. The Hue TREATY.—The French pipers publish the text of the Moo rreatv, the principal provisions of which have already been indicated. Telegraphing frorn Hong Kong, the correspondent of the Mites, referring to the difficulty with the Black Flag, says M. Dupuis, who has arrived, is of opinion that an amicable agreement is impossible, and that the Mick Fl ig must Fe extirpated. The Yellow Flag com- mander, who has reached Hong Kong, reports that owing to the French authorities interfering with his command the Yellow Flags disb anded, in st of them j)ining the enemy. There has been a serious riot at Foochow, which was sup- pressed by the French Consul, TIIE WHOLESALE POISONING IN LlVERPOOL.—Catherine Flannagan, the woman accused of having carried on a horrible traffic in human life for the sake of the pittance accruing from small policies of assurance, was arrested on Monday evening at Wavertree, near Liverpool. She was found drinking in a public-house, but was sober. Margaret Flantr,gan, a girl of 14, her daughter, was liberated, but Mrs. Higgins, wife • of the deceased man and sister of Catherine Flannagan, was detained. On I'Vednesday morn- ing, Catherine Flannagan and Margaret Higgins were brought before the Liverp.,ol stipendiary magistrate, charged on suspicion with having murdered Thomas Higgins, by poisoning him with arsenic. After a short statement of the case for the prosecution, the prisoners were remanded till , Tuesday.

e- HORRIBLE CHILD MURDER.—At London Central Criminal Court, on Thursday, James C9le, labourer, was indicted for the wilful murder of his son, Thomas Cole, aged three years, on August 19tie, at Thornton Heath, near Croydon. Fur some time before the crime prisoner had been out of work, and on the evening of the murder he quarrelled with his wife. During the night he got up and seized the boy by his lees and dashed his head against the wall. The pri- soner was found guilty, and sentenced to death. THE GALE AND FLOODS.—Daring the whole of Wednes- day night and Thursday a heavy gale from the west pre- vailed generally over the kingdom, and an enormous amount of damage to property has resulted. Very high tides were experienced at many places on the coast, and at Cardiff especially the lowlying portions of the town were flooded. Inland, also, rivers have overflowed th,ir banks by reason of heavy rains, and miles of land were submerged. In the north of Scotland snow fell in large quantities, cover- ing the corn which is yet in the Highland districts standing in the fields. On the east coast the tides were very high, and the waters invaded the fishing villages with disastrous ' result. Very heavy weather was encountered by Channel steamers. At Southport and Lytham damage was done to the promenade works. About a mile in length of the Mire. head branch of the Great Western Railway, which traverses the :omersetshire coast, was swept away, and traffic com- pletely stopped. At the Severn funnel works, where the engines for the last few days had been gradually gaining on the water with which the works were flooded, a huge tidal wave on Wednesday evening dashed over the river bank, Clang the Marsh Pit and its connected workings. Of 75 men who were at work at the time, one was killed as he was asceosi:lng the ladder, and the retreat of the remainder was temporarAly cut off. The same wave flooded the recently iltboilteeehouses find extinguished the engine fires.

I THE uNirED KINGDOII ALLIA.NCE. GREAT MEETING AT WARRINGTON. A densely crowded meeting in suppert of the United Kingdom Alliance, was held at the Public Hell, on Monday evening lest, a large number of la lies being among those present; and whilst the vast audience was assembling a selection of music was discoursed from the organ by Mr. F. Booth. The proceedings were very successful, the utmost unaninnity being displayed in the adoption of the several resolutions presented-to the meeting. J. G. McNlinnies, Esq., M.P., presided, supported on the platform by Dr. F. R. Lees, of Leeds, Rev. Thomas Hutton, rector of Stilton (deputation), the Revs. Father Furniss, Father Beauvoisin, Father Thompson, J. Eglinton. J. Yonge, E. Moore, I'. Rippon, W. Mules, W. Pilling, Messrs. F. Monks, J.P., R. I Garnett, J. H. Gornall, Herr Cohen, D. Garnett, Councillor Dixon, R. Roberts, John Green, John Tuft, N B. Percival. J. Shaw Green, Thomas Hale, R. Siddall, J. Summersgill, Joseph Harrison (station master), D. Houghton, W. Hud- son, L. Gillooley, J. Skelland, W. Roberts (hon. sec.), T. Weaver, J. Critchlev, W. Gleave, E. • Ford, J. W. Hall, James Handley (Runcorn), J. R. Frith (Runcorn), E. J. Guest, T. Holbrook, and others. The CHAIRMAN opened the proceedings by calling upon the Rev. T. Rippon te read certain replies he had received to the invitations sent out for the meeting. The Rev. T. RI/PON said he had sent out GO invitations to Conservatives and Liberals, to the clergy and dissenting ininilers of the town alike. He had received replies from the following gentlemen who could not possibly be present: —Mr. Peter Rylands. M.P., Rev. Father Feeny, Rev. E. J. Willtocks, Rev. W. Cullen (Oughtrington), Rev. M. Schon- berg, Mr. W. Beemont, Mr. John Feirclough, J P., Colonel Bell. The Cifeinetaer, who was warmly received, then said:— Ladies and gentlemen, I suppose that there is no [movement of modern times upon wh'ch those who have taken part in it can look with greater satisfaction than the agitation in fav3ur of temperance. The change in the habits of the people in my time in reference to this wetter his b:en most remarkable, and the change in the habits of the people has not been more remarkable than the change of sentiment in reference to the indulgence in intoxicating drinks. Nobody now defends drunkeeness. I remember the time when a clean who invited his friends to dinner, and m tde them n extre,nely jolly on the occasien, was thought to be a very good fellow indeed. (Laughter.) And I remember the time when the m In who locked his guests up in his dining-room, and did not allow them to go until they were fresh indeed, was considered a very good fellow too. (Iteeetved laughter.) All that has passed away. There is nobody now who will condone or excuse the excessive use of intoxicating liquors. Even the men who are engaged in the sale and the manufacture of these drinks will not excise the excessive indulgence in them; and I think that this change of habit and change of senti- ment in reference to this practice has been brought about in no small degree by the efforts and the agitation of the Alliance. (Hear, hear.) As regards legislation in the direction that the Alliance points out, they also have a good deal to say in their favour. The House of Commens, on one, two, or three occasions, has given its voice in favour of the restriction by legislation of the means and facilities for drink- ing; and within recent time a great statesman has formulated a scheme which, in his opiuion, might be adopted by the Leglslatare as a mean of restricting the insane and facilities for drinking. I do not mean to say that the scheme of Mr. Bright has been accepted, or is even acceptable—(bear, hear); but I do ma in to say that a question upon which a great st,tesinan like Mr. Bright—a man of acknowledged re- putation—(cheers)—has thought it worth his while to say what in his opinion might be the scheme that the Legisle- tnre would adopt,—l mean to sly that that fac: is of itself a proof that,the agitation of the Alliance has reached a very great degree of prom'se. (Cheers.) It appears to me that we are now within what has been c illed measurable distance of legislation on this subject, and as far as I Can , judge I should say that the present position of public opinion in reference to legislation is this : I believe that the people of this country have come to think that excessive facilities for drinking leads to excessive indulgence in drinking. (Hear, hear.) In the second place, I believe that the people of this country have come to think that the facilities for drinking shonld be diminished. And I think further that if any existing interests should be damaged lay any legislation upon this subject, that those interests should receive compensation. .( Applause.) Now, I have no doubt at all that whatever legielation takes place upon this matter will not give satisfaction to extreme opinion on either side. Reform in this country never takes place by single acid complete steps. All great changes, in my time at least, have been in the nature of compromise. I remember the abolition of the disabilities of Dissenters and Roman Catholics; I remember the passing of the fiat Reform Bill, and of the last; I remember the abolition of the corn laws ; I remember the abolition of slavery; and I remember the reform of Corporations; nod what I re- me.nber in reference to all these great changes is that they have been in the nature, as I said before, of compromises. I won't go into particula/ s in reference to any one of those great changes except one—the abolition of the corn laws. When Cobden and the League entered into the great agita- tion which in the result was the abolition of the corn laws, what they said was "We contend for the immediate and to- tal abolition of the corn laws," and they carried on the agi- tation for seven years with that object; but when the states- men of the country took it up, and although the country itself had come to the conclusion that those hews were eminently injurious to the people—that they injured trade, that they led to the diminution of employment and reduc- tion of wages, to a great deal that militated against the material proeperity of the people—yet wben Sir R. Peel pro • posed the repeal of the corn laws he left a sliding scale for three years in favour of laws which the country at that time believed to be eminently injurious, and ought to be repealed. Notwithstanding this, Cobden and Bright and the League accepted the compromise of Sir R Peel, and the sliding scale was sanctioned for three years. I only men- tion this as the most prominent instance I know of the acceptance of compromise in reference to greet reforms. As regards legislation in reference to the restriction of drink I have never myself been able to understand the objection. that the publicans interest have to those mdsures that are advocated by Sir W. Lawson and others —(hear, bear)—and which, while! suppose they are no pert of the platform of the Alliance, yet are supported, and I suppose accepted, by the Alliance. I am sure I have never quite understood why the publican interest should object to them. It seems to me that the complaint that we tradesmen have to make in this country is the amount of com- p2tition that we find in our various trades. I am a cotton spinner, and my great complaint is —if I put it in the shape of a compiaint—that there is too much competition in the cetton trade. I slmuld be very glad indeed if there were fewer cotton mine in the ceuntry. But the publicans object to diminished competition in their trade. I cannot understand this at all. If any trade, if the competition in any trade can be diminished without detri- rnent to existing interests, well, I say we should all be very glad indeed to see that diminished eompetition. But it seems to nee that the publicans, somehow or other—from having been badly led in my opinion—have taken an entirely erro- neous view of their interests in this matter. My own opinion , is that the interests of the publicans and of those who retail drink in this country have not been regarded by the men who have pretended to lead them; but that the interests of the great brewers and distillers have been regarded to the disadvantage, I think, of the publicans. I do not, however, despair of the time coming when we shall find that the publicans of this country will lselieve that those who are anxious to see a diminution of the facilities for selling drink are their best friends, and I should not be at all sarprisei in fact—although Artemus Ward tells us we should not prophesy unless we know—to find that the time will sooner come when the publican will join the Alliance in promoting some scheme for the reduc- tion of the facilities for selling drink rather than that the Alliance itself will see the time when everybody will join in this country for the total suppression of the sale of in- toxicating drinks. (Applause.) Well now, geptlemen. I am reminded you dial not coins here to listen to me, and that I came here to listen and not to speak, and I au going to cell upon a gentleman to meve the first resolution. But before I do so, I have to announce eotne very bad news. I reserved it. until this moment for a reason of my own, because for one thing I would rather address an audience who were disposed to be good-natured and to listen with a great degree of good humour to any imperfect remark that I may have to make. That you know is selfishness. But I am grry to tell you that our friend Mr. Caine will not be present here to-night. I have received a telegram from him—" Have sprained my I leg, and am laid up tere (LI infivrfechan) for day or two. Impossible travel. Please explain to meeting. Vere, sorry." I am quite sure that we all are very sorry that Mr. Caine not present here to-night. I am particularly so, because I have great respect and admiratioa for Mr. Caine personally. I He is a man who is making a great position he the House of Commons in reference to this and other questions, and I am quite sure :hat if he had been here he would have been able to have pat his *views before you in a manner which would have met with general acceptance, and which I have no doubt Wall would have contributed in a great degree to the success of this meetinto ( Applause.) However, we have representatives on this platform who, I have no doubt at all, will be able to put the position of the Alliance before you in a manner that you will all appreciate. I be now to call upon the Rev. J. Eglinton to move the first resolu- tion. (Loud applause.) Rev. Jenne &fulmar then moved the following resolu- tion : " That recognising the numerous evils inevitably resulting from the traffic in iutoxicating liquors, this meet- ing deprecates the policy of legalising and supporting such an evil system, and protests against the injustice and cruelty of thrusting it into or maintaining it within any parish or district, centrary to the will of the inhabitants of the locality, who are the moat deeply affected thereby, and who ought to have an effectual vote for the protection of their houses and families from such a grevious injury and terrible wrong." He said that with regard to nine circumstances in this matter, so far as Warrington Via 9 concerned, they were exceptional. For many years he had been a familiar ob- server of the staggering gait, of time tattered garb, of sunken eye, and of the meaningless :peed:, which told the drunkard. He had known sonnething of the deeolatiou sue sorrow of the inebriate's home, and it had been a very pad sight to see not only drunken men but drunken women ale°. (Hear, hear.) For years he had lived in that great tlity

which had hem styled—he thought not happily—the "black spot" on the Mersey (Liverpool). He knew there peelaeAssau rgc-eiant id,earanl etshseind ttrhkantecssi tyi,vabsu ug that it l thine ni n ehd withoh many powers of hum in light, and he rejoiced to hear of the ' good that was being den?. Bet he had never read until he came to Warrington of drunken girls—(hear, htar)—of such scenes that they had had in their court-house lately. Young people who should be fine blushing maidens, a credit to their churches, and the flower of their country, were defacel, and frequently, he believed, debauched by that wretched habit of drinking. (Hear, hear.) He read a letter in a local contemporary last week siened by a War- rington clergyman to the effect [bat some means should be adopted to rescue those poor girls from their pitiless state. (flear, hear.) fie wished to Fay that he would pledge him- self, his colleague, and people to join in any movemen' in such a direction. (Cheers.) Rev. Father BEAU VOISIN seconded the resolution. lit stood there as the representative of a body of men in War- !ineton who were clubbed together not to legalise drin'ting in any place. Ile represented the Total Abstinence League of the Cross. (Hear, hear.) Thouela he adnette I that moderation would be better, still he could not help express- ing his views to that a semblv in face of the fact that there was a CISSJ of men working men, those engaged in hard labour and exposed to great te nptations, for whom moderation would not do. (Rear, hear.) The previous speaker had ' told them what he had witnessed and what he had heard with regard to the great qu-stion of drink. He (Father Beauvoisin) had for the last twelve months residee;ll, ire War. rington in the very midst of the drink and to his shame he had to utter it, that among his own people, m and girls, professing the same relie,ion as tiiinself, there were to be found the greatest drunkards and habitual drunkards in the town of Wertington. Theet were se-ong words to utter in an assembly like that, but they were strictly true, and in associating himself with the great League of the Cross he did so because he felt that the Catholics bad a work to do. (Applause.) it had been said that the drink question had been overdrawn, and that they had talked too much about it, but he wanted to say a wc.rd or two more. (dear, hear.) The words of the r4sol mkt] stated that the men and women had a right to choose whether they should have public-houses in the town or net; they had a right to choose Local Option. (Hear, hear.) But he wanted to ask the people of Warrington why they had not chosen it? Why did they not rfse as one man and in one voice te ask for Local Option, and which had been granted in other couatries ? (Hear, hear.) They were that evening under the presidency of a very venerable chairman, and one who was highly respected by them all-- (applause)—and he was sure that the words they expressed and the resolutions they passed would not step there but would be carried elsewhere. (Hear, hear.) It was alleged that if they abolished the drink that the revenue of the country would decrease. That he emphatically denied. If they took away the drink the revenue of tie: country would increase. (Applause.) They should consider what drink led to. It led to the prison, their people were there, as also were they in the workhouse and the lunatic asylum. If they dispensed with the drink those houses would be half empty, if not totally so. (Hear, hear.) The United Kingdom Alliance was a grand and noble society, and although he was not in a position to join, being already a memle,e- of the Total Abstinence Society, still he wished it, God speed and he could only hope and trust that it would receive into its ranks many of those present that evening of their Warring- ton friends. (Applause.) Father athew, the great ten. perance orator, recognised the importance of the society when it was first established over mere individual enterprise in the cause, and had wished it as he (the spaaker) did, God speed. (Cheers.) Rev. THOMAS Harrow supported the resaluti m and. ex- pressed a hope that their worthy chairman would give the country the benefit of his knowle4go with regard to the questien during the next session o Parliament. (Applause.) The resolutioa was carried unanimously. Councillor Mowns, J P., moved the following resolution: —" That this meeting congratulates the friends of temper. ance, and of social, moral, and religious progress, on the acceptance by Government of the Local Option Reselu- lion ' of Sir Wilfrid Lawson, as a basis for early and effi- cient legislation, so urgently required in the best interests 'of the nation. rile meeting:, however, deplores the sub- sequent inaction of the Government, and records its core.° ' viction, that whatever may be the future constitution of - the licensing authority, any legislation to be satisfactory I must include clauses empowering the inhabitants of parishee and districts to exercise a direct popular veto upon the issue or renewal of licenses for the sale of intoxicating 'ignore within their boundaries, and hereby calls Upoll the Cabinet no longer to delay, but at the earliest moment in the next session to introduce a measure inciteding such clauses." He' heartily endorsed the resolution, and. added one word in reference to their position in Warrington. He was sorry Mr. Eglinton had referred to a subject which he was sure would bring sorrow and regret to the heart of every Werrington men the custom of girls drinking in public-houses. Without waiting fer ; the passing of any measure which would enable them to deal with this matter as satisfactorily as they would like, • I he would urge upon the Werrinetou Temperance Union to I make the best of the means they had to compel the magi— strates to withhold licences—(epplause)—where they are forfeited by the breaking of the conditions upon which, those licenses are held. (Applause.)

Mr. R. GARNETT expressed his pleasure at seeing Mr. McMinnies in the chair, and so large an audience, which cantrastA wonderfully with the audience at the meeting last year. The meeting was a very enthusiastic one, and a meeting neither Warrington nor any town in the Kingdom. need be ashamed of. He was sure the influence of the meeting would tell very substantially upon the resolutions put before it that night, resolutious which would go forth to the country and the world at large, and would be a dis- tinct testimony that in Warrington at least they were sound upon the point brought before them. (Hear, hear.) Re— ferring to legislation upon the liquor traffic, he said if the present House of Coin none intended to do anything in the matter it would have to be sharp. He had some fear as to whether they would get the credit of it, or whether the House which succeeded them—which might possibly be from the opposite side—would not have the privilege of carrying it, and thus render themselves exceedingly:popular with th country. If the present Government do not do something very substantial—they made promises enough— in the way of restricting the present ve,y large sale of in- toxicating drink., and give the people what the country di- mands—Local Option—:he play which will succeed them will very likely see that it is one of the first things they will do. (Applause.)

I Dr. F. R. Lees, in an earnest, powerful, and eloquent speech, supported the resolution. Adverting to the chair- ; man's reference to Mr. Bright's suggested scheme of placing licensing matters in the hands of Town Councils, he strongly- condemned any such scheme, asserting that Town Councils Iwere the very worst bodies in existence. Show him where a single town was over purified of this evil they all deplored Iby Town Councils. He proceeded to show the beneficial effecte of prohibition in America, and asked if such legislation could be worked successfully across the ocean whether it could not be worked with equally good effect in England. Herr CoHEN morel a resolution offering the thanks of the meeting to the chairman for presiding, and requesting him to send copies of the resolutions to the Prime Minister, the Home Secretary, and the members of Parliament for the county. Herr Cohen depicted the evils of excessive drink- ing, and spoke of the want of more s.ringent legislation with regard to the traffic. He asked the young men present to help the Alliance in their work. He believed in enthusiasm, but he recognised still more the power of individual progress. (Hear, hear.) , The drunkard was a bed politician. He (Herr Cohen) once heard the ques!ien asked, "Why is a drunkard a bad 1 politician 2" and the reply was, "Because he puts his no ! into ineesures that will spoil the constitution." (Laughter and applause.) The question before them was pre- eminently a social ens, and concerned everybody. (Hear, hear.) In conclusion, Herr Cohen urged all who could to I assist the Alliance. THE Conference of the Liberal patty held at Leeds this week has been in every respect a decided success. The object of the gather- ing was "to express the opinion of the Liberal party upon the subject of Parliamen- tary Reform," and in order to get at this opinion accurately every care was take to make the Conference thoroughly representa- tive. The gentlemen attending it consisted exclusively of delegates of Liberal organisa- tions accredited by the bodies to which they belonged, Liberal Associations in places with a population under.so,ooo sending five repre- sentatives, above 50,000 ten, and above 100,000 twenty. When it is remembered that about 2,000 delegates attended, and that these representatives doubtless took the pre- caution before attending the meeting to ascertain the views of their constituents upon the subject to be discussed, there need be no hesitation in accepting the decision of the Conference embodied in the • resolutions passed as the united voice of the Liberal party on the Reform question. That its in- fluence will be felt throughout the country, and that it will have great weight with the PRIME MINISTER and the Cabinet in shaping their course in reference to this important subject there can sea-cely be two opinions. It may be accepted, we think, as a foregone conclusion that the franchise will sooner or later be extended to the counties. On this point both political parties appear to be pretty well agreed; but the question of the redistri- bution of seats is one not so easy of settle' ment, and over which there will undoubtedlY be a hard party struggle. In previous reforni bills the representation of the landed interest has been carefully guarded, and there is no reason why it should not be protected in the future. There are, however, unanswerable arguments why the territorial interest should not longer be allowed to have an undue share of representation, and no future Reform Bill will be satisfactory which does not remeclY this standing grievance. Unless this is done we may again find, as was the case in the Parliament of 1874., a majority of the House of Commons elected by a minority of the electoral body. During last session Mr• RYLANDS obtained an important return of the, Parliamentary constituencies in the Unite' Kingdom, the counties and boroughs being classified according to population. Thl9 return shows the increaso and decrease in the population of each constituency since IRV, together with the number of members allotted to each, and the number of electors in these years. It also gives some interesting details as to the payments to income tax. From this return Mr. NosLf, the author of the " Parliamentary Reformers Manual," has compiled some interesting facts illustrative of the inequalities of the present system of distributing political power:. and from that Manual we quote a few °.` these facts in support of a scheme of redistri- bution. These returns, then, show that the constituencies which manifest vitality have population of 5,093,04.5, and have 64. meor bers allotted to them; while those wh° are either in the declining or stationary state with their population of 619,299 have 8i a very ridiculous state of things. £3,24.2,396 to income tax, are represented by 183 members; while 251 cities and boroughs, With a population of 14,811,118, having 1,850,477 electors, and paying £5,400,235 to income tax, are represented by 300 members. This, Mr. NOBLE says, is wholly "inconsis- tent with the old constitutional principle of g-overnment:by the majority." The popula- tion of tv.ie counties exceeds that of the boroughs by 5,226 003, yet the boroughs have 652,830 more electors than the counties and pay £2, 1 57,8 39 more to the income tax. Mr. NOBLE shows that apart from the ques- tion of the due proportion of borough and County members, the returns reveal a series of startling- anomalies. "Dividing the borough representation at the limit of So,ooo inhabitants, it appears that below that line 4.38,387 electors return 231 representa- tives, while above the line 1,412,090 return only 129. A similar anomaly exists in the counties. Taking the .constituencies below 150,000, 660,132 electors return zo6 mem- bers; while above the limit 537,515 electors return only 77 members." These figures re- late to the United Kingdom, but if England and Wales be taken alone, it is found that the town population of 17,285,026 is represented by 24.1 members, while the rural population Of 8,683, z6o is represented by 243. It would be interesting to know how this state of things can be justified. The anomalies of distribution are, however, more clearly brought out in examining the representation of the counties in England and Wales than in anything else. For instance, 'Worcester has a population of 452,538, andit has eleven representatives, the same number as Surrey With a population of 1,419 176. The popula- tion of Lancaster is 3,437,633, and it is re- presented by 32 members; but Yorkshire has Six members more, though its population is 56z 138 less than that of Lancashire. Cam- bridge, with a population of 185,475 has five Members; the population of Oxford is 3,000 Less than that c.f Cambridge, but it has seven representatives. Westmoreland, with 6408+ of a population, has only the same number of representatives as Monmouth with 211,374 of a population. Anomalies such as these could be easily multiplied. The system of grouping boroughs in Scot- land is, we are told, the cause of compara- tively fewer anomalies being found there; but in Ireland, as in England, they are plen- tiful. The number of representatives for the Irish counties, with a population of 4,258,385 and 168,217 electors ,is 64; and the boroughs, with 901,454. inhabitants and 57,497 electors, return 37 members. More than one-half of these boroughs, it should be stated, have less than soo electors, Portarlington only 142 and Xinsale 190; yet the votes of the members -or these constituencies are as potent as the votes of members representing counties or boroughs with 50,000 or more electors. The only ground on which these few of the many anomalies of our representative system can oe defended is that the landed interest may be represented to the detriment of every other interest. At present there are 47 Par- !lltnentary boroughs with an aggregate popu- lation of 662,262, which are in reality county constituencies, and in these, strange to say, •the householder, whether agricultural labourer or not, has a vote; on the other hand, several counties contain a large number of unrepre- sented towns—amongst others St. Helens— in which householders of only LI 2 value and Upwards have a vote. That is a state of things which can no longer be tolerated, and I;_he sooner a remedy is applied the better. ne are glad to find the Leeds Conference has Spoken out on this matter with no uncertain Sound, and we have every confidence the course that they suggest should be adopted be generally approved by the country. -the present Government was, we believe, elected to power for the purpose of passing, above all other things, another Reform Bill, and it only remains with them to set about the task in earnest. If such a bill is not pro- ceeded with next Session, there is a danger of postponement to another Parliament. This Would give great -dissatisfaction and disap- Pointment to all Liberals throughout the country, and we doubt not to many Tories as

IN4I:3EST AT RUNCORN.—At the Royal Hotel, Runcorn, 1311 Wedaesday morning, Mr. J. E. Worsley, the deputy coroner, held an inquest on the body of Bridget Kilconnell, a child two years of age, daughter of Thomas Kilconnell, of 4.9, Vicar-street. Mr. J. W. Woodland was the foreman of he jury. On the 20th of Slptember the child overturned a Cup of tea, and part of the heated fluid fell upon its breast. Abe amther dressed the scald, but no doctor was called in, a d the child gradually became worse and died on Tuesday Zorning last. A verdict of "Accidental death" was re- corded.

The number ~31 paupers relieved in Lancashire during the quarter ended Nptember last was 20,740 indoor and 46,895 outdoor. Of these 1,790 indoor and 6,500 -outdoor were adult able-bodied, ,Igainst 21,530 indoor and 47,980 outdoor in the correspon- 'ing quarter of 1882. Of these 1,810 indoor and 7,500 out- uoor were adult able-bodied. In the county of Cheshire the tluttiber of paupers of all classes was 2.937 indoor and 10,605 °iltdoor. Of these 530 indoor and 1,290 outdoor were adult able-bodied, against 3,190 indoor and 10,965 outdoor in the rresponding quarter of 1882. Of these 590 indoor and 1,403 outdoor were adult able-bodied. Some of the makers Who were showing an anxiety to secure orders have been pnabled to till up their books for the present, but the year Closing with no real weight of work ahead; and, although there is little or no margin upon the present prices to work 4Pon for any further reduction in prices, there is apparently Want of confidence in the future, which is keeping buyers ro,al placing orders. Lancashire pig iron makers are well 5f0141 over the present year, and are firm at 45s 3d, less 21, or both forge and foundry qualities delivered equal to s!anchester.
