RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB.—In the county trial match. at Sale to—day the Runcorn Football Club will be represented , by Messrs. H. and W. Hughes, W. H. Broady, W. Wright, ' and Wilkinson. THE LIBERAL ASs)CIATION.—Messrs. E. K. Muspratt, J.P., J. Handley and H. B. Shores were the representatives of the Widnes Liberal Association at the great Reform Con- ference held at Leeds during the present week. A DEGRADED COrPLE.—Yesterday, at Runcorn Police Court, John Venables and Agnes Ford, a woman of bad character, were charged with vagrancy. Early that morn- ing P.C. Robinson had found the couple sleeping on the floor of a bedroom in an unoccupied house in Cooper-street. They had nothing in their possession, and could not give a satisfactory account of themselves.—They were each sen- tenced to a month's imprisonment with hard labour. THE HEAVY RAIN: SHEEP DROWNED NEAR WIDNES.—

The continuous heavy downpour of rain during the last few days has occasioned considerable damage in various parts of the country, and large tracts of land have been sub- merged in many places. At an early hour on Thursday morning, Cuerdley Marsh, a low-lying spot, situate between Warrington and Widnes, was flooded by the high tide in the river, and a number of sheep owned by Mr. Rolaan, salesman of Liverpool, were drowned. WESLEYANISM AT HALTON.—The Rev. George Hack on Sunday morning and evening, preached a sermon in the Halton Wesleyan C'aapel on behalf of the Wesleyan Foreign Missions. On Tuesday evening the annual missionary meeting was held, and there was a good attendance. Mr. R. Shaw, of Runcorn, delivered an excellent opening ad- dress, and Mr. I'. Norman took the chair. Appropriate ad- dresses were given by the Revs. George Hack, S. Mees, and S. T. House, of Newcastle. The collections amounted to upwards of .£B. CARPENTER AND LORRAINE'S MINSTRELS.—This troupe of minstrels are announced to give their diverting entertain- ments at the Public Hall, Runcorn, on Thursday and Friday next. The company, which has only recently arrived in this country from America, is making a tour of some of the princi;.-al towns on their wax. North. They will in all pro- bability precede their entertffhment on each night with a procession through the streets. The company are favourably, spoken of, and both originality and mirth may safely be cal- culated ts be in store for intending visit& ro. MISSIONARY MEETING AT WESTON.—The annual meeting in aid of the Wesleyan Foreign Missions was held at Weston, on Wednesday evening, and although the weather was furiously boisterous there was a good attendance. Mr. T. Norman presided, and delivered an appropriate address, in which he referred to his connection with Weston, of which he had many pleasing memories, and declared his willing- ness to do all he could to forward the interests of his native village. Addresses were also delivere-j. by the Revs. George Hack and S. Mee', and Mr. Robert Norman, who related some interesting facts regarding the establishment of Wes- leyan Methodism in the village. The collections realised 16 shillings more than last year. •

EVADING THE RUNCORN BRIDGE COLLECTORS. At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, Samuel Nash, a chemical labourer, was summoned to answer a charge of attempting to defraud the London and North-Western Railway CJnap tny.—lt appeared from the evidence that, early on the morning of the 29th September, Nash succeeded in getting on Runcorn bridge, at the Widnes end, without paying his fare. When he had nearly traversed the length of the bridge, he removed his clogs, and, in his "stocking feet," crept quietly down the slope, but rushing past the collector's office at the run. The collector followed, how- ever, and having overtaken him ascertained his name and address.—The defendant, who did not appear, was fined 20s. and costs, 135., or, in default, 14 days' imprisonment, with hard labour. ACCIDENT TO A RUNCORN YOUNG GENTLEMAN IN AUSTRALIA.--" The South Australian Register" has,the fol- lowing paragraph :—On Tuesday, Auguet 28th, Dr. F. Salkeld, of Gawler, met with a very serious accident. He had been visiting a patient on the awler plains, when his horse bolted and went off at a terrific rate. Near the back entrance of the Mill Inn tho doctor was pitched off on his head. He was picked up by Mr. Betts. Dr. Dawes fortunately happened to be passing at the time of the acci- dent, and so assisted in carrying the sufferer into the inn, when it was found that he was suffering from concussion of the brain. Consciousness did not return for over an hour after the fall, and the doctor now lies in a very bad state. It will be remembered that Mr. Salkeld left Runcorn early in the present year for Australia. A DISORDERLY HOUSE AT RUNCORN.—At the Chester Quarter Sessions, on Tuesday, Elizabeth Abbott (42), shop- keeper, of 14, Fryer-street, Runcorn' was charged with keeping a common ill-governed and disorderly house, at Runcorn, on the 18th August —The charge was brought by Henry Pocknall and Jam Grarvy, neighbours, and Mrs. Abbott, who said the proceedings both inside and outside the house were very discreditable.—Evidence was given in sup- port of the charge by Mary Spencer, agol 18; Ellen Hulse, aged 23, living at the Brickkiln houses, Runcorn ; Elizabeth Ellen Bird, without a proper home, all "unfortunates ;'' and Sergeant McMichael and Inspector Hollingworth.—Mr. Royle's agent proved that prisoner was the tenant of the house in question on the 18th August, and had been for some time prior to that date.—Prisoner was found guilty, and was sentenced to twelve calendar months' imprisonment with hard labour.

UNLAVVECLLY REMOVING A COW TO SANKEY.—At the Warrington Borough Police Curt, on Wednesday, Thomas Wiles, cow-keeper, Widnes, was summoned for having, on the 13th inst., removed a cow from the district of the borough of Warrington into the district of the local authority of the county of Lancaster, contrary to the regulations of the county in pursuant of the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Pattinson said on the afternoon of the day in question he met the defendant coming out of Warrington with a cow. He stopped him and asked him if he was aware cattle were not allowed to be removed out of the borough into the county. Defendant said Mr. Bennett, from whom he bought the cow, told him to keep clear of Warrington, and he did not know that he had been in the borough.-Mr. J. Hylands said it was a very natural mistake, still it was a breach of the law. Defendant had rendered himself liable to a fine of not exceeding £2O. but the Bench were willing to take a lenient view of the case, and believe that he did not know he was breaking the law.—The case was dismissed on pay- ment of costs. ALLEGED HOUSE BREAKING AT RUN'CORN : A VIOLENT PRISONER.—Before Mr. W. Bankes, at Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, Joseph Rowlands alias Porter, a rough character, who has made upwards of 20 appearances before the Bench, was brought up in custody charged with breaking into the dwelling-house of Jane Hicks, of Cooper-street, on Tuesday night, and stealing therefrom a pair of boots and 2s. 6d , the goods and monies of Eliza Garnett.—From the evidence adduced, it appeared that Garnett is the wife of a flatman, and usually lived on the boat, but on the night in question she went to Mrs. Hicks' house. About half-past seven Mrs. Hicks went out, locking the door behind her, and slqortly afterwards witness went to bed. At that time the prisoner's brother John was lying on the sofa in the kitchen. After the lapse of a few minutes Mrs. Garnett heard the outside door burst open with a crash, and immediately afterwards the priso- ner, followed by two men whom she did not know, entered i the bedroom. He attempted to criminally assault her, but she struggled from his grasp, whereupon the prisoner took up the boots which were near the bed-side, saying, "Well, I have got a raise now for the morning; we can have a drink in the morning." He and his companions then de- camped, and the half-a-crown was afterwards missed.— Whilst Mrs. Garnett was giving her evidence the prisoner cursed her in most vile language, and attempted to rush from the dock with the object of striking her, but Superin- tendent Williamson with great promptitude prevented him. —The prisoner was remanded until Tuesday next. A MAN ATTACKED WITH • POKER AT WIDNES —Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell junr., at Widnes Police Court on Mon- day, Edward James Ryan was brought up in custody, charged with unlawfully wounding Richard Wallace, a copper smelter, who lives at 12, Dock-street. About half- seven on Saturday night Wallace was in his house, when 1 he heard a disturbance in the street, and followed by his wife went to ascertain the cause. In the meantime the neighbourhood had become quiet, but Wallace had scarcely stood in the open a minute, when he heard a footstep behind him, and immediately received a blow on the back of the head which partly stunned him. He could not swear that th,f, prisoner was his assailant, but his wife Mary Alice de- poTed to seeing the prisoner leave his own house and strike , her husband with the short, heavy, iron poker produced. 1 Ellen Roach, of 15, Dock-street was called, but gave her evi- dence in an unsatisfactory way. She said she could n9t identify the prisoner as the man who struck the blow.-IYr. j McLeanau deposed that Wallace went to his surgery on I Saturday night. He found him suffering from an incised scalp wound, 21 inches long, on the back of the head, peue- trating to the bone. Blood was flowing freely. Witness stitched and dressed the wound which was a dangerous one, and it would probably be two or three weeks before he was out of danger. The poker produced would cause such a wound.—P.C. Thompson said he apprehended the prisoner in bed on Saturday night. He at once said "I know what you want me for. He hit me first and I struck him with the poker. I ought to have given him more."—The prisoner was formally committed to the Liverpool Quarter Sessions , for trial.

Mr. PIERPOINT'S•CONCERT AT RUNCORN.—The following I remarks on Miss Thudichum, who is to appear at Mr. Pier- point's concert on the 13th ult., will be read with interest. The "World," speaking of her appearance at the popular concerts, London, says :—" But quite an event, in my opinion, is the dant of Miss Thudichum. An exceptionally fine dramatic voice—formed by the best singing master we have, Manuel Garcia—evident musical intelligence, and re- I fined feeling, could only lead to one great artistic result. Although I have seen in no paper very much made of her, ' I say this day, February 6th, that here is a coming great English singer. The evenness of her timbre, the equal power of her medium, the warmth of her expression, the superiority of her conception, the purity of her intonation, the clearness and correctness of her ascending chromatic scales and shakes show what she will do." The Manchester Guardian says of Miss Thudichum at Mr. Halle's concerts— "Miss Thudichum is a young singer of great promise. All her her selections were of an exacting character, though in different styles. Handel and Pergolesi have something in common in the antique forms of their melody; and Handel in the "Lusinghe pin care " has written a number of pas- sages as awkward of execution as any that can be found in his works. These were mastered in a way which spoke highly for Miss Thudichum'straining and intelligence, and her singing of the florid Rossiman aria "Di placer " proved that she had something more than a merely flexible voice and a capacity for using it. The latter song needs consider- able feeling, much finesse, and more self possession in order to its successful accomplishment, and in none of these was Miss Thudichum detieent."

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 20, 1883. OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 20, 1883. OUR LONDON LETTER.

DRAMATIC ENTERTAINMENT AT RUNCORN. - The St. Edwards' Catholic amateurs will give another of their in-. teresting dramatic performances in the Public Hall, on Monday evening. Full particulars will be found in our announcement columns.

CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY, FARN— WORTH.—The members of the juvenile section gave an en— tertainment in the girls' school, on Tuesday evening. Mr. J. W. Davies presided, and delivered a short address, as did also the Rev. J. Holden. Mr. Harnpson, of Liverpool, gave a blackboard address, inculcating many useful lessons into the children's minds. An excellent programme of recita— tions, songs, and dialogues was gone through. ST. AMBROSE CHURCH, WIDNES. There was a good congregation in this church on Tuesday evening, on the occasion of the annual harvest festival. The sacred edifice had been neatly decorated with various fruits of the earth. The preacher was the Rev. G. Hardwick Spooner, vicar of Litherland, and the other clergymen present were the Revs, George Bond, M.A , S. A. Spooner, M.A., and J. Holden. The collection in aid of the boundary wall fund realised £6 ss.

LODGING•TIOUSE ROBBERY AT RUNCORN.— Yesterday, at Runcorn Police Court, before Mr. W. Bankes and Captain C. W. Hazlehurst, John Coghlan was brought up under a warrant, charged with having, on the lith inst., stolen a pair of boots, the property of Peter Murphy.—Murph:- is a labourer at the Old Quay Y aril, and lodges at Barratt's house in Mersey-street. The prisoner had lodged at the same place for about ten days. The boots, which were valued at 12s, were safe on Tuesday night, but on Wednes- day morning when the prosecutor got up, they had been taken away. The same morning the prisoner pledged them at Mr. E. Imison's pawnshop, for the sum of 2s. GJ. P.C. Wallace apprehended the prisoner at Widnes, on Thursday afternoon. He acknowledged his guilt, pleading in extenua- tion that he was drinking.—lnspector Hollingworth said the prisoner was a stranger to the town, and the Bench sen- tenced him to one month's hard labour.

IMPENDING CHANGES IN THE CABINET-THE SPEAKER AT GLYNDE - THE ATTORNEY- GENERAL - SIR FARRER HERSCHE L- AN ALHAM BRA-FASHIONABJ,E MARRIAGES-THE ANIMAL SEASON-INSURANCE OF PARCELS- THE BISHOP OF LONDON AND HIS SUC- CESSOR-ROYAL APARTMENTS AT KENSING- TON.
LONDON, THURSDAY.,

When October has so far advanced as that we are very near November, when all the people who have to come to town are back, one hears year after year the familiar cry of impending changes in the Cabinet. It is sure to come, and it has come this year only a little earlier than usual. The changes said to be impending are indeed very impor- tant. I suppose the first is that we are to have a new Speaker. I saw Sir Henry Brand at Glynde, last week, walking with his little grandson by the hand over the downs, upon which his sheep were feeding industriously. The Speaker at Glynde—he is always called " Mr. Speaker" there—wears the leggings and gaiters of a country gentle- man, and looks, as an old country gentleman should, hearty and vigorous. But the last session was a trying one, and it is no secret that before next February comes Sir Henry will have arranged to be relieved from a very dignified but very onerous office.

IWho is to succeed him? That sets the snow ball called "Impending changes in the Cabinet" rolling. The present Home Secretary has shown a desire and an aptitude for all kinds of otY,ce. It was said he was to be Lord Chancellor, and now it is slid he is to be Speaker of the House of Com- mons. I think he would well govern, but I greatly doubt whether he would well moderate such an assembly. He is certainly a strong man, a vigorous politician, and of un- doubted ability. With him for Speaker we should want a new Home Secretary, and there can be no doubt that Sir I Henry James would be the favourite. Sir Henry does not care for judicial rank. He is a bachelor, rich and though not self-indulgent certainly not anxious to throw himself i away. After all there is something very austere about the Bench. You know no one but your legal brethren ; yon are condemned to sit daily from ten to four in a draughty build- ing, and you must listen to every counsel who addresses I you. Sir Henry has the social qualities too strong developed to allow him to tolerate the idea of high judicial rank. He 'is a good billiard pliyer, a good card player, a good sports- man. ILI enjoys the confines of parliamentary life. If Sir William Harcourt is moved elsewhere, I think there is no doubt Sir Henry will be his successor. And then it is said that Lord Selborne is going to resign, and that the present Lord Chief Justice will be the new Lord Chancellor. It is very likely to be SO. The promo- tion comes regularly, and the fusion of law and equity seems to be accomplished. Who, then, would be Lord Chief Justice of England ? The present Attorney-General would not. He tikes of choice a different rank. 'The Solicitor- General is spoken of for the post; but I do not think this at all a probable appointment. Sir Farr er's ability is well known, and highly as he is esteemed by the public, I think he is even more highly esteemed by the profession. Still I do not think, at this juncture, he is likely to be Lord Chief Justice. The post is much more likely to be given to the present Master of the Rolls. But all these forecasts are I premature. We are in October, 1883, not February, 1834; and all we know is, that Sir Henry Brand will probably re- sign, and that it is said Lord Selb)rne will resign at the ' same time.

I hear there is prospects of the Alhambra introducing to to the London public the famous ballet of Excelsior. I have this year seen it performed in Milan, Rome, and Paris. At Paris there was the best danseuse, but the strength of the piece lies in the drilling of the subordinates,and nothing ever seen on London boards approaches the unanimity of an Italian ballet. If the piece is to have the continental success it would be necessary to import the whole troupe, and that Ido not think is likely to b 3 done. Nothing for a long time in its line has had such a success in Italy, and the army of ballerices who gave it passed frona town to town throughout the winter.

There were fighting bishops in old days, but the presrnt Primate is winning or himself distinction as a marrying hierarch. It will get to be quite fashionable to be married by Dr. Benson. St. Margaret's, Westminster, is also coming into note as a church which the upper ten affect. Canon Farrer's sermons have none that for it. It would be an in- delicate thing to enquire, but I wonder what art etiquette is in feeing an archbishop for his services at a wedding. In o'd days a bishop got a pair of gloves with a guinea in each finger and a guinea :n each thumb. Is the benediction of an archbishop more costly? By the way, I observe that the bride wore a very small white bonnet. It seems Vie Princess of Wales is winning in her millinery crusade all along the line. •

The fishery fever is dying out, and its successor is declar- ing itself. The animal season is coming on. By the end of the month the DuKe of Wellington Riding School will 1 be inhabited by St. Bernard Dogs. There are entries already for over two hundred. Then there is the cat show at the ! Crystal Palace, more popular and better stocked than any previous exhibition. I have been looking through the catalogue, and I fancy that some of the prices put on these feline pats must be intended to be prohibitory. And yet an exhibitor is quite at liberty to wind up the description of her exhibit with the simple sentence," Not for sale." Dogs at Knightsbridge, cats at Norwood, and bulls at the Aquarium. The trained bull calves do indulge in strange ; sports, and one jumping over the back of the other is a reversal of the fable of the frog that tried to seem a bull. I notice that the critics in speaking of the performances at the Aquarium dwell much on the wonderful wit of the trainer. But in reality a bull calf is very docile and very intelligent. It is only when he reaches the age of puberty that he gets intractable. The London show of dogs will not be confined to St. Bernard. Baghton in November is prac- tically London, and the show of fox terriers will be held Hearly in that month. It has always been a favourite exhi- • bition at London-on-the-sea. But fox terriers--I am told— are going out of fashion. Of course I mean out of fashion with ladies. They keep their hold on the masculine affec- tions. Their supplanters with the other sex are the tribe of black Potneranians.

In the struggle bctween the railway companies and the Post Office as to which could offer to the public the most profitable terms, the com- panies, or at least certain carriers who employed them, had the pull. .They offered to insure for a small ex- tra fea the value of the goods entrusted them for delivery. And now I hear that the Government are going to do the same. A halfpenny for fifty shillings, a penny for the first £5, and a halfpenny for every extra £5 ; this is slid to be the

actually before the vacancy arises. it is said that the vicar 40 Kensington will be recommended to the Queen by the Prime Minister for a bishopric. He has claims. He has married a daughter 0r the Duke of Argyll. He is wealthy, ' and Lord Wolveton is a great personal friend of the Pi ime Minister. .Moreover, he is a hard-working, conscientious Ems ,n, who tills his church and takes ewe of his parish, and is as far as possible removed from the wealthy clerrymau who tinls it eisier to get a bishopric than to in lunge a diocese. :it;11 I do not think Mr. Carr Wynne will be made a bishop, and I do not think he ought to be. He is a young man. He 'is young even . for the post he holds, and he has not had the opportunity to show himself of that kind of stuff of which bishops are made. He is a good preacher, but not an excellent one, and I have never heard it said that he was either a great administrator or a great scholar. He deserves to be " reserved for promo- tion."

The royal apartments at Kensington are stillivacant. Her Majesty has, of course, the patronage of them and has uot yet exercised it. The rooms do not pass out of the occu- pancy of same members of the Royal Family. The Duchess of Teck was the last occupant—it was said that the Prin- cess Louise would be the next. The Duke of Sussex, one of George lll.'s family, lived in them for years, and when the Duke died his widow, who, after her marriage—a morganatic one—was created Duchess of Inverness, resided there till her death in 1873, when the Princess Mary came. Kensington, ae court suburb, sets some store on royalty being what the Americans would call "located " at the Palace. The idea of the Prince of Wales coming there, once a very favourite theory of the inhabitants, is now quite abandoned.

div.head: AFFAIRS OF THE RUNCORN GAS COMPANY.
div.p: THE AFFAIRS OF THE RUNCORN GAS COMPANY.

At the Cheshire Quarter Sessions, On Monday, Mr. ! Horatio Lloyd and other magistrates heard during the after- noon a case in which Mr. Marshall appeared in support of a petitiot signed by the proprietors of the Runcorn Alkali Works, and Messrs. Wegg Brothers, who craved the Court to appoint someone to make an inquiry into the finances of the Runcorn Gas Company. It is alleged that the Company have been appropriating more profit than they are legally authorised to do, to the injury and loss of the consumers of gas in their district. After Mr. Higgins had been heard on behalf of the Company, Mr. Lloyd said the magistrates were of opinion that a prima-facie case had been made out for appointing someone to examine the ac- counts of the Gas Company, and they had therefore come to the conclusion that it was their duty to comply with the prayer of the petition. If the petitioners turned out to be wrong, the Court bad full power to make them pay the costs.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL B )A RD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL B )A RD.
SMALL-PDX STILL SPREADING: INTERESTING
DISCUSSION.

A special meeting of Widnes Local Board was held on Tuesday afternoon for the purpose of affixing the seal of the Board to the agreement of the purchase of Mr. Ireland's property at Appleton. Mr. F. H. Gossage presided, and there were also present Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. Carey, Pankhurst, Wright, Midwood, Dutton, Houghton, Johnson, Webster, Sadler, Handley, Kershaw, J. T. Alien (clerk), Dr. Cooper (medial officer), Iligginson (surveyor), Dickson (nuisance inspector).—Before commencing with the business which had brought them together, the members considered a report with reference to number 1 contract of the main sewerage scheme. It was decided that Mr. Allen give legal notice to Mr. Jeffries, the contractor, of the termination of the contract.—The CLERK read a letter from the Local Government Board, in which it was stated that the Board could not give their approval to the proposed site for an in- fectious diseases hospital until it had been examined by one of their inspectors. An endeavour would be made to arrange for such an examination during the present week.—Dr. O'KEEFFE, in the face of that letter, could not move that the seal be affixed to the agreement; but Mr. CARET con- tended that the letter did not alter the case.—Mr. KERSHAW did not think the Board should affix its seal to any agree- ment until it had the approval of the Local Government Board.—At the request of several members the CLERK read the agreement, which was made between Thomas Ireland, farmer, of the one part, and the Board of the other part, for the purchase of Mayfield House, stables and gardens, now in the occupation of the vendor, two cottages, and a plot of land (one acre, three roods, and six perches in extent), in the occupation of John Valentine. The cast was £1,400. The agreement was to be entered subject to the approval of the Local Government Board.- -Dr. O'KEEFFE moved that the consideration of the agreement be deferred until the visit of the Government inspector, and suggested that the gentlemen should be shown ov,:r the town, and empowered to select a site. He (the doctor) had no desire for any particular site, and any site selected to meet the views of the members would be agreeable to him. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Hounirros seconded the proposi- tion.—Dr. O'KEEFFE observed that three additional cases of small-pox lead been reported that day. One was in Gladstone-street, one in Lathomestreet and one in John-street. In one case there was a little chance of isolation, but in the other two cases there was none whatever.—The CHAIRMAN : And they are not paupers?—Dr. O'KEEFFE: No, they are not. —The CHAIRMAN: Then we cannot insist upon them going to the workhouse.—Mr. WEBSTER remarked that the Board Was like a shuttlecock, going up and down and doing noth- ing, while in the meantime the disease was spreading.—At the request of Mr. Kershaw, the clerk read same correspon- dence that had passed between himself and Mr. Hartley., clerk to the guardians, with reference to the case of a woman named Cox. Mr. Hartley replied that the guardians did not feel justified in interfering with the case, as the Local Government Board objected to them having anything to do with any but pauper cases. —The CHAIRMAN intimated that a deputation of property owners with reference to the proposed hospital were waiting for an interview, and they were called into the room. The following gentlemen, headed by the Rev. Geo. Boni, vicar of Parnavorth, then entered the room, via :—Messrs. Ernest Bibby, Bullough, Barker, T. Robinson, Riley, Mercer, and Horabin. The Rev. G. Bond read a petition, signed by 128 persons, which stated that as property owners in Halton- view and the immediately surrounding district, they begged respectfully to protest to the Widnes Local Board against . the purchase of property in the above-named district for the purpose of e-ecting an infectious diseases hospital. As property owners in a gradually improving and rising neigh- , bourhood, they considered it would certainly tend to the depreciation of property, and they believed that a temporary building in a more isolated situation would better meet the requirements of the Case without inflicting injury upon property. They thought the proposed site too near a public thoroughfare, to St. Ambrose Churei. to Albert-road Wesleyan Chapel, to Warrington-road Board Schools, and to Page-lane Mission-room and Sunday school. Mr. Bond remarked that the signatures had been obtained in one day without a single refusal.—The CHAIRMAN said the Boaid in receiving the deputation did not pledge itself in any way. The Board would he obliged to act in the manner they thought best for the good of the whole inhabi- tants of Widnes.—Mr. T. Rom:ewer personally objected to the proposed site because the erection of a hospital would depreciate land upon which he intended to build a house for himself, and on general grounds because the sewage would have to flow into Bower's Brook, which would be turned into a disease spreading stream. Many years ago at St. Helens a similar brook was the cause of a serious epi- demic of fever. He thought a superior site ready for im- mediate occupation might be found at a less cost than that proposed. The cost of the land and building proposed would not be less than £4,ooo.—Mr. BIBBY said the erection of a hospital at Halton View would completely spoil his land there, and he should be happy to negotiate with the Board for a site in another part of the district —Dr. O'KEEFFE pointed out that the epidemic in St. Helens was not caosed by the sewage from an infectious diseases' hospital. There was not one in the borough at the time.—Mr. KERSHAW contended that there were 20 landewners who had not been approached, and protested against rushing into the matter.—The CHAIRMAN said it was hardly right to reproach the Board in having rushed into this business. The Board had been met at every turn with refusals from the landlords to allow a hospital to be erected on their land, Mr. Kershaw had also refused. Mr. Bibby was the first landowner who had shown himself willing. The Rev. G. BOND said the Bishop was coming next week to consecrate St. Ambrose Church, but he did not see much use in the church being consecrated at all if the infectious diseases' hospital was to be as near as proposed.— Members of the deputation suggested various sites, but it was found that the Board had had most of them under con- sideration, and terms could hot be arranged.—Dr. Coopnn made a few remarks to the effect that the supposed hospital could not injure the neighbourhood. Mr. BARKER said there was not one good drain in Halton View, and there was a drain that ran past the Board School that was enough to poison half the neigh- bourhood. Mr. Roniersota remarked that whatever might be the medical opinion the public would exercise their own judgment, and if the hospital was erected at Halton View people would give it a wide berth.—The CHAIRMAN said the suggestions of the deputation would have serious consideration, and on behalf of the Board would pledge the members not to do anything rashly.—The depu- tation then withdrew.—Dr. O'KEEFFH charged Mr. Kershaw with being concerned in getting up the petition, and stated in the course of half a day. Mr. Kershaw was like the dog in ' that he ceuld get any number of signatures to any memorial the manger, for he would not give land himself nor allow a site to be selected.--Mr. KERSHAW protested in emphatic language that he had had nothing to do with the memo- rial.—lt was then unanimously resolved that the sealing of the agreement be deferred.—The CLERK read a comm unica- tion from the medical officer of the borough of Stafford offering to sell the Local Board two infectious diseases tents, one to accommodate 12 patients, for £5O, and one to accommodate 8 patients, for £3O. They had wooden floors raised 18 inches from the ground, and were admirably suited for the purpose.—Mr. T. HANDLEY moved, and Mr. DuerTore seconded, that the tents ke purchased and tern• porarilv erected in Ditton Gas-yard.—The motion was agreed' to.—Arrangements having been made for the Go- vernment Inspector's visit, the meeting terminated.

div.head: THREE WIDNES CABMEN IN TROUBLE.
div.p: THREE WIDNES CABMEN IN TROUBLE.

Enoch Simcock, Thomas Lee, and 'William Didebury, Widnes cabmen, were each summoned at Widnes Petty Ses- sions, on Wednesday, for obtaining drink during prohibited hours, from Mrs. Clare, landlady of the Ring-o'-Bells, Farn- worth, by making false representations.—Mr. J. W. Knowles appeared for the defendants.—Mrs. Clare was put into the witness box, and Superintendent Barker was proceeding to conduct the case when Mr. Knowles objected to his doing so, saying that it was not a police case, and Supt. Barker net being a solicitor had no right to conduct it.—The Magistrates' Clerk : Show the magistrates that.—Mr. Knowles said that Superintendent Barker could not act as a solicitor, and the learned clerk must know that to be so. The superintendent was, liable to a penalty of £5O if he conducted the case.—Superintendent Barker said that the case was instituted at the instance of the police, and be maintained that he had a right to conduct Mr. Knowles said that the summonses were taken out by ; Mrs. Clare, and it was therefore a private case.—The Magistrates' Clerk ruled that the Bench could allow Superintendent Barker to conduct the case.— Mr. Knowles asked the Bench to take a note of that.—Mr. H. S. Hall (chairman) : Well, we can take a note of it, Mr. Knowles ; but if your interpretation of the law is right, the law has been very often broken.—Saperintendent Barker then went on with the case ; and Mrs. Clare said that about three o'clock on Sunday afternoon, the 7th instant, the three defendants came to her house, and were admitted. They were questioned as to where they came from, and Siinceck replied that they came from Hale, Lee said he came from Woolton, and Didsbury said be came from Gateacre. She then served each with a "small rum." While de- fendants were standing at the bar, Sergeaat Coutts came in and told her that be knew all the defendants, and that they came from Widnes. Sergeant Coutts stated that he went into the Ring O'Bells, Farnworth, about 4 o'clock on Sunday afternoon, the 7th inst., and found the three defendants standing with glasses of rum before them. Simcock, in reply to a question, said he did not come from Widnes, but subseqsentty admitted it. The other two de- fendants also admitted that they came from Widnes. He called the landlady's attention to the matter, and she replied that they had represented themselves to be bond-fide travel- lers. On questioning the defendants they admitted that they had done so. Simcock seemed to think he had a right to be there, and was unwilling to give his name.—The Clerk said the defendants were liable to a penalty of £5 each.— Each defendant was ordered to pay 22s each.

div.head: WIDNES CHORAL SOCIETY'S SOIREE.
div.p: WIDNES CHORAL SOCIETY'S SOIREE.

The annual soiroe of the members of the Widnes Choral Society was held in Lacey-street sclsoal-room, on Thurs- day evening. About 80 persons partook of the tea which had been provided, the following ladies presiding over the various tables :—Mrs. Bond, Mrs. Carey, Mrs. Richard White, Mrs. Hunter, Mrs. Kershaw, and Mrs. John Taylor. The tables were adorned with a number of beautiful plants, lent by Mr. Farrant, of Appleton Villa. Subsequently a concert took place.—Mr. W. A. WATTS presided, and after congratulating the members on the success of the soir6e, called upon the Glee Party to sing " The wrecked hope." Mr. Black, a recent acquisition to the society, and who will certainly render valuable assistance, then sang "The desert," a song requiring great powers of vocalisation. His fine, heavy voice, however, proved equal to all the demands made upon it, and he was deservedly applauded. The sweet song, "The children's home," was giten by Miss I. Bond with true taste and feeling; and Mr. E. Carey sang his old favourite, "The Muleteer," to the delight of the audience. A harmonium solo by Mr! Argent was the next item, and the genial conductor exhibited his usual delicacy of touch and finished execution which distinguishes his performances on all occasions. He was heartily encored. Mc. Broadlake, of Liverpool, sang "The old arm chair" with a keen ap- preciation of the beauties of the peace, and with good effect. Miss Lily James, of Runcorn, contributed "The kingdom blest." She possesses a voice of great harmony and power which she uses in an accomplished manner, and the fin.! cadences of the song were rendered in a style that drew hearty plaudits from the audience. The song, "Dream, fairies," was sung by Miss Leatherbarrow in a pleasing manner, and Mr. Morrison showed that he had lost none of his old power in the song, " Dids.t thou know how much I love thee." Mr. Smith gave "Come into the garden, Maud," with good exoression, and Miss Haddock was heard to advantage in "The children's kingdom." Mr. Brown sang the powerful strains of "The diver" in a lusty but not unmusical fashion, and "Baby mine" received a pleasing interpretation from Miss Leatherbarrow. Miss Oakdeu, who pessessas considerable elocutionary ability, gave a recitation, and Mr. White executed with skill a pianoforte solo, which was followed by the singing of "Powder Monkey Joe," by Mr. J. R. Lea, whose efforts were heartily appreciated. The soirée was brought to an appropriate conclusion by the glee party singing "The bells of Eve" in the harmonious style that characterised their first efforts. The thanks of the company were accorded to the ladies and gentlemen who had assisted in promoting the harmony and success of the soirée.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

A meeting of this Board was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuealiy afternoon. Mr. J. Ashton presided, and the. other gentlemen present wera the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, J. Lockwood; Messrs. Handley, Highfield, Norm in, Whittaker, . _
, . Wallington, Hamilton, Weir, Mclntyre, Smith. Whitlow, and Rigby, with H. Linaker (clerk) and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk.)

THE APPOINTMENT OF A NURSE. At the last Board meeting a Mrs. Wright was appointed nurse at the Workhouse, at a salary of £2O per annum, on condition that she obtained a satisfactory testimonial from the nurse at the West Derby Hospital. The nurse now wrote the Board saying that as Mrs. Wright had only been at the West Derby Hospital about four months she would rather that a testimonial V 1,14 obtained from someone else. The Board thought that if a nurse was again advertised for, and £25 per annum offered, more persons would apply for the post, and the Board would therefore be able to make a better selection.—lt was acordingly decided to adve. rise, on the motion of Mr. HANDLEY, seconded by Mr. Locitwoon.

VES SUDDEN DEATH OF A WIDI, MANAGER.

Mr. William Hopkins, manager of the refining department a, the Tharsis Sulphur and Copper Works, Lugsdale died under somewhat singular circumstances on Tuesday Morn- ing. Up to about a week ago, when be complained of a slight pain, Mr. Hopking bad enjoyed extremely robust health, and the services of a doctor has seldom been neces- siry. o member of the medical faculty was consulted in the present instance, and on Tuesday morning he went to the works apparently in the best of health. In the fore- noon, however, he complained of a violent pain in the stomach, and told Mr. W. S. Pritchard, the manager of the works, that he thought he had got the cramps. Mr. Pritchard despatched a messenger for Dr. Cooper, who im- mediately proceeded to the works, but arrived too late to be of any aid. Just previously, Mr. Hopkins said " Let me have some cold water; I am dying." Mr. Pritchard obtained a glass of water, and Mr. Hopkins, after a futile attempt to swallow some, fell back in the chair dead. The deceased, who was highly respected in the town, was 51 years of age and unmarried, and resided in apartments at Laurel Mount, Albert-road, Widnes. The Coroner has been advised of the death, but he considers an inquest unneces- sary, and has reterrtd the case to the registrar.

div.head: WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS.
div.p: WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS.
MEETING AT WIDNES.

The annual sermons in behalf of the' Wesleyan Foreign Missions were preached in the Victoria Road Chapel, on Sunday last to good congregations. In the morning the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. J. Ilothersall, formerly a missionary in the West Indies, and in the evening by the Rev. R. Harper, superintendent of the Widnes circuit: On Monday evening the annual meeting was held in the same chapel, under the presidency of Mr. R. Shaw, of Runcorn. The weather being very boisterous there was only a mode- rate audience. The speakers occupied seats on the plat- form. Devotional exercises having been engaged in, the Chairman delivered a brief address in which he referred to the vast extent of the missionary work. He said they Could this year congratulate themselves more than they had been able to do for many years past, for whilst the amount spent during the last year was £109,446, the amount re- ceived was £169,361, leaving a deficiency of only .£B5. He believed that it was many years SinC3 the society was in such a position as that. He saw in looking over the figures that had Widnes given last year what it did in 1877 there would have been no deficiency bat a balance. However, they knew that there had been special claims upon the people of Widnes. But it was one of the great privileges of Christian people to unite themselves in haying done what they could around and about them with that liberal heart which Christ had put in each one.—Tne Rev. J. HOTHER- SALL then read the extracts from the general report, and Mr. ROBINSON explained the diminution in the contribu- tions during the past year by the state of trade in the town, , and referred to the time when comverts from a mission sta- tion were brought over to England and exhibited before the people. In those times missionary meetings were scenes of great commotion. Perhaps it was desirable in those days, but Christian people now took a different view of the subject. Some years ago they did not know the world. It was a terra incognito. lately a great deal had been said in depreciation of the Foreign Missionary Society, ,but he asked what was the state of the country before the advent of the missionary society, and spoke of the numerous advantages which had accrued since missionaries bad learnt heathens to lead civilized lives.—The Rev. R. HARPER drew the attention of the audience to the fact that the Misslonary General 2ornmittee asked the Methodists of the country to bring up the annual subscriptions £20,000 ' higher than they were last year. That seemed a large sum, but it was not much when spread over all the congregations of the country. The income of Widnes circuit, last year, was £75, and he thought they ought to make it £lOO. Speaking of India, Mr. Harper said that country was 5,000 miles away from where he was standing, and had a popula- tion of 160,000,000-40 times as great as London. Fcr two centuries missionaries have laboured there, and they had been blessed with great success, although there had been immense difficulties in their way. The could not take the Gospel to the ladies of India, who were brought up pri- vately in great ignorance and superstition. Very few people knew how closely confined were the ladies of India. They were prisoners for life. They were not even permitted to walk in their own garden. The rooms in which they dwelt were miserably furnished. In that of a princess there was only a miserable sofa and a chair. They generally sat on the floor, and wore seven jewels in their ears. Their nose was pierced three times, they had six ornaments on the head, ornaments on the wrist, fingers, ankles, and toes, and a band of gold or silver or something pretty round the waist. Nobody saw these ornaments but their husbands. It was an utter impossibility for the missionaries to get into the society of these women, but a few ladies had started a society called the Auxiliary Society,- which was attached to the general society. These missionaries told them that they saw as many as 49 females in one establishment. Mr. Harper then , spoke of the difficulties caused by caste distinctions, described the state of the Hindoo widow,, and stated that a class met in the vestry at Widnes each Saturday to further the cause of the missions, and he hoped the members would be received with a smile when mothers were asked to allow their little girls to attend and assist in making clothing. , (Applause.)—The Rev. J. HOTTIERRALL spoke of his labours in India, when he said the missions had 302 ch ipels, 210 preaching places, 99 missionaries, 326 day school teachers, 2.70) Sabbath school teachers, 569 local preachers, 47,562 full and accredited church members. with 2,311 on trial. They had 276 Sabbath schools, and 28,000 scholars. They had 212 day schools, and 21,648 scholars, and it was cilculated Ciat 15,5,000 people heard the Gospel each Sunday. (Applause.)—The Rev. T. HOUSE, the deputation, then delivered an eloquent address on the spread and power of Christianity.—A collection was then made, and the meeting concluded with the usual votes of thanks.
DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MR. S. COLLIER, OF RUNCORN.

Mr. Samuel Collier, wholesa.le provision merchant, Run- corn, died at his residence, Church-street, on Friday night week last, and the town mourns the loss of one of its oldest public men. Born of a Lancashire family in the year 1811, in a village where the name of Primitive Methodism had left a strong impression, Mr. Collier was trained in that faith, and early showed an aptitude for preaching. When only 16 years of age he delivered a discourse in a Primitive Methodist Chapel, and, at the request of the Quarterly Board, he joined the staff of local preachers. A few years later he was admitted into the regular ministry. He often recalled with pleasure the fact that the first money he received for displaying his oratorical powers in the pulpit was at an Indep,mient Chapel, and he expended the gift in the purchase of a useful dictionary—an early sign of the wise discretion which marked his lata years. For several years he held his position of minister' and laboured in that capacity in Runcorn, but marrying, he resigned, and after- wards followel several occupations. In 1810 he commenced business as a grocer, in the shot) in Church-street which is now occupied by Mr. Thomas Leach, draper. His business aptitude and untiring energy were rewarded with abundant succs., which his enterprising spirit took the utmost advantage of. Purchasing a large plot of land from the late Mr. C. Hazlehurs', he erected the block of fine business premises in Church-street, known as Victoria Buildinga, and subsequently he acquired property in other parts of the town. The deceased gentleman occu- pied a very prominent public position. Oa the Ist April, 1857, he was el:cted a member of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners, and from that time up to the autumn of 1882 he continued to hold a seat at the Board. He then voluntarily retired in consequence of failing health. He was what may be termed an "independent member," and fearlessly expressed his opinions on all occasions. For 1 many years he was a valued member of the Board of Guar- dians, and he also held a seat on the Burial Board. In 1881 ' he was appointed chairman of the latter body, and the duties I rappertaining to the office were discharged with thorough impartiality. He tilled most of the offices in connection with the Wesleyan Methodist body in the to wn,.and was the oldest local preacher whose name appeared on the local plan. His discourses abounded in trenchant and original ut- terances, and were heartily enjoyed by the congregations he addressed. In politics Mr. Collier was a Liberal of a pro- nounced type. The deceased gentleman, who was 72 , ' years of age, was twice married, and leaves a numerous family of grown up sons and daughters. . One of his sons, Sir. S. F. Collier, is a Wesleyan minister ' with a rising reputation stationed at Twickenham, Mid- dlesex, in the Brentford circuit. On Sunday the Rev. E. J. Robinson, preaching to a large congregation at St. Paul's Chapel, referred in kindly terms to Mr. Collier's death. At au inquest on Wednesday morning, Mr. J. E. _rW_orsiev, the 1 deputy coroner, made a feeling reference to M . Collier's , i demise. The interment took place at the Cemetery at noon on Wednesday, the body being followed to the grave by a large number of public men and tradesmen. The funeral cortege, which consisted of a hearse, a carriage and three mourning coaches from Mr. S. Yarwood's establishment, left Ithe residence of the deceased a few minutes before noon. A : considerable number of people lined the streets to watch the mournful procession pass, and the windows of the shops and houses on the route were darkened. Preceding the hearse walked the following gentlemen, headed by Mr. J. Meadow- croft (chairman of the Board of Commissioners), and Mr. T. Norman, viz. :—Messrs. J. Dobson, W. Fisher, Joseph Williams, W. Whittaker, H. White, J. Pritchard, J. W. Lightburn, W. H. Linaker, W. Brookes, M. Barker, G. Moss, W. Handley, W. Sutton, T. Simister, R. Norman, G. Marshall, J. Ball, W. Spearing. B. Kinveton, S. Coventry. John Timperley, J. Heyes, W. Shaw, J. Bowyer, J. W. Woodland, G. Bellamy H. Randle, W. Kay, W. Croley, F. Fairhurst, i. Stringfellow, T. Poole, P. Harrop, T. Lydiate, and A. Sayles. Thu first carriage was occupied by the Revs. E. J. Robinson, George I Hack, S. Mees, and J. D. Thomas, and Dr. MacDougall ; Ist j mourning coach, Mrs. Collier (widow), Rev. S. F. Collier, I Mr. W. Collier (son), and Mr. R. W. Kettle (son-in-law, Southport) ; 2nd, Messrs. F. Bate (son-in-law), R. Collier (Runcorn), S. Collier, W. Collier, and J. Collier, all of Low- ton (brothers of the deceased); 3rd, Messrs. J. Gleaye (Middlewich), W. Littler, and W. Marsh (brothers-in-law), W. Parry (nephew), and W. Collier (cousin, of Helsby). The service in the church was conducted by the Revs. E. J. Robinson and G. Hack, prayer being offered by the Rev. J. ' D. Thomas. The two former clergymen also conducted the • burial ceremony at the grave side, where the body was borne I by Messrs. A. Savles, Hughes, T. Lydiate, and McKennan. • , gr. F. Fairhurst conducted the funeral arrangements.

SMALL-PDX IN RUNCORN. Two cises of small-pox have broken out in Duke's Field. / The disease is supposed to have been imported from Wid. _ Dr, Mouritz, the medical ofßcer of bealtb, has issued ,ing to the public, and advises that ail children under la2wyaera-rsf age shall be re-vaccinated.

div.head: G2i,riE AT RUNOORN.
div.p: THE G2i,riE AT RUNOORN.

DRO WIVF D. - --- Tuesday hare been excep great inten< The tides at RulAtco3rlnAlsssi-net, clonally high. On I'Vednesday n4,:ht a gale or sity was blowing up the river, anti t;"e water washed over che pier walls at Runcorn Docks. No si-bzn's Land WAS corn-, pletely submerged. About midnight a furicus wind rushed round Hale Head upon Westou Point, and the waves dashed violently over the pier. At this time the flat Succass, be- longing to the Cheshire Acnalgamated Salt Company, attempted to ewer the dock, and Edward Williams, a flat- man, of Barnton, jumped ashore to fix a roue. He informed the pierman of his intention, and immediately hrryras blown into the water and was not seen again. The body was re- covered from the Dock Basin on Thursday morning. Yesterday afternoon, Mr. J. E. Worsley, the deputy-coroner, held an inquest on the body at the Weaver Hotel, Weston Point, and a verdict of "Accidentally drowned" was re- turned. On Thursday the gale was still blowing, and at noon the tide reached a height of several feet above that recorded in the tide table. Hundreds of people assembled on both sides of the river to watch the advancing water. It was with great difficulty sailing flats succeeded in sailing under Runcorn Bridge, where the wind had almost the force of a hurricane.

div.head: RUNCOi,N RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCOi,N RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

An ordinary meeting of this anthority was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday afternoon. M. J. Ashton presided, and the other gentlemen present were the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner and J. L3ckwood ; Messrs Ilandley, Highfield, Rigby, H. Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk), and J. Farrington (surveyor).

div.head: MEDICLL OFFICER'S REPORTS.
div.p: MEDICLL OFFICER'S REPORTS.

Dr. BRIDE (medical officer) rep,ried-7 that during the quarter ending September 30th the Ristrar's returns ' showed there had been 154 births and 73 deaths in the four sub•districts comprised in the Union. Of the births, 80 were miles and 74 females, giving a birth-rate of SO per 1,000. Of the deaths, 39 were miles and 34 females, givinga death- rate of 3 8 per 1,000. In the corresponding quarter of last year there were 123 births and 67 deaths. Or the deaths in the present quarter 25 were under five years of age, 15 of these being uuder one wear, and 48 were five years of age and upwards.

div.head: HOTBED OF FEVER.
div.p: A HOTBED OF FEVER.

Dr. BRIDE, in a special report, sta•ed that he had to re- port the death from scarlatina dropsy of George William Shilland, at a cottage situate in Lunt's Row, Weston. This Leing the second death in the same cotge he must again remark upon the careless and uncleanljr-habits of the occu- piers of the cottages in this row, more particularly for the reason that scarlatina fever had infected' almost every cot- tage in it since June. The custom of "neighbouring" was an important factor in the spread of infectious diseases, and as the result of personal observation he was able to state that notwithstanding every eff.at to prevent it by advice and warnings this abominable habit had been largely in- dulged in at Lunt' s Row, Weston.—The usual instru:tions were given to the surveyor respecting the !natter. There was no other business-of public interest.

WIDNES SUNDAY SCHOOL UNION. The first annual tea party in connection with the Union of Nonconformist Sunday Schools in Widnes:took place in Lacey-street schoolroom on Tuesday evening. There was a large attendance, and the following Ladies presided:at the tea tables :—Mesdames Harper, Hothersall, B. Brown, Cozen, Coverley, Williams, Moore ; Misses Thomas, Barker, Pinches, and Wiles. Subsequently a public meeting was held, Mr. B. Brown, the president, occupying the chair. The room was well filled, and the following gentlemen occupied seats on the platform:—Revs. R. Harper, J. Hothersall, D. Davies, Messrs. R. Shaw, S. B. Stringer, E. Seddon, S. Drought, F. Lawrinson, T. Reay, T. Perry and T. J. Peters and Past (secretaries). A choir of 150 voices, assisted by a string band, sang during the evening a choice selection of music in admirable style. Mr. S. Lamb conducted, and Mr. J. Robinson was at the harmonium.

In the opening address the CHAIRMAN explained the aim of the Union, which was to make the schools mutually bene- ficial and useful, and to excite a deeper interest in the study of the Bible. He advocated a more dogmatical or doctrinal teaching of the Word of God, and an extended use of catechisms, on the ground that no relizious instruc- tion was given in the board schools to which the children of Nonconformists were compelled to attend as they had no denominational day schools. The committte of the Union were rather disappointed that so few scholars bad presented themselves for examination on certain parts of scripture, but they coped for better success next year. The Rev. R. HARPER delivered an address on the sys- tematic study of the Bible, and Mr. S-. B. STRINGER followed with a speech on the same subject. j In calling upon Mr. Robert Shaw to distribute , the prizes to the successful scholars, the CHAIR- -1 max congratulated him on being elected to servo ; the Nonconformists on the School Board for the Ifourth time, and observed that in various ways he had , always been found ready and willing to further the cause of ' education in the town. (Applause.) Mr. Straw said he looked-npon that meeting as one of the most important meetings that had ever been held in I Widnes—(hear, hear) —and went on to speak of the religous education 20 years ago. They had now arrived at a point when knowledge of the Word of God was to be put into its right place, and while he would not underrate in, any degree the prizes given in the town to successful students in I science and art, he was sure that they would agree with him that they met together that night for something far higher and nobler than that—(hear, hear)—because there could be no study to which young people could direct their thoughts and bg of such benefit to them as that of the Bible, which they had now commenced in connection with the union. He spoke of the educational advantages now offered to chil- dren in the day schools, and impressed upon parents the im- portance of sending their children to the Sunday schools, as their minds were stored with secular knowledge five days out of the week. Mr. Shaw then presented the priz?s as follows:

Senior Division (scholars over 16 but under 20) : Ist prize awarded to Wm J. Bagbridge, aged 16. Wei.h amgre2ations.l Chap.!. Middle Division (scholars over 12 bilt under 16) : Ist ptize awarded to John Reid, aged 12, Milton Cougreptional ; 2nd. Frederick W. Ooxon. aged 13, Hutchinson street Primi- tive Methodist Chapel. Junior Division (scholar,' under 12): Ist prize, Mabel Williamson, aged 11, Albert-road Wesleyan ; 2nd, Henry Mcßeth, aged 10, Hilton Congregs,:i•ual Thomas Arthur Moor, aged 10, Welsh Congregational. Junior certificates were awarded to Frederick Gui,e, of Milton Con- gregational School; Jessica Poulson, of Lacev-street Wesleyan I School; Ann Reid, of Milton Congregational School; Minnie Sadler, of Lacey-street Wesleyan School; and Wm. Teesdale, I of Milton Congregational School. I The Rev. J. Hothersall delivered an address on "The I Spirit of Obedience ;" after which IVar. PErwas moved a vote cf thanks to Mr. Shaw, to whose interest in secular I and religious education he made a complimentary allusion. Mr. F. Liwnitisos seconded the motion, which was carried by acclamation. In the course of his reply, Mr. &Law expressed his wil- i lingness to aid the Union pecuniarily if required. There I were something like 2,220 children in the Widnes Board schools, and they knew what they were capabl of laccomplishing, because they weie subjected every year to a very severe test by the Government Inspectors, and the Widnes children were among the first in the kingdom for ; the amount of grant earned per head. (Applause.) There- fore, seeing that there was a capacity for reaiving instruc- tion, he thought Sabbath-scnool teachers should be alive to , the fact that if they would only pour into these young 'spirits the truths of the Gospel, there would be accomplished Isuch a work as would astonish those who expected most. (A ppla use). On the proposition of the Roy. D. DATIES, seconded by iMr. FOGG, a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. S. Lamb, the ;conductor of the chair; and a similar acknowledgment was made to the trustees of the building for the use of the room, t: on the motion of Mr. Coxori, seconded by Mr. SEDDON. I A vote of thanks was passed to the Chairman, en the motion of Mr. STRINGER, and the meeting concluded.

CIIAPTEE XXVII.—LEFT Ano The utement 6-entleraan Jack disappeared the terrible inward conflict that had been kept under during thoTassage through the streets, broke out; and Stephen had an hour of such misery as be lead never before known or contemplated as possible. But as yet it was not the loss of his home on-the terror of the future he enie,he have to meet that lee thought of. His whole heart and •soui were engrossed with the remem- brance of the late scene with Miss Vandeleure and -of the ' probableconsequence--her marriage ere long with the Earl. He felt with remorse Low deadly was the ineultiif rightly perceived and felt, as -it evidently had been by her while the fact of her so receiving it, showed laireAto late be must have cruelly misjudged -her. Then her beauty, her-winnine•' manner, her grace alleer of person and sunny beightnets of mind seemed to come before his vision more vividly than ever, now that she was lost ; now that his own hehaviour had called -forth irresistible evidence of that quality ihe had so wench -donlete.;—a strength ,a 1 character., thatermner or later waneol redeem her from besetting faults. He tried to remetnber her faults, to reconcile himself to himself br again pia:wino her. behaviour to Lord Harlax- ton. "It wae unwomanly. It wee an act that might be the sore- runner in life of—." ffiut he stopped and tanned with dis- gust from his own thoughtsrard patiently strove to ferget them, and &7.4310te himself to the business of the hour, the consideration—what was he tode ? Then his aged and sad mother seemed for a few moments actually te stand before him, sa-eing nothing, butelookiag se piteously and reproachfaell.7,in his face, that te -escape it he began to walk rapidly to and fro in the room, to the groat wonderment of the bar cronies --helow, who were discussing his appearance, his portmanteau, hie object in ceining here, and, on the whole, getting decidedle- suspicious. Suddenly ties steps ceased:; Stepieen had broteeelet .hirazel: to by the words. "What's done is done. The .otly question LI OW is— What's to folloa-R What aic. Itodo ? Which means-- What can I do? A. narrowing of the question that should be satisfying, for .see but one thjr in all this world for which I am fit, and which Natere, in .:ler bounty, is quite ready to give mee—the inestimable carder of a private:sol- dier I "And can I herd with such men.? eienow no other nein- panious? Able neither to join in their habits of life, apart from the military rcutine of dutr, nor in their ways of thought—if they eve: do think. -..P.epelled ceaselessly leer their ccmpanionship, having nothing in common with them, and forbidden to keep apart by the penalty of their general dislike, and tae of the ,_ruore despicable among their number. "Well, If the life .does not leek attractive, choose another! "Fool! you knew vaguely before you eceentnitted your- self, theme. you would not then stop to think the matter out, you had no choice. You saw that plainly and only hesitated so long in your ,mouldering dissatisfaction with your home, yourself, and pretty well everything beside, be- cause the enth-vas so clear and humiliating. "This is idle talk. I have no choice! I have ;no friends te appeal to, and if I had; I -cculd not go to -them ..xithout suggesting all felts of mysteries, or giving explanations ,thee: are equally .eut of the question. " Is it not worth while to tern the shield and look at the other side? "Suppose I could bear all the jealousies of the barrack- room end its squalid life—the ham l occasional iabou ree-ebe routineof duty unettenled by a angle circumstance fiat can mate the private. look fore:aid to it with pleasure or

„eatisfacCon. "Suppose I could acts steer my.course between all !mar of possible outrages, while conqueri,rg all provocations te anger, and ;zever giving way so as tc bring down humiliat- ing or cruel punishments.; could I not then achieve my ovvn reward, and pass throug to a commission, then return to my home independent—cc longer ashawed of the wazte of life? .

"But make,ra) mistakes. Let me be sure I can do and bear all this: for if not the great humiliation of a return home would be the wiser courze. And le3fore I could do that, under present circumstances, I think a touch of my razor on my throat evould be on the whole peeferable. "Where now have I brought tnereelf—but tc this—l must go to a hard life, a bitter life for teeny months,at least, and yet I do not know but I may fail—and so come to the razor at last after so much added pain. "My past—it is no ute denying it—has been one of sheer indulgence. And yet I think to be a peiaate sol- dier !" "Hew I should have laughel any one of my former asso- ciates out of such a ridiculoue fancy ! Am I, then, com- pounded of better stuff than these other gilded youtLe-- myeelf having been foremost in all their follies, weaknesses, and !eve of habitually making things pleasaet—no mattes at whoze cost." "One only thing do I see—and surely that is the mad- dest thing in the way of temptation that ever mortal man devised for his own, or other people's solace. " But that Ido see. Once in,! must go on. What comes to be borne I must bear; for else I shall find something in- fiaitely wors3 in the b ickground. It may be only one of the delusions a man takes up when all others have flown, but I think I could fight my way through, if only I ceuld persuade myself to the trial. A queer weed to use, seeing that once I have made the plunge, judgment follows; and the sentence is—No retreat." lie stopped, appeeently without any decision but imme- diately took up his hat, went out, and took a cab to a street way, where he remembered to have seen on a book- seller'e stall a Feo9nel-hlnti, Army lelig fee the current This List he bought, then hurried back in the same cab and began to turn bick the pages to find out where Nis the bast place to enlist, if he should have courage and resolu- tion finally to decide on the serious step he meditated. This took a long time, for wherever he looked there turned up the name of some officer known to him, or that he might be known to; but at last he settled on the part relat- ing to the Curragh Camp, Ireland, for not one of the officers there mentioned could he recognise directly or indirectly. So far satisfied, he was going on, when suddenly he stopped the driver, and discharged him, causing the portmanteau to be put down on the pavement by his side. What could be the meaning of this movement? It was a bye-street he stood in, dark, without shops, and with no apparent building near that he could possibly want. But he had seen Gentleman Jack, at the moment the cab- man, with that love of short cuts that characteriserethe fra- ternity, had turned into this gloomy street. He hardly knew whether to laugh or be angry. How had the fellow managed to keep up with him? Then he remembered (here !lad been §CYeral delays on the road he had tiOt thonght 3f k the pre-becupation of his tnind. But where was he now? That question was soon answered. Gentleman Jack's vision dawned upon him by the aid of light from a window, advancing, cheerily humming a tune, perfectly unconscious, so it seemed, of Stephen's proximity, till they almost touc_hed. Then he started, looked at the portmanteau, and exclaimed in a tone of wonder, "Well, of all the coincidences I ever knew or heard of this is the most astonishing!" Stephen could not help laughing outright, at what he esteemed Jack's consummate 'impudence and consummate acting; who, however, left him no time for comment or in- terruption. "Cab broke down? Waiting for another P Oh, soon -find one. How lucky I came this way, but my lodging is in this neighbourhood. "My dear fellow, go to it. Its' a raw night. I envy you with a quiet fireside, and, perhaps, with a pleasant com- panion; I want no help, and since I must speak plainly I wish in the fullest sense and meaning of the words to be left alone! " The friendly tone of the beginning was succeeded by one so stern as he came to the end, that Gentleman Jack promptly succumbed to what he esteemed the mere humour of the moment, and said, "All right! I'm glad anyhow to be able once more to wish you good-bye. But don't be hard on poor Jack when at times you do think of him." "Trust me for that," said Stephen, as he again, with renewed friendliness, shook him by the hand; mad Gentle- man Jack went on his way, which naturally might be to his lodgings, but was certainly the direction in which Stephen wanted himself to go. Ile watched Gentleman Jack the entire length of the street, where he turned and disappeared. By this time an empty cab came up going the same way, but when Stephen had stopped it, thrown in his portmanteau, taken a last look down the street and saw no person whatever, then he caused the cabman to turn back for a considerable distance, and then, as if changing his mind, again turned, bet by quite a new route, into his first course, and drove rapidly to the London and North-Western Station. THE LA.NCASHIRE IRON AND ENGINEERING TRADES. The iron trade in the Manchester district keeps :above the actual level of depression, as occasional orders which come in give sufficient employment to neake;s to prevent them being absolwely under the necessity of forcing sales, but there is a general want of buoyancy in the market. The renewal of a few expiring contracts for pig iron at the close of the quarter bought buyers to a moderate extent into the market, and here and there makers who were getting some- what anxious for orders were able to fill up their books. The general inquiry le very small, and there is little doubt that if the market were really tested by the offer of any weight of business buyers would still be able to find weak points. Quoted rates for delivery equal to Manchester are firm at 45s 31 for forge and foundry Lancashire, 44s 61 to 443 101 for forge, and 45s 61 to 45s 101 for forge Lincolnshire lees 2'; as the minimum, but very little business is being done at these figures, and very low sales of Scotch iron are reported, which is certainly not a healthy sip. Manufactured iron makers are kept going on present busauees, and for prompt specification] buyers have to pay the full rates of £b' 2s 61 to £6 53 fer bars, £6 12s 61 to £6 153 for hoops, and £3 to £3 5s for sheets ilelivered into the Manchester district. There is no pressure on the part of buyers, and the weight of forward business offering is very limited. In the engineering trade there is a continued unmistakable quietening down, and the rapid slipping away of Hee recent activity in shipbuilding does not improve prospects for the future. Heavy tool makers are still fairly off for work, and locomotive builders e3ntinue very busy on old contracts, but these are not at pre- sent being replaced. Small stationary engine builders ate but indifferently employed, and the same may be said generally of ths machine trade. In the coal trade bueiness has quietened down considerably during the present month. The supplies now offering in the market are in excess of re- quirement?, and prices if anything easier, although not quotably lower. Comparatively very little actual change in the industrial coalition of the ceuntry, so far as the engineering trades are concerned, is shown in the returns for the past month received from the various districts of the trades' union societies connected with the above branch of industry ; but from the point of view as indicating any recovery from the decreasing activity which has recently been recorded they are mot encouraging as to ;ley prospects of an improvement in trade. With the exception of several important districts affected by wages disputes, the returns sent in to the Amal- gamated Society of Engineers report employment generally as still fairly goof. and the number of members receiving out-of-work suppert is practic ally the same as last menth*, what little variation there is being in the direcion of a slight decrease, if anything. The secretary of the Steam Engine Makers' Seciety reports that no improvement has taken pl ice since last inenth, but that in some cases the reports sent in are of a more despondent nature; the number of unemployed had not increased to any large extent, but the list was far heavier than they carol to see.

He reviewed the old state of things before the country was conquered, but solely to show how the people had a positive share and right in the laud; in order to point the moral that England in using her conquest for the purpose of establishing her own land laws, which took away the people's right, had made herself responsible for the misery and disaffection that ensued, and which nothing but a re- versil of such policy could possibly remove. At the Cheshire Quarter sessions, on Tuesday, Eliz tbeth ,Brazendale, F.. 3, fustian cutter, was sentenced to o no month's imprisonment for breaking into the dwelling-house of Wm. A FUSTIAN CUTTING CUSToll.—Yesterilty, at Lyturn Petty sessions, Frederick Danby, of Gyrnm, was summoned for unlawfully leaving his work, by which his master, Matthew Woodhead, had sustained damages to the amount of £1 128. Bd.—The complainant stated that on the 16th September, he paid the defendant .£1 4s. Bd. in advance for two "pieces." From that day the defendant was absent from his work four wc2ks, and the complainant claimed 2s. per week for the loss of the use of his frame. Ihe de- fendant. after receiving the money, spent a fortnight drink- ing, and then went to work at the Spread Eagle, but had since returned to his own employment. The defendant could have finished the work in seven days. Paving wages in advance was a custom in the fustian trade.—As the defendant promised to finish the work the case was dis- missed.

ASSAULT ON A WOMAN AT LYMM. Joseph Hurst, of Lymm, was charged, on a warrant, at Lymm Petty Sessions, yesterday, with assaulting Hannah Marsden wife of Joe Marsden, Sandy-lane.—The prosecutrix stated that about four o'clock on the afternoon of the 9th inst. she hid occa- sion to go into an open space behind her house. The prisoner, who was there, fighting with some men, began to use very abusive language to her, calling her foul names. He said it was jut her that he wanted, and he then dealt her a blow en the side of the face. Before she hal time to recover, he struck her again, but his wife then interposed and prevented him from using further violenca. Her face was black for several days. She did not use any provocation, but about three and a half years since she charged him at linutsford Sessions with attempt- ing to c..m.nit a criminal assault on her. The prisoner was under the influence of drink.—Tt3e prisoner said that he was having " a little bother with to men, one of whom was the prosecutrix's brother, and the prosecutrix came up and put herself in the way, and he struck her."—The prisoner was ordered to pay 103 and costs, in all .£1 103. 61., and to be bound over to keep the peace fowards the prosecutrix.
