SCHOOL BOARD.—The monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Board School, on Tuesday evening. Pre- sent: The Rev. T. P. Kirkman (chairman and clerk), and Messrs. James Hatton. Lewis Birchall, Richard Turner, and Alfred Dixon (school attendance officer).—The At- tendance officer presented his monthly report, which stated that he had visited the various schools in the dis- trict during the month, when he found that 37 children had been away sick, and that most of the children whose parents were warned last month were now attending school more regularly. H,3 also stated that he had served one notice for children to attend school, and warned several parents that unless their children attend school more regularly they would he samononA to appear before the Board. Ho als3 'reported that he had summoned three parents before the magistrates (as instructed at the last Board meeting), viz. : Mary Monks, James Hatton (Hermitage Green), aad Thos. Dickenson, all of Croft ; the cases being heard at the War- rington Petty Sessions. on the 3rd inst., when each of the defendants was fined 5s including costs.—The report having been adopted, it was unanimously resolved that a precept be made on the overseers of the township for the sum of £3O, to meet the expenses incurred during the half-year ending the 25th March next. Several accounts having been passe-I, the proceedings terminated. STRETTON.

THE Pentstr Cuunca.—Harvest thanksgiving services were held here on Sunday. The work of decoration was carried out by a number o! ladies and gentlemen, who appear to have apportioned it among themselves; but though thus, as it were, executed in sections, it formed a most harmonious whole. The screen was the work of Mrs. Dodd, and in its ;id)rnment wheat, oats, barley, fruits, flowers, &c., were tastefully employed. The pulpit and font were entrusted to Mrs. Charles ‘Vhitley, while Mr. Whitley had the east end and the altar under his charge. The lectern fell to the lot of Miss Downing. Besides these notable portions of the building, there were the chancel arch, I ha walls, and the side windows, and in the ornamentation of these, as well as in other particulars, hearty assistance was rendered by Mr. and Mrs. Kerr, Mr. John Bennt.tt, and others. Flowers and fruit for the purposes of the decoratio4s were given by Mr. T. H. Lyon, Appleton Hall ; Mr. J. Marson, Prospect Hill ; tbe Vicar (Canon Dodd), and others. The vegetables, fruit, &c., which adorned the side windows were the gift of the farmers and cottagers. The sermon in the morning was preached by the Vicar (Rev. Canon Dodd), and in the even- ing by the Rev. T. P. Williamson, Vicar of Thelwall. The offertories amounted to £22 43. Mr. T. M. Pattison presided at the organ and the choir acquitted themselves creditably. - WARBURTON.

AN AWKWARD LODGER.—On Saturday. at the Al trincham Police Court, Ann Sullivan was brought up in custody, charged with being drunk, and breaking windows, the pro- perty of Joseph Higginson. at Warburton.—Prosecutor, a farm labourer, stated that when he got home on Friday night, his wife said that Sullivan had been calling her names. He gave her a week's notice, and she com,nenced blackguarding him. He put her out of the house, and then she broke the windows.—His wife corroborated this.—De- fendant denied having used bad language, and Mrs. Thomas, wife of the foreman at the new church at Warburton, informed the Bench that the defendant was very badly treatel by her husb ind, as well as the other people in the house.—The officer in eaartze of the else said the woman was not drunk, but had had drink.—The Bench said they could not deal with such a case, and discharged the prisoner.

div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

SUBSIDENCE. Daring the week the work of raising Christ Church, Winsford (Weaver Church), his been going on once more. It had got cut of the level nearly a foot. The east end having a tendency te, bow down, has, by the liberal use of jicks, to be r,stored to its normal condition, or rather its upright state. The picture of desolation witnessed when it had to be taken down is no longer to be dreaded, as a few hours and as many nun can soon rectify its abnormal tendency. BRINE SUPPLY.—TIie supply of brine continues yet very far below the requirements of the trade. The only firm which seems to have a good supply is Stubbs Brothers, of the Nitional Works. Their supply, if not inexhaustible, is far beyond the rest, as their shaft seems to be deeper; but the reservoir under the afore-mentioned works, which was formerly one,of the rock-salt mines of the district, is now. and has long been, tilled with the best brine. The other 'firms are sinking their shafts deeper.

LIBRRAL Cucs.—The advertenca a few weeks ago to the formation of a Liberal Club was followed on Friday last by still more active steps, by which sach a body as the Liberals at Winsford will b 3 more fully consolidated and augmented, and the principles of progress in which they believe be more ardently carried out and more widely disseminated. On the motion of Mr. Robert Verdin, J.P., Mr. John Buckley took the chair; and after all the needful arrangements for furniture, billiard-table, &c., had been >.nide, members were elected, and a committee of manage- ment formed. Mr. Joseph Slater, Mayor of Over, was elected first president; :Messrs. Buckl-y, Robert Stubbs, Holland, John Stubbs, J. Bradbury, William Dagnam, and Thomas Johnson, were elected vice-presidents. Mr. Reuben Stubbs was :nade treasurer, with the Union Bank as bankers. Mr. Tolfree WAS chosen secretary; and the formal opening will soon be effected.

ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS. INCREASE OF ASSESSMENTS IN CIIESHIRE.—TiIO Assess- ment Committee of the Northwick Union district have been re-valuing the public buildings and works in the neighbour- hood of Northwich, Winsford, and Middlewich, for poor. rate purposes. The Northwich gas works have been raised from £265 to £1,150, Winsford gas works from .£lOO to £69, and Middlewich from £lOO to £2lB. The committee have also raised the assessment of the Northwich water works from £lB5 to .£548. The Winsford water works, which belong to the local authorities, had net until recently teen assessed. For rateable purposes they ha',•o now been assessed at £270.

Thelwall Haves, Warrington: Mr. Fredk. Rigby, Wavendale, Frodsham ; Mr. Thomas Beeley, Dun- kinfield ; Mr. Arthur Palmer Aspland, Werneth Lodge. Gee Cross, Manchester; Mr. William Mark Ashton, Ford Bank, Didsbury ; Mr. Robert Verdin, The Brockhurst, Northwich ; Mr. Delves Louis Broughton, Doddington Park, Nantwich ; Mr. William Young Craig, Alsiger ; Mr. Gabriel Looker Davies, Old Hall, Helsby Mr. James Handley-, Weston, Runcorn; Mr. Edward Rose: Marple; Mr. James Leigh, Brinnington, Stockport; and Mr. David Duncan, Gayton Hall, Neston. CHESTER GREAT CHEESE FAIR.—The great cheese fair of the year was held in connection with the dairy show at the Linen Hall, on Wednesday. There was a pitch of quite 70 tons of cheese in the fair, and about 80 tons in the show yard. There was a very large attendance of buyers from London, Liverpool, Manchester, Leeds, Birmingbam, Brad- ford, Sheffield, Leiceeter, Carlisle, Wolverhampton, Hanley, and Crewe. There was the keenest competition to obtain the exquisite dairies of cheese which had taken prizes in the show, and some of these passed hands more than once. Mr. Erown's dairy, which took the prize for the best in the yard, w2s sold by the owner for 87s per cwt., and was immedi- ately sold again for 883. A second prize dairy realised 85s per ewt. Tne prize cheese, made at the Duke of West- minster's factories at Aldford and Balderton, realised 70s per cwt. It is unusual for a faotory-made cheese to sell for as much money as home-made. In the fair there was the keenest competition, and erery dairy had been sold out at noon; the better class dairies at an enhanced price of quite 3s per ewt. over that current last fair. Quotations :—Ex- tra fine dairies, 72s 6.1; fine, 65s to 70s; medium, 55s to 655; and inferior to middling, 45s to 50s.

div.head: CHESHIRE DAIRY FARMERS' ASSOCIATION.
div.p: CHESHIRE DAIRY FARMERS' ASSOCIATION.

The annual exhibition of the Cheshire Dairy Farmers' Association was held on Tuesday in the Linen Hall, Chester. The exhibition was inaugurated last year under the patron- age of the Duke of Westminster, as president, and has been a thorough success. The object of the Association was, by offering prizes, to bring the fine cheese makers together in competition at an annual dairy show. The Association also keeps a keen eye, through its Standing Committee, upon all matters affecting transit and sale of all kinds of dairy pro- duce, the collecting and giving information thereupon, and devising means for its more effectual distribution. The show was in every sense a succss. The entries in the half- dozea classes for cheese numbered 94, against 72 last year, and in the classes for cheese 65, against 51. There was a keen competitioa in class 1, for the best 20 cheeses of not less than 10 cwt., owned and exhibited by any dairy farmer within the Association's district. The first prize was taken by Mr. W. Brown, of Handley. He also t)ok the first prize of 12 offered by the Cheshire Lend Agents' Association for the best dairy of cheese in the county, and also prizes for the beat lot of cheese in the fair, and for the best twenty cheeses in the fair. One of the prize cheeses was afterwards cut up and dis- tributed. and was pronounced to be of perfect flavour and quality. The Duke of Westminster's factories at Balderton and Aldford took the first and second prizes respectively in the class open to factory cheese made in the United King- dom. The competition in class 5, and the cheese exhibited therein demands no special notice. Mr. Pym well woa the honours. The entries in class six were not numerous, but the flavour of the cheese was exquisite. Mr. Bate, of Duddon, Tarporley, took the prize of a offered by the Cheshire Land Agents' Association. This Association offered prizes amount'ng t) £2O for the best average dairies of cheese. The judges were required to visit the dairies and judge the cheese at house. The butter classes were well title!, and the produce pronounced excellent.
THE LO WTON 11.IURD RR. THE PRISONER BEFORE THE MAGISTRNTES

On Wednesday, John Gibbon was brought before the magistrates at Leigh on a charge of murdering his uncle, Joshua Rigby, at Cheethatn's Fold Farm, Lowton, during the night of the 17th or morning of the 18th of September. —Mr. W. Cobbett appeared to prosecute ; Mr. Richardson defended the prisoner. Mr. Cobbett said the evidence to be adduced was mainly ; circumstantial, but he thought after hearing witnesses the magistrates would consider it to be their duty to send the case for trial. Prisoner and his wife had lived with the de- ceased since May. Up to that time Joshua Rigby, another nephew of the deceased; and a sister of the deceased, lived with him. Old Joshua did not seem to be an amiable man. It was alleged that he struck his sister, in con- sequence of which she and young Joshu I left his house. There was some talk of his being arrested for the assault on his sister, and atethis time he made his will under somewhat remarkable circumstances. On the 2nd of June prisoner c tiled upon Mr. Page. schoolmaster, and stated that his uncle wished to make his will. When Mr. Page went to the farm deceased gave hie own account of the quarrel with his sister, and nephew, Joshua Rigby, and prisoner on being aopealed to, stid his uncle's state- ment, was correct. During the conversation prisoner left the room for about ten minutes, and on his re!uro, having noticed some hesitation on the part of the d.ceetsed. he said he had just heard that they (meaning deceased's other rela- tives) were sending for a constable to arrest him. Mr. Cobbett asked the Bench to draw the inference (het prisoner, having been taken into favour by the old man, vouched for the statements he had made with a view to get him out of a scrape, and the old man's apprehensions having been ! acted upon, he made the will in prisoner's favour. The property appeared to be worth about VOO. Between that time and the Saturday or Sunday before the murder nothing unusual seemed to have taken place. His will was made in favour of the prisoner under circum- stances of pressure. Prisoner had nothing to gain by the will, but if the old man had changed his mind and made another, prisoner's interests would have been seriously in- jured, and if any quarrel took place between prisoner and deceased or prisonees relatives and deceased an alteration of the will was imminent. In putting the will into his pocket deceased made a remark that he might alter it, but he would see how they (his relatives) went on. Prisoner was therefore not altogether safe in considering himself the old man's legatee. On the Saturday or Sunday before the murder a quarrel took place between the old man and pri- soner's wife. It did not seem a quarrel of much consequence, but an undoubted rupture of some kind took place. I They had no very definite and certain evidence as to the nature of the quarrel, and prisoner's wife could not be celled. About seven o'clock in the evefiing of Mon- day prisoner's wife left the farm and went to her father's house and informed them of her intention to stay during that night. That same night deceased appeared to be in his usual health. He seemed to have gone to the Jolly C trter, where he had a little drink. He left the public- about 10-30 and went home. Prisoner stated that this was the hour his uncle arrived. About that time prisoner made 'his appearance at his father-in-law's house. They were all in bed, but prisoner's wife and mother-in-law got up and went down stairs. A conversation ensued, of which practi- cally the prosecution could not get particulars from Mrs. Bent, except that Mrs. Gibbon complained of ill-usage from the deceased. Prisoner remained until midnight, and then went back to the farm, and he remained there until the fol- lowing morning, when the murder was discovered. It was upon evidence on prisoner's own admission that during that night no persons occupied the farmhouse except the de- ceased and the prisoner. About 4-20 on the morning ef Tues- day, Sep. 18, a man with a cut saw a light burning steadily in the kitchen or houseplace, showing that some person was tip and about the house. Prisoner, on his own statement, got up at five and went about his work in the ordinary way. This was important. Prisoner occupied the front bedroom, and there being no doer to the room of the deceased he must have discovered the condition of the old man, if he had not known before, when he got up at five o'clock, the two door- ways being exactly opposite each other. Prisoner called at his father-in-law's house for a cup of tea at 5-45, stating that he had a headache. There were 11 injuries n the body of the deceased, and the throat, according to the medical evidence, had been cut after death. Some of the injuries on the body were of the same shape, and he thought it would be pretty clearly established that some of those wounds corresponded with the shape of the nails on the toes of the prisoner's boots. Though prisoner had made a state- in(•nt that he had very little money on him, when searched he had over LIO on him, and had possession of the will of the deceased, bankbook, and other papers. Some evidence was called, and the hearing was further adjourned until this day week.

SMALLPDX AT WIDNES. Mr. HARTLEY said he had received a further cornrnonitir Lion from Mr. Allen, clerk to the Widnes Local Board, regard to the admission of small-pox patients into thy Workhouse Hospital. Mr. Allen now asked that the Guar: dians should admit into the Workhouse Hospital a P‘t %victim named Cook, who was suffering from a severe eta" of small-pox. He (Mr. Allen) thought the Guardiane ought to receive this patient as a pauper, but if not he haf; no doubt the Local Board could arrange to make a snaa" payment to the Guardians on her account. Mr. Hartlei read a long letter which he had written to Mr. Allen el" plaining the position of the Guardians with regard to the question. In reply to this letter, Mr. Allen wrote that be did not consider the difficulties were raised by the Guar; dians, but by the Local Government Board.—Mr. HARTIns said lie had been afraid the Widnes Local Beard were under the misapprehension that the Gu„rdians were throwing difficulties in the way.—Mr. CHAMBERS: Yet they continue to write to us.—Mr. HARTLEY said he believed the Board were in pressing difficulties at present with regard to the small-pox.—Mr. FINEGAN was sorry to say there had been nothing done at Widnes yet to provide for the present epidemic. There had been many mettinge of the Local Board, and a site had been thought about, tint the Board had now another scheme in hand. He 01,r' Finegan) was in a position to say that this week they lar had three or four fresh cases of small-pox ; and although be was a representative for Widnes he must say that he thouga' the authorities there were not without blame in the matter. They had, he believed, at present a scheme in hand for bar ing a tent and erecting it in a glass yard, but as yet there was really nothing done, although the epidemic was spread' ing. lie himself rather agreed with Mr. Hartley in his stir' gestion that a general hospital should be erected at the worlv house.—Mr. NEWSOME said considering the very dangerone state of things at Widnes they ought to make an exception of the present cases, and adm t some of them into the work" hence infectious hospital. The hospital was at present empty, and if the epidemic were to spread he thought the Guardians would be somewhat to blame, though he would not say culpably. He considered they ought to stretch a little to stop the spreading of the infection.—The Citaineati, said that although he looked upon the cases as very hara ones, yet he did not see why they should alter the decision they had already arrived at. The cases were now in Widnes, but they did not know but what there might be a similar outbreak in other places, and if the, forced the authorities at Widnes to provide a hospital aS soon as possible other Boards would see that they must aleo provide for themselves.—Mr. NEwsomE : In the meantitne these unfortunate people are dying of this disease.-141:' HALL said the subject had been ventilated several tireo, before the Board, and it had been proved that th-lives es five paupers had been lost through admitting small-polr patients HAIG the hospital at a time when they were PI getting better. He thought it was unfair that the Loca, Board of Widnes should call upon the Guardians to taßie their places in providing hospital accommodation. He sail' they bad not room in the hospital to admit these patiente from Widnes.—Mr. NEWSOME said Mr. Hartley had just re' ported that there were only throe cases in the hospital. Lle thought it would be cruelty to leave the p. or people to be neglected.—The CHAIRMAN said it might be very bard at , present, but he would be very sorry to see the IVorknooSe ! hospital in the deplorable condition it was a, few months ago, when there was no doubt that several deaths occurred through the introduction of small-pc:Or patien's.— Mr. FIDLER said that in the face of the decision, of the Local Government Board, the Guardians could tin nothing towards admitting non-pauper patients into 01 Workhouse hospital. It behoved the Widnes Local BOO' ' to show inure energy in providing a hospital of their own,'" Mr. LEATHEntiennow asked, if the epidemic should splead, had they, as sinitary authority, made any provision 10, meet hit—Mr. HARTLEY SAM that was a matter for the Rural , Sanitary Atulioritv.—Mr. MEADOWS said there were plentY of empty houses in Widnes, and the Local Boird might take one or two for a hospital, and disinfect them after' wards. Mr. HARTLEY thought it was unfair to the Gag' dians that that matter should be brought up fortnight after fortnight. They had given the Widnes Locil Board an exhaustive answer, and they ought not to be troubled svirli it any more. Mr. HALL moved that non-pauper C-1.5e..9 not admitted into the workhouse. Mr. JACKSON seronde“ this motion, which ,was a;iii st un ininioasly carried.

LADIES' MECHANICAL TALK.—Mr. Hue, I think it is, tells us some very good stories about the way in two Chinese gentlemen contrive to keep up a long 14'rt, without saying a word which has any meaning in Something like this is occasionally heard on this side ve the Great Wall. The best Chinese talkers I know are 003, pretty women whom I meet from time to time. Pleasa" airy, complimentary, the little flakes of flattery glinoie; ing in their talk like the bits of gold-leaf in eau-dc-ri€ Dantzio • their accents flowing on in a soft ripple—never s wave, and never a cairn; words nicely fitted, but never .% coloured phrase or a high-flavoured epithet; they turn 118 into syllables so gracefully, that we find meaning for music they make as we find faces in the coals and fa_il palaces in the clouds. There is -something very though, about this mechanical talk. You have Emnetieu; been in a train on the railroad when the engine was tached a long way from the station you were approachillbro Well, you have noticed how quietly and rapidly the kept on, just as if the locomotive were drawing them. deed, you would not have suspected that you were tral'„e ling on the strength of a dead fact, if you had not seen ta engine running away from you on a side-track. thlon_ns conscience, I "believe some of these pretty women their minds entirely, sometimes, from their talk—,n(3,lg:Tef is more, that we never know the difference. Thefr off the fluty syllables just as their fingers would sPr“!.74 the music-drops from their pianos; unconscious habit VI/ the phrase of thought into words just as it does' tl.ta% music into notes. Well, they govern the world for all —these sweet-lipped women,—because beauty is the iroi, of a larger fact than wisdom.-0. Wendell Holmes 'in' Professor at the Breakfast Table."

r.vrvoN V. SALFORD (2nd team).—These teams met on the ground of the latter for the first time, and after a pleasant and fast game ended in a draw, each side scoring three minor Paints. ST. HELEstcs V. VULCAN.—PIayed at St. Helens, and after a hard-fought game the "Saints" won by owe goal, two tries, and four minor points to one try and four minor points. Parr seared the tries for the home team. NEseToss v. LEIRII (A Teams).—Pfaved on the grqund of the latter on Saturday, and after a capital and even game resulted in a victory for the home team by two goals, one try, and two rhinos points, to Newton one goal, two tries, and six minor , Points. ST. ELPH/N'S V. OUGHTRINGTON.—A. match between the above clubs was played at Oughtrington on Saturday, and re- sulted in a victory for the visitors by one goal (dropped by Relshaw), two tries (Lawless and Molyneaux), and three minor Paints, to Ougntrington two minor points. ALTarrestam V. BIRCH (a team).—This match was played on the ground of the former on Ssturday, and resulted as follows: —Altrinolaam one goal and one minor point; (Arch one try and • one minor point. 'the goal for Altrincham was kicked by U. Smith, from try by J. Harrison, sad the try for Birch was Obtained by S Hamnett; Thorley failing to kick a goal. WARRINGTON WANDERERS (2ND) V. RUNCJRN The match between the above teams took place on the ground Of the former, and a well-contested game resulted in a victory for the home team. Both sides playei in a vigorous manner, but nothing of note took place daring the game, except that the home team forwards shswed a considerable improvelnent O n the previous Saturday's performance. The Wanderers WOO by one goal, two tries, and six minors, to one goal and one minor. RH:scores V. WALVDEN (2ND TEssts).—Played at Walkden on Saturday. and after a pleasant and wed-contested game ended in a draw slightly in favour of the home teams Score— Walkden, four minor points; Runcorn. nil. Teatns—Runcorn : %rods, back; Jones, Riley, and Howard, three-quarter backs; Stubbs and Speakman, half-backs; Dunbavand (captain), Bur- rows, °rale, Cox, Janion, Mullaney, Antrobus, Ford, Clarke, and Banner, forwards. Walkden: J. Yatei, back: Jones. ' Grnmiy, and Hurst, three-quarter backs; Lane and T. Yates, ha;.-saeks ; W. Yates (captain), Shepperd, Green, Cook, As'oe, W. H. Hayes, Leach, J. Hayes, Jackson, and Howell, forwards. WIDNES RECREATION V. NEw SPRINGS (ASPULL).—On Saturday last the New Springs Club met towether for the leeona time thas season, and with a mi2ced first and second team journeyed to Widnes to meet the Recreation Cie) of that town. A very fat and pleasant game was played, victory in the end resting will the home team, who secured a try, but it was not improved upon The home team playe an excellent Combined game throughout whilst for the visitors Roberts, Law- °n, and Silcack were c nsricious. Roberts gaining the applause of both spectators and players alike for his efforts to cc ire. On the conclusion of the game the New Springs team sat down to an excellent tea, which had been kindly provided by the home t 'am. Score :—Welses, one try six minor points; New Springs, one touchdown. THE LANCASHIRE FOOTBALL UNION.—A meeting of the Lancashire Rugby Union took place at the Albion Hotel, Man- chester. on Wednesday evening, Mr J M•Laren presiding. The following clubs were represented :—Manchester, Preston. Old- ham, Walton, Werneth. Brougiston, Broughton Rangers, Salford, Bolton, Free Wanderers, Swinton, Cheetham, Chest- ham Hill, Rochdale Hornets, Widnes, and Royton. The busi- ness of the evening consisted principally of the election of ()Filters for the ensuing season. The following were chosen : President. Mr James M•Laren; vice-presidents, Mr E Rowley and Mr W Brierley ; hon. secretary and treasurer, Mr J H Payne. Committee—Messrs W E Openshaw (Manchester), F M Hull (Liverpool), F A Groves (Swinton). T Deane (Brough- ton Hangers), A Herrington (Walt)n), A Hillkirk (Free Wan- derers), R H Selby (Oldham), E Healey (Roehdale Hornets), W Hunt (Preston), and Jif Kevan (Bolton). LATCHFORD (A ThAM) V. RUNCORN TAM O'SHANTERS.—The Latchford Football Club reayed the second match of the season On Saturday, their opponents being the Ituucorn Tarn O'Shan-* ters. Immediately alter the k'ck-off the home team began to shaw their superiority, the ball being permed in lips visitors' quarters during the whole of the first half. The Latchfordltes, consequently, were not slow in availing themselves of this op- Pnrtunity, and at the call of time had scored three tries and six touehdowns t 2 the visitors' nil. After changing ends, the Visitors tried hard to equalize matters. Thy. however, lacked the dash of the home team's backs and forwards, and again had to assume the detensive. Notwithstanding all their efforts, they esuld not stall off the rushes brought to bear on their territory, and the home team, playing in splendid style, added four tries and nine mince points to their previous score. At the call of no-side, the game stood as follows—Latchford, one goal, six tries, twelve touchdowns, and three (Pad balls to nil, the tries being got by Burgess, Cannon, Acton, Sudlow, Jones, and Hilgarry. The last try (tsqiicii was got by Cannon list before the ca.l of time) was converted into a neat goal by Acton. EARLESTOWN (2nd) V. ADLINGTON (2nd) —A match between the second elevens of the Earlestown and Adlington clubs was Played on the ground of the former on Saturday last, in the Presence of a large number of spectators. The home team won the toss, and cho Ise to play with the wind in their favour dur- ing the first half. Taylor kicked off for the visitors, but not Many minutes had elapsed before Helcroft cc red the first goal for Earlestown. Up to half-time the play was all In favaur of the Earlestonians. who were frequently applauded for their good and accurate passing, James adding two more goals. On the Change of ends, the Adlingtonians created considerable interest by securing the dowafall of the home fortress, Monks sending the leather through the uprights. The home team afterwards severely pressed their opponents, and at the call of time the aeore was—Ea, lestown five goals, Adlington One. The teams were—Earlestown : 0 Birknead. goal; T Champion and J Gray backs; G 0 Roberts and 1.1 Silver half-backs; J Greenand Holcroft right wing; J James and W Cameron centre; J Cameron and W Whittle, left wing; T Whittle, umpire. Ad- iington : 11 Smith, goal; Brogden and Gent, backs; Makin- son, Mullineassx and J Whittle (sub.), half-backs; A Gray (sub ) and Harper, right wing; .1 Taylor, centre; Monks and Lighthouse, left wing. ItexcoHN V. Waiiinest.—An et enly-c3ntested match between these clubs was played at Runcorn on Saturday, about 600 spectators being present. Yates kicked off for Walkden, and the ball was returned by a fine run. Harper passed to Grundy, who ran the ball in touch in the Runcorn 25. W. Hughes re- lieved the pressure, punting into centre field, when Andrews Put in a dodgy run to the goal line. Within a few minutes of half-time, W. Hughes got possession, and neatly dripped the ball over the crossbar amid tremendous cheering. On the Change of ends, Dean started the ball, but Owen returned It well in touch. From a scrimmage Marsh got possession and made a fine run to the Runcorn line, when he most unselfishly Passed to his captain, Owen, who ran behind the posts, Yates kicking the goal. On hostilities being resumed, the ball was kicked over the Walkden line., and Wilkinson following up aimed a try, which was disputed on the plea that the ball, having passed over 15 yards beyond the line, was dead. Lewis took tare place, but no goal resulted. When "no side" was called the score stood—Run .orn, one goal, one disputed try, and three minor points, to Walkden one goal and one minor 'Point. The teams were—Runcorn: Wainwright, full back; Broady and W. Hughes, three-quarters; H. Hughes (captain) and Andrews. half-backs ; Lewis, Cox. Wright, Clark, Galley, Mason, Dean, Barnes, R iberts, and Wilkinson, forwards. Walkden: Prescott, full back; Grundy, Marsh, and Yates, three-quarters ' • Owen and Harper, half-backs; Barnes. Jones, Kay,Rusidon, Miller. Aidred, Welsby, Gardner, and llrmson, ferwards. EARLESTOWN ASSOCIATION V. ADLINGTON.—The Earlestown first team journeyed to Adlington on Saturday afternown last, and met the first team of the Adlington club on their ground. There was a considerable number of spectators who manifested the greatest interest in the game, which was well contested throughout though the play was considerably in favour of the Adlington eleven. The visitors won the to s, and in the first half had the advantage of a strong wind, whieh blew almost from goal to goal. For some time after the game had been ''intnenced the play was of a very even character. but after about a quarter of an hour's play an exciting scrimmage occurred pear to the A dlington goal, and Ogden sent the leather through, drawing first blood for Earlestown. No sooner was the _ill again in motion than the home forwards dashed in front of 6 Earlestown uprights. and Emmett by a mis-kick sent the 4bather between the score thenceforth standing at one goal l'ach• Up to the change of ends both teams strove hard to secure an additional point, but half-time wascalled before either enuld do so. Ten minutes after the recommencement of the rme, the home team secured a corner kick, and the Earles- „ goal-keeper in knocking the leather back acsidentally put th iscr, rough the uprights, and Adlington were thus awarded a eond goal. A short time afterwards the home team put on a tplerniid spurt, and finished by scaring a capital goal. The tarie(t wu pioyers once or twice endangered the home goal.

-- -- THE COMING K_.—Cammack.—Ad. The Primate, on Thursday, consecrated the Rev. A. W. Poole to the Bishopic of Japan. The ceremony took place in Lambeth Palace Chapel, and amongst those present were the Japanese Ambassador, his wife, and suite. The body of Mr. Henry Herbert Speight, who, with an engineer named James Marler, was drowned a fortnight ago through the capsizing of a boat in the river Onse, was re- covered en Thursday at Swinefleet, near Goole. A spinning mill at Waterhead, near Ohlharn, was des- troyed by fire on Thursday night, the damage being est 3. mated at £B,OOO. A temperance hotel at Lindley Moor, Huddersfied, was also burnt to the ground on Thursday, in- volving a partially covered loss of £1,500. GOOD TEMPLARS' ENTERTAINMENT AT EARLESTOWN.-- There was a very good attendance at the weekly meeting of the members of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars, held in the Lodge-room, Bridge-street, on Monday evening. Brother Henry Warburton, W.C.T , occupied the chair. Two new members were initiated; otter which ceremony arrangements were made for the holding of the annual tea-party In connection with the lolge, and a commit- tee was appointed to draw up the programme. Brother John Taylor subsequently read an essay on "My Lodge," clipped from the Good Templars' Watchword ; and Brother John Warburton gave one or two excellent recitations. The pro- gramme for the evening was "a night of sacred melody ;" and a selection of hymns from Sanke,y's and the Gospel Temperance Hymn-books were sung by the members. The proceedings were of an enjoyable character. THE EARLESTOWN GOSPEL MISSION.—It is a pleasure to record that the Earlestown Gospel Mission, under ita new committee of management, still continues to be favoured with the support of a large number of friends. On Sunday I the afternoon preacher was the Rev. James Allatt (Newton I Congregational Church); and in the evening Mr. J. Prescott, I of Earlestown, was the preacher. There were large atten- dances, the room being filled on each occasion. We may add that 1! goodly number of scholars attend the Sunday school, held in the same. place both morning and afternoon, and on the whole the mission appears to have met with no small degree of success. Oa Tuesday evening a public entertain- ment was held, and the attendance was very fair. Mr. Jamison presided; and M!. Cordingly gave an excellent address. Sews, recitations, and readings were nicely given by several friends, the entertainment being greatly appreciated by those present. LITERATURE.

IDictionary of Pts—ra-se and Fable (Cassell dr. Co., Limited). —This work, which is by Dr. Brewer, gives the derivation, source, qr origin of many thousand common phrases, allu- sions, and words that have a bile o teil ; and to it has recently been added a concise bibliography of English literature based upon the larger work of reference on the same subject by W. Davenport Adams, with additions. As an evidence of the popularity of this dictic,nary, it need only he stated that it has now passed through fifteen editions. To the student such a work as that now before us is invalu- able ; whilst to ths man of learning it must be a great assistance in his researches. The dictionary is something more than a mass of dry facts, for it contains much readable matter, a thing rarely to be found in a work of reference. No library can be said to be complete without this dictionary. We have received a espy of the Autobiography of a Lan- cashire Lawyer, being, as the title page states, The life and recollections of John Taylor, Attorney-at-Law, and first coroner of the borough of Balton, with notice of many persons and things met with (haring a life of seventy-two years lived in and about Bolton. "v The volume must be of considerable value to Boltonians, because it treats of many episodes in the history of that borough in which Mr. Taylor has borne a part; at the same time the writer is a gentleman who is well known, espe- eially to the legal profession, throughout Lancashire, if net i beyond its borders, and the autobiography will, therefore, be ' read with interest by many not connected with Mr. Taylor's native town, but who have learned to esteem the author for his sterling worth. Mr. Taylor possesses considerable histrionie abilities, he has performed on the boards of many a Lancashire theatre with some of the celebrities in the dramatic profession, and his experiences, good and bad, of those with whom he thus came in contact are related with a transparent honesty to be admired. The story of the author's life, the ups and downs he encountered in his profession, his record of the criminal causes of note in which he has been engaged, are told in simple but telling langn4v, from which old and young may alike profit; but the part of the work which is the most interesting, as it is the most touch- ing, is the author's description of his struggle when throwing off the ties of this world and its vanities and concentrating his thoughts on that which appertains to the next. On the whole we think it well that this autobiography, which was at first only intended for the family circle,should have received much wider publicity, and we are satisfied it cannot fail to be productive of benefit to those who peruse it. The work has been edited by the author's friend, Mr. James Clegg, one of the proprietors af the Bolton Chronic e, at which office it has been printed, and4he letterpress reflects credit on the establishment. The publishers are Messrs. Tubbs, Brook, and Chrystal, Manchester.

CLEVER CAPTURE BY AN EARLES- TOW N POLICEMAN. A STRANGE RAILWAY PORTER. An unusually smart and clever capture of a man wanted by the officers of the law, was effected by P.C. McMullen, resident in Earlestown, but having the oversight of the Wargrave and Vulcan districts. It appears that on the Ist August last, William Mains, a labourer, living in Vulcan- cottages, should have appeared at the Newton Petty Ses- sions, to answer a charge of trespassing in pursuit of game, on land at Winwick, in the occupation of the Rev. Canon Hopwood. He failed to do so, however, and after hearing the evidence the Bench im- posed a fine of .10s and costs, or in default of payment, one month's imprisonment. Evidently aware of this. Mains absconded, and succeeded in eluding the police up to Monday last. His apprehension was made more difficult by the fact that he very well knew the features of the local policemen, and as he was a remarkably swift runner, the chances of escape were in his favour. On the day in ques- tion P.C. McMullen heard that Mains was working as a labouter in a field near Winwick Quay, and that officer adopted a rather novel mode of effecting his apprehension. About noon Mains and a man named rent were engaged in ioading a cart with straw when a man attired in the garb of a railway-porter, with a soft low hat, and an overcoat buttoned up to the neck, sauntered tnwsrds them, apparently unconcerned and unsuspected. Mains was evidently ignorant who the strange "railway psrter " was, for when the latter suddenly grasped him and said that he was " wanted " by the police, he looked up as- tonished and exclaimed with surprise, " Whi do thi send railway-pooarters neaw to lock fooaks up? I waint go wi' thee." But when the assumed railway official cooly unbut- toned his overcoat and exposed to view the familar bright buttons and dark blue clothing of a full-fledged constable— minus the hat—the state of mind in which Mains found himself can be better imagined than described. Thus cap- tured, Mains quietly submitted to be locked up, and the same day he was conveyed to prison for one month, in de- fault of paying toe flue.

SERIOUS WOUNDING CASE AT RUNCORN. STABBED WITH A FORK. At Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, 1- mr. Banks, Hannah Silk was bought up on with unlawfully wounding James Brie charged of eight or nine months Brightoe For a period .. had cohabited with the woman, and together they Iravelled through various parts of the country as ehnh polishers. On Monday they arrived in Ruoc,orn an took up their quarters at Mrs. Allaby's lodgin uotts its Merseyea'reet. In the evening they both r.'eturned to the house in a state of intoxication Silk cl',arged Brighton with having entered a public-house wit.`a another woman, and a wrangle ensued, Brigivon rising from the chair on which he was sitting and striking the woman several times. Suddenly she jumped to her feet, seized something from the table, and was seen to aim four blows at her assailant's head. Two struck their mark, and the man fell to the floor in an unconscious state. The woman decamped, and the police were sent for. When they arrived, the man was still unconscious. It was discovered that he had three punctured wounds over the left eye, and a similar number behind the left ear. An ordinary three- pronged fork was found lying on the floor where the prisoner had been standing. Dr. MacDougall said .he had compared the prongs of the fork with the wounds, and the width of the wounds was exactly the width of the prongs. The wound over the eye was a very dangerous one, the weapon having narrowly escaped penetrating the ball of the eye. Had it done so, the man would have lost his sight. The fork had also penetrated the babe of the ear. The prisoner was apprehended on Monday evening by P.C. Wallace, who charged her with the offence. She replied, "Wounding ! I don't remember anything of it."—The prisoner now in- formed his I,Vorship that Brighton was very good to her when sober, but when drunk he was very "nasty," and ex- cited her temper. He was so on this occasion, and struck her three times, and she did not remember anything further until she found herself in the custody of the police.—She was committed to take her trial at Chester Assizes.

In the committee-room of Lacey-street School, on Monday morning, a meeting, convened by circular, VMS held for the Dfirpose of avoiding a contested election of School Board ineini,ers by A col.pr9rniee• The following candidate* and their supporters attended :—Revs. J. Wright Willdeesee Geo. Bond, T. Finegan, J. Clarke,. Dr. Ca. ineeffe, Messrs. T. Sutton Timmis, Peter Glover, 1. B. Imison, Joseph Robin- son, K. Shaw, J. W. W?:reing, J. White. Crawford, Fogg, B. Brown, W. T. husband, J. Morrison' T. S. Swale, J. E. Johnson, and G. H. Danby (clerk to the School Board). At the request of the meeting, Mr. T. SurroN TIMMIS (the chairman of the School Board) presided, lie said be had received a letter from Mr. Tenon, who expressed regret that he could not be present, and hoped they would be able to avoid a contest. On previous occesions, the chairmate added, when there had been a necessity to elect a School Board, he bad not hesitated to express his opinion that a contest was desirable, as inanv people who seemed dissatis- lied with a "nomination Bused" would have An opportunity of recording their votes. While he had not changed his mind as to the principle of the thing, he might explain that it would be a mistake to have a contest on the present oc- casion. In the first place the Board, which was now expir- ing, had worked extremely harmoniously, and he had reason no believe that the ratepayers had been satisfied with the course of action they had taken. (Hear, hear.) M all events he had heard nothing to the contrary. (Hear, hear.) Then to have an election there would be considerab'e cest. The expenses would be at least £290, which would be utterly beyond the control of the Board. The election was under the control of the clerk to the Guardians of the Prescot Union, and he was entitled by law to certain charges, which the School Board had nothing to do but pay. In the pre- sent state of trade in Widnes and the pressure of rates, he thought it was very undesirable that they should spend £2OO, which would to all intents and purposes be thrown away, and therefore he was quite willing to subordinate any views he iniglit hive as to the policy of a contest to what was consideredto be for general good of the town. If there was not to be a contest a number of the gentlemen nomina- ted will have to exercise a little self-denial and withdraw. Now there were three parties represented on the Board, and with two exceptions the retir- ing members were willing to be re - elected. The question, therefore, was who would the Church party select to fill the vacancy caused by the retirement of Mr Brunner, an by whom would the Nonconformists replace Mr. Hartland. If two gentlemen could be agreed upon, he had no doubt the other gentlemen who were nominated could be induced to withdraw their names. Mr. Deem then read the list of candidates, classifying Mr. Wareing and Mr. Husband as the nominees of the Church party. Both gentlemen objected to the classification. The CHAIRMAN explained that although nominally gentlemen had been elected to represent certain parties, vet when they came to the Board they simply represented the town. (Hear, hear.) No question of party had ever arisen.—Mn. WAREING: Ex- cept in the nominations.—The CHAIRMAN was sure that each member of the Board had bean actuated with the desire to carry out the Education Acts for the benefit of the town, wad to promote elementary education. The question of party had never cropped up, and wnen gentlemen were called the nominees of certain parties the phrase was to some extent a misnomer. He took it for granted that if two gentlemen could be agreed upon to take the place of the Mr. Brunner and Mr. Hartland, the nine retiring members ehould be elected. Mr. B. Bearawer said from what he knew of the feeling of the ratep tyers it was the general wish. —ln answer to an invitation from the chairman, Father Finegan said he had no objection to any one retiring member, or to any gentleman in the room. The Catholics would be content with the same number of gentlemen on the Board they had at present, and they were prepared to withdraw their fifth nomination, if by so doing a contest could be avoided.—Mr. Sasw said that meeting might decide the question, but they did not yet know whether a portion of the community was satisfied with the operations of the Board up to the present time. If there was any disagreement with the policy of the Board, that would be a reason for a contest. What that policy had been was well known. It had been to provide accommode- thin for the childaen of the district, and at the same time to do nothing prejudicial in any respect to the denominational schools—(hear, hear)—for the experience of the Board for the past nine years had been that these schools had been benefitted by the operations of the Board. If the ratepayers, or a large portion of them, said they were not satisfied with the policy, and wished for a contest, a contest ought to be entered into, but if they were satisfied, then it would be wrong to have a contest. He took it that all the gentlemen nominated were supposed to have some responsible and con- siderable number of persons behind thern—(hear, hear)— because two or three people in a town had no right to force a contest upon the inhabitants. In that room they had one or two gantlemen who had not been nominated by the recognised parties in the town, and it must, therefore, be taken that they bad a considerable following who were willing that a contest should be entered into for some reason or other. If there was any objection to the Board's policy it ought to be stated so that they might know exactly where they stood. So far as he had gathered a large por- tion of the ratepayers was satisfied with the harmonious end efficient way in which the business of the Board had been managed. div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday, Mr. John Simpson presided. There were present—the Rey. Father Fennelly, Messrs. T. Norman, J. Pritchard, R. Lea, and F. Rigby, J.P. (clerk).

_ _ FINANCES. The annual statement of the accounts, as read by the Clerk, showed that the receipts included a balance of £72 15s 101, grants from the Committee of the Council on Edu- cation, £132 16s 6d , payments made, to treasurer by rate authority at 2d in the Z, £400; and school fees, £75 5s sd. The total receipts amounted to £684 14i 2d. The expen- diture amounted to £525 4s sd, and included the following items—salaries of the officers of the Board, £l9l 2s 24; legal and other expenses of administration, including rent of office, &a., £72 7s 2d; salaries of teachers, £147 12a 2d contributions to industrial schools, £l5 13s 3d; repayment of principal of loans, £24 lie 44 ; interest on loans, £25 23 14. _ . .
The accounts were passed and signed by the Chairman.
AN AWKWARD TENANT.

The CLERK submiAed an application he had received from Mr. Cunningham for the use of Mill-brow school on ' certain evenings during the winter for tea parties and lec- tures in cennection with the Holy 'Trinity Young Men's Society, and remarked that it would be in the recollection of the members that an application for the use of the room , for a special purpose was made to the Board in May. On the 6th of June he addressed a letter to the Rev. W. Preston stating that the use of the room would be granted on the Board receiving an assurance from him / that an annual rent of £7 would be paid. The letter also pointed out that Mr. Preston's present errangement with the Board was to pay the rent quarterly in advance, and there were then twe quarters still unpaid, and a third would be- come due en the 24th inst. A few days subsequently Mr. Preston forwarded half a year's rent, but it was now the 17th October and no reply had been received to the first part of the letter. He was given to understand that the yeung men had taken charge of the room for a penny bank on certain evenings, but the Board had not received the assurance from Mr. Preston. Mr. NORMAN: I don't Clink that is right. If they were to pay the rent in advance why is it not done? The CLERK: There is half a year's rent owing now. Mr. NotterAer : We cannot allow this to go on. They have taken charge of the school in face of the Board. It Mr. Preston doesn't pty the rent I think we ought to stop the tenancy. Anyone else might claim the same privilege. The CHAIRMAN: It seems to me that we shall not be do- ing right if we don't let Mr. Preston know that we cannot allow the use of the school beyond a time we may fix unless the rent is paid. Mr. LEA: That is the best thing you can do. The CHAIRMAN: It will be a great pity if we have to take any decided steps. Mr. LEA moved, and Mr. NORMAN seconded a resolution in conformity with the Chairman's suggestion. Father FINEGAN : Their action is a gross violation of the agreement with the Board, and a contempt of the Board for not answering the letter. The CLERK remarked that in connec:ion with the Holy Trinity Young Men's Society using the room, there had been great complaints from the cleaner, and she had come to personally speak with the Board The gas meter had been damaged, locks broken on two occasions, and a key had been smashed. The CARETAKER was then c died into the room, and said vtood. tho room woro v.rr Mr. BowYeet (attendance officer) said there was a desk broken now. The CHAIRMAN: It seems to ins from experience that it is a very awkward thing for day schools to be used for any other purpese, unless the caretaker was always On the pre- uni.esi and unless such a rent is piid as to enable the Board to pay the caretaker a proper amount of wages for that duty. Otherwise, we shall always be liable to unpleasant- ness of this kind. The CLERK said the Board could close the agreement to- morrow if they liked. 'rime CHAIRMAN said it was awkward for that meeting to take any decided steps, as there were three Nonconformists present .
The CLERK stated that the remuneration the ciretaker got for her labours each Saturday and Sunday was an annual payment of 4s 41 or Id per week. (Sensation.)_
• Mr. NORMAN and Mr. LEA each stated that Mr. Prest®n ought to be charged with the cost of repairing the damage . . . .

_ that had been done. _ Mr. rIZITCII.B.RD said after these statements it was a matter for consideration whether they should not charge an increased rent, so that the caretaker could be adequately paid for her extra labour.
The CARETAKER said there had been held in the room in
connection with Holy Trinity two tea parties and a magic lantern entertainment, and a shilling was given to her. She had to scour the floor on each occasion.
Mr. NORMAN: Perfectly alnminable. --- •

The CHAIRMAN : They seem to take the advantage of get- ting the room on cheip terms, and paying the caretaker at such a miserable rate in order to save their own premises. The CLERK pointed out that before the school became the property of the Board it was frequently used for a polling booth, and taking the average, 15s was fair remuneration. After two tea meetings and a m;s:gic lantern entertainment a shilling was considered a fair remuneration. Thet'discussion then ceased, it being understood that the clerk would communicate with Mr. Preston.

div.head: ASSISTANT MISTRESS.
div.p: THE ASSISTANT MISTRESS.
The salary of Miss Dumbell, assistant mistress at the Board school, was increased to £35, on the motion of Mr. NORMAN.

A letter from the secretary to the Commissioners with reference to the School Board's occupancy in Waterloo llouse was read. Consideration deferred.
TI.IITOR'S REPORT.

Returns from the public elementary schools for Sep- temlnr :—Certified Government accommodation, 2,716; total number on the rolls, 3,030 ; number on the rolls corres- ponding period of last year, 2,912: increase in the number on the rolls, 118; total average attendance, 2,283 5 ; ave- rage attendance corresponding p-riod of last year, 1,918 ; increase in average attendance. 335 5 ; percentaze of attend- ances, 753; average attendance for the year 1874, 1,2:52 ; increase in average attendance as compared with the year preceding the formation of the Board (1874), 1,031.5; accom- modation in excess of average attendance, 432.5; number on the rolls in excess of accommodation, 314; number attend- ing private adventure sch)ols under niaepeoce per week,;46. The rettalts for the past month show a large increase in the attendance at the various schools, as compared with Sep- tember 1882. Measles and scar! Aiwa were exceedingly prevalent in the corresponding period of last yetr, which considerably reduced the average attendance; the returns, therefore show a large increase over that period. Since my last report I have completed the list of cases ordered to be dealt with for c3ntravention of the bye-laws. Two cases were then in abeyance ; both have now been dealt with, and the usual fine of 5s imposed.
