"THE pHIL(f-ellY OF PVI`i'ERBS"
PAR -- % BY THE REV. CANON DODD.

• The op'„ing meeting of the session of the War- r,ingif.in Literary and Philosophieal Society was aeld In the Lecture-room at the Museum, on Thursday evening. There was a large attendance of members amongst those present being the President (the Rev. Gam Dodd), Rev. R. Pilcher, 8.A., Rev. H. Stubbs, Rev. H. G. Smith, Major Hamilton, Messrs. John Dun, C. Broadbent, T. Morris, W. D. Jeans, C. White, J. C. Young, J. R. Young (hon. sec.), and others. After the transaction of routine busi-
ness. The PRESIDENT proceeded to read a paper,on the "Philo- sophy of Proverbs." He said the study of ptivitrbs was both

curious and instructive. The common sayings which we were accdstomed frequently to use and to hear used, but into the origin of which we rarely think of inquiring, were in many cases much older than we supposed. Moreover, they were only a few members of a very large family with whom we had perhaps chanced to form an acquaintance, while the other Members of the same family whom we did not know far exceeded in number and antiquity, and often in importance, our more familiar friends. Proverbs cer- tainly existed long before books. "The words of the wise, and their dark sayings," formed the homely learning of a people that could not read. Short, pithy, easily remem- bered, easily applied, sparing of words, and prodigal of sense, such sayings would be jealously treasured from one generation to another, • handed down from father to son, from mother to daughter, from master to man, till they Came to form a kind of unwritten philosophy, expressing accepted maxims in art, and morality. mad life. Ihe very words he had just quoted carried them beck to the days of Solomon, and Solomon's name reminded us of the great antiquity of proverbs. "I'o underst end a proverb and the interpretation" was the mark of a wise man. Some of these might have been abtrueive sayings difficult to inter- pret, like the replies of the Greek oracles, the proper study of sages. But the greater part of the proverbs of Solomon were simple exhortations to virtue and purity of living, suggesting rules of self-government in every relation and condition of life. The Book of Proferbs in Holy Scripture, which bore Soloman's name, consisted partly of a miscellaneous collection of ancient sayings previously current among the nations, and also of a collec- tion of original proverbs by the great seer himself. To these weie added some further proverbs attributed to Solo- mon, which "the men of Hezekiah, King of Judah, copied out," together with the words of Agar, and certain admoni- tions given to King Lemuel by his mother. The proverbs were chiefly given in the form of poetry peculiar to the Hebrew language, and much of their elegance and force was due to the antithesis which characterised almost every sentence. Aristotle, who wrote over 2,000 years ago, in his observations on proverbs, regarded them as fragments of the earlier wisdom, the wrecks of an ancient philosophy over- thrown and lost in some convulsion of human affairs, and leaving only these specimens of its pristine vigour. It was well known that the Tartars, Turks, Arabians, and Persians, and indeed almost all Asiatic tribes had possessed sentences of a proverbial character, expressing their peculiar genius and art, while the Chinese language, of which he had not a profound knowledge himself, was arid to be rich in proverbs bearing on every kind of subject. Of the antiquity, there- fore, of proverbs there could be no question, and they might fairly believe that before men could read and write their observations of nature, of cause and effect, of Nemesis, found expression in these proverbial forms. For what was a proverb? Many and various definition, had been given by students and collectors, and the very number and variety of these definitions seemed to prove the difficulty of pro- viding an adequate answer to this question. The learned Erasmus rejected the definitions of all who had preceded him, and called the proverb a "eelebre dictum," that is "a famous saying." Lord Bacon, in his collection of apo- thegms, after regretting the loss of Cmsar's collection, and expressing the poor opinion he had of subsequent collectors, proceeded to cell them muerones verborum, that is "pointed speeches." They serve," he said, " not of pleasure only and ornament, but also of actions and business, whereby knots.insrbuline.ss are pierced and severed." He reminded us Cicero celled them "salient" that :was 'salt pits, as though one might extract silt out of them and sprinkle it where they would. "They serve," added Bacon, "to be interlaced in continued speech. They serve to be recited upon occa- sion of themselves. They serve, if you take out the kernel of them, to make them your own." Dr. Johnson's defini- tion ran thus : "A proverb is a short sentence frequently I repeated by the people," but such a definition was plainly insufficient. Some good proverbs had never been familiar, and the people frequently repeated a great many objection- able things that were not proverbs at all. One old writer, Howel, analysing a good proverb, declared that it consisted, and that all good proverbs always must consist, of three things, "sense, shortness, and salt." The sense of these three ingredients was perhaps the only original element in his definition. the saltness being probably borrowed from the "ealinx" of Cicero, and the smallness from the corposis exigui of Martial's verse. Still essre was merit in the de- finition of what had been called the three S'9. Sense formed the staple body of the dish, the shortness imparted a cha- racter and tone (and in this particular distinguished it from the apothegm, which had no special regard for extreme brevity), while the salt added a flavour, and 'served a whole- someness calculated to tenant the palate of the most dainty. Martial's epigram on an epigram run thus : Omne epigramma sit ihstar apis, sit aculeus ipti. Suit sea mella, sit et corposis exigui. That was, let every eptgram-be nue a Dee ; "let it have a sting, honey of its own, and a little body." Archbishop Trench had thus translated Martial: Three things must epigrams, like bees have all A sting, and honey, and a body small. The saintly George Herbert made a smell collection of proverbs. To these he gave the name of Jacula pruden- tium '—a wise saying that was, which could be darted or hurled on occasion, and might be expected to strike deeply and stick fast. With regard to the shortness of a proverb it was evident that this was an essential feature in its composition. Otherwise an approach was made to a fable, and indeed there were cases in which a proverb might b- said to be the summary of a fable. Thus the fable of the fox and the grapes was briefly comprehended in the saying "sour grapes." The fable of the old men and his sons and the sticks was amply expressed in saying " Union is strength," and so on. But the proverb itself must of neces- sity be short. It was only thus it could expect to be used, and use alone could keep it alive. After explaining the meaning of the epithet " laconic," the president said no proverb, as far as he knew, had ever been condensed into less than two words, though it was impos- sible to say what the learning and skill of the future might pro.luce. For a long time it was thought impossible to arrange a problem in chess which should con- sist of less than two moves, "White to play and mate in two moves." But an ingenious composer a little tiara ago contrived a problem of considerabledifficulty, in which white was to mate in one move, and immediately an ardent competi- tor for chess honours (he need hardly say he bailed from America)—(laughter)—composed a problem in which white should mate without moving at all. It WAS therefore within the range of possibility that a proverb might be discovered consisting of one word or even of no words at all. And indeed they already possessed indications of s mething of that kind. The historical nod of Lord Burleigh's head was as good as any proverb, while the wink of an artful tricksler or the shrug of a Frenchman's shoulders expressed a great deal of meaning without having recourse to the employ- ment of words. As specimens of two-worded proverbs they could all rec ill" Extremes meet," Forewarned, forearmed," " Noblesse oblige," and many others, while in Latin they had several that did net really consist of only two words, but of which through an ellipsis, only two words were used. Thus " Sus Minervarn "(" docet " being understood), Expede Herculem " (" noveris " being understood), " Verbum sap" (the whole sentence being " Verbuin sapienti, sat eat"). This was also sometimes abbreviated into " Verbum sit." As regarded popularity, though they could not accept Dr. Johnson's defini!ion, which referred to this as the only necessary qualific talon. yet it was evident that a saying, however good and pointed in itself, unless it was widely known and used, could not be correctly celled a proverb. "[hey seemed, therefore, to arrive at the following conclusion with regard to the necessary ingredients of a proverb, viz , that it should consist of only a few words having nothing superfluous in it, that those words, by their wit and wisdom, should commend themselves to the people generally, and that there should be a certain flavour or tastiness in the expression which should sive it from becoming at any time insipid or tin wholesorne. Thus they saw that a proverb must grow in public estimation, making its way naturally by virtue of its own intrinsic goodness of strength, and therefore that anything like the artificial forcing of a pro- verb was altogether impossible; and indeed the origin of a proverb was usually difficult to trace. In many cases it could not be traced at all. Hence there was some truth in that dstinition of a proverb, which declared it to be " s tying without an author," as though it were the result of spontaneous generation, and could only give the same account of itself as the immortal Topsy did of herself, " I 'specs I growed." (Laughter.) But there were c eses in which sharp pointed sayings, first produced on occasions of special inter est, had afterwards on account of their general application been adopted as proverbs. Of these he would now endeavour to give them a few examples. In the let Book of Samuel they read as follows, about Saul :—" And it came to pass that when all that knew him beforetime saw that, behold, he prophesied among the prophets." Then the people said one to another " What is this th it has come to the son of K,sli ? Is Saul also amongst the prophets ?" Therefore it bscame a proverb "Is Scut also among the prophets?" the interpretation of which he took to be this : On the occasion referred to Saul became another m to, and had another heart given urro him. He joined the com- pany of prophets and prophesied with them. So sudden a change and such an unexpected proceeding astonished all who knew him. Some one asked the question in words which embodied the astonishment of all, arid ever after- wards when a man was found acting differently and better than his antecedents would have led people to expect the general surprise found expression in the proverb, "Is Sml also amongst the prophets?" When Cseaar, after deliberat- ing as to the good policy of crossing the Rubicon, decided to make the passage and. burn his boat, he exclaimed, "The die is cast." A Theban officer, merrymaking with a party of his friends, received news of a conspiracy which he was urged to suppress. "Business to-morrow," he cried, and

plunged further into the dissipation around him. Before " to-morrow" came be fell a victim to the plot he had. delayed to unravel. A woman brought her cause before King Philip, but on account of the King's intoxication received an unjust sentence. "I will appeal," she said. "To whom will you appeal ? " asked the King. "From Philip drunk to Philip sober." Ibyeus, a famous lyric poet of Greece, on his road to Corinth, being attacked by robbus, called upon a flight of cranes, the only living things in sight, to avenge his death. The appeal, at the time it was made, seemed useless enough, but the robbers some time after be- ing seated in the theatre at Corinth, observed some cranes searing above their heads. "See," they said to one another, "there are the avengers of the Ibeyus." Enquiry followed. In their confusion the murderers betrayed themselves, and ultimately confessing their crime received the first reward of their evil deeds. Thus "the cranes of Ibeyus," or, "murder will out," became a common saying, indicating a feeling still largely prevalent that while other sins might

escape-discovery- , the sin of bloodshed was almost sure sooner or later in some way or other to be brought home to the guilty. (Applause.) The remarks of Lord Chesterfield respecting proverbs were very frequently quoted, not indeed with approbation, but to show how false and foolish was the fastidious fashion of his day. "A man of fashion," he said, "never had recours3 to proverbs and vulgar aphorisms." However true that might have been of the so-called "men of fashion" in Lord Chesterfield's time, it was certainly not true of men of learning and intellectual power at any period of history. Every classical scholar was aware that proverbs of every description lie thickly embedded in the works of the great authors of Greece and Rome. Many of these had been transposed, rather than translated, for modern use. Cicero made a very large use of proverbs, and many of these were to be met with in a modern form. He might especially refer to one of these. In his "Dv Seuectute," or " Treatisdhpon old age," he made the elder Cato refer to the friends with whom he associated in early life and quoted what he called an ancient proverb, or as they had it in modern fashion," Birds of a feather flock to- gether." They had already referred to Plato and Aristotle. Plutarch's remark might also be added, "Under the veil of these curious sentences are hid those germs of morals which the masters of philosophy have afterwards developed into so many volumes." Proverbial expressions were frequently to be met with in the Greek tragedians, while Horace, by the pithiness of his verse and his wonderful knowledge of human life, might himself be said to have frequently created pro- verbs that had been atelmost universally accepted by the educated world. The learned Bentley, master of Trinity College, Cambridge, and one `of the greatest scholars of his own or any time, was reviled by certain superficial and jealous wits among his contemporaries on account of his pedantic use of pro- verbs, but he defended himself by showing how frequently Cicero quoted proverbs from ancient Greek writers, and how generally men of learning had not disdained their use. Our own Shakespeare (the lecturer continued) was a very fre- quent citer of proverbs, and often referred to them without actual quotation. He used popular proverbs, as the titles of some of his plays, thus, "Much ado about nothing," "All's well that ends well," "Measure for measure." If they took any of Shakespeare's best known plays, such as " Hamlet " or "Macbeth," and carefully marked all the proverbial expressions they met, they would be astonished at their number. They were, indeed, "familiar in our mouths as household words," and partly accounted for the profound criticism of a wonderful wag, who said he did not think much of Shakespeare.whose writings seemed to consist of a quantity of common sayings strung carelessly together. (Laughter.) The learned Erasmus was particularly fond of proverbs and made a very large collection of them. The " Adagia "of Erasmus contained about 5,000, collected from all sources of ancient learning (this work passed through 12 editions in his lifetime). Julius Caesar also made a remarkable col- lection, though it had been unfortunately lost. Lord Bacon from a sick bed dictated from memory a number of proverbs he had met with in his reading. In " Dan Quixote" Ler- vantes had made Sancho Pansha hardly ever to open his mouth without speaking a proverb. How could he forbear to refer to the writings of the New Testament where they found Our Saviour did not disdain to make use of expressions with which the common people were familiar, such as "Physician, heal thyself," "A Prophet is not without honour save in his.own country," and again after His con- versation with the woman of Samaria He said to His dis- ciples "Herein is that saying true, one soweth and another reapeth." The epistle St. Paul, at least on two occasions, quoted well-known sayings of ancient Greek writers. In the 15th chapter of the Corinthians. which was usually read at the burial of the dead, they had "Evil communications cor- rupt good manners "—a verse taken literally from th'e writings of Menandey, and, again, when preaching to the Athenians on Mars Hill he said, "in Him we live and move and have our being, as certain also of your own poets have said." Those words were found in the writings of two Greek poets, Aratus and.. Cleanthes. The Apostle had never read those works, and did not even know the names ,of the authors of the words he quoted. If proverbs and proverbial expressions were the contemptible and unworthy things the quite too exquisite Lord Chesterfield would have them believe, they might be well satisfied to go astray in such company as that. (Applause.) Proverbs were cos- mopolitan, national, local, and even personal. One of the most interesting studies in connection with proverbs was to trace in the case of some of them how they appeared and re-appeared in various forms among almost all nations under the sun. As Sam Slick reminded them " there is a great deal of human nature in men"—(laughter)—and they fohnd that the people in the sheds and markets of Athens and Rome and Alexandria were very much the same in sen- timent and logic as they were at the present day in Paris and London and New York. Thera were still mea of every variety of character and temper to be met with, honest and false, noble and mean, gentle and churlish. The same 0,“31000tilI prnrinnerl the game residte, the same deeieee .n 4 hopes, the same de'ays and disappointments, the same joys and sorrows, the same surpeses and regrets to still affect the human heart. These attributes of humanity were indepen- dent of time and place, and therefore he imagined it was that they often met the same thought in various dresses among nations as far asunder as the Poles. Whether the existence of the same proverb in different languages simply meant a transLition from the same original, or whether the differeet nations had a separate proverb for themselves, illustrative of a common idea that commended itself to the universal sense of mankind it would be difficult to say. Many pro- verbs had transferred themselves in their entirety from one nation to another. Others could not bear such a transference, having some speciality about them indicative of the soil whence they sprang. He migh here translate and quote the beautiful words of Erasmus, Many proverbs have this peculiarity that. they require to he spoken in the language in which they were born, but if they migrate into another language much of their beauty departs." Still it was evident that besides the proverbs which a nation had of its own, it inherited, so to speak, the common property of the world, and found a number of wise and witty sayings ready made to its baud. Hence it was that a vast number of the proverbs of Greece and Rome, and also of mediaeval times still remained among all the modern nations. And here it was that the collector of national proverbs found it so difficult io.determine what proverbs were really the production of the nation and what had been borrowed. Be was often deceived into claiming for his special nation a proverb that was not indigenous, but only nationalised, the true origin of which was to he found in an earlier age and in another tongue. Sach a proverb as "Man proposes, God disposes," or, as it had been cynically framed, Man appoints, God disappoints," carried them back to the Greek tragedians with their frequent declarations as to the futility of resisting the will or the Gods. That proverb, or something closely resem- bling it was said to be found in almost all languages and among all nations. However originally it might have had its birth is the thought of a stoical yielding to necessity the well instructed mind might still employ the phrase in signifying nothing more than a glad submission to the Divine will. But they saw the cause why such a proverb as that should be cosmopolitan. It was a kind of universal acknowledgment of the existence of a Superior Being, and an expression of the helplessness of man to arrange the future. Another proverb showing the folly of sending to a place whatever it already possessed in great abundance was found in various forms under various languages. They said "To carry coals te Nexcletle," the Greeks said "Owls to Athens," the Hebrews "To carry oil to the City of Olives," in the East "To carry pepper to Hindostan," among the Egyptians "Enchantments to Egypt," in mediaeval times "Indulgences to Rome." National proverbs or distinct from cosmopolitan would betray some peculiar mode of thinking or acting which belonged to that special nation only. The proverb of the Greeks showed a wonderfully intimate knowledge of the antiquity and myth- ology ef their race. They were keen and clever, humourous and sly, and clearly showed the intellectual power and high mental culture of the people. The proverbs of the Romans, on the other hand, were more solid and matter-of-fact, less poetical and subtle, full of stern cimmon-sense and the patrons of rugged virtue. The literature of Spain was ex- ceedingly rich in proverbs, and the antiquity of many of them was shown in the fact that they were found in the old romance. The Spaniards called theirs "the sayings of old wives by their firesides." In number they seemed to far exceed those of any other nation, one enthusiastic collector having succeeded in gathering together 50me20,500 or 30,000. Many of theirs betrayed the pride and haughtiness of the race, together with that chivalry for which all Spaniards were famous. Thu., "The king goes as far as he is able, not as far as he desires," indicating a jealousy of the adop- tion of supreme power by the head of the State and a deter- mination on the part of the nobility that he should be curbed in his ambition. "What Christ takes not the Exchcqier carries away," sounded like the complaint of an over-taxed people from whom the priests were ever exacting extravagant dues, as though Spain had always suffered from the excessive priestcraft and irregnlar finance, which were its chief characteristics still. It was indeed curious how frequently the greed and avarice of the priesthood formed the prominent points of a Spanish proverb. The Italian proverbs were shrewd and selfieh. The Elder D, Israel, mai& : "Every tenth proverb in an Italian collection is some cynical or selfish maxim—a book of the world for worldlings. Their political proverbs, no doubt, arose from the extraordinary state of a people sometimes distracted among Republics, and sometimes ser- vile in petty courts." "Who knows not to flatter, knows not to reign." "An open countenance, but close thoughts." He who talks sows, he who is silent reaps." "Revenge is a morsel for God." Enough had, he thought, been shown to prove that while many proverbs were citizens of the world, and appeared in various forms in various countries, there were otbers that by some peculiarity of thought or expres- sion distinctly betrayed their nationality. The question (a

Very interesting one) was rtlCient to form the subject of an entire lecture, for. doubt every nation had proverbs of its own which would lose much 9f their point and interest if used in a foreign land. But there was not 1 time to pursue this branch of the subject any further. But`i besides these cosmopolitan and national proverbs, there were, as he had already-said, proverbs that were distinctively local, and even personal---." Make hay while the sun shines ;" "Better to wed over the mixon than over the moor" (a Cheshire proverb); "I will make a shaft or a bolt of it" (that is one use or the other of a thing); "Those who will not be ruled by the rudder must be ruled by the rock" (a Cornish proverb) ; "If Shiddaw hath a cap, Scruffel wots full well of that ;" "It were better to hear the lark sing than tb.e mouse cheep" (a Borderproverb), ctc. Many proverbs bear the jingle of alliteration and rhymc,. Swift was slid to have invented many of this kind, and then to have passed them off in conversation as "old and true sayings." After quoting examples of personal proverbs, the Rev. Canon said they frequently found the same thought expressed in two or more different proverbs. Some- times a national or local peculiarity explained the change, not always. In English they often met with proverbs entirely distinct in the images and words employed, but almost identical in idea.

The river passed. and God forgotten. The river passed, and the Saint forgotten. Make hay while the sun shines. Every dog has his day. A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush. Half a loaf is beter than no bread. It's a long lane that has no turning. Silver lining to every cloul. Many proverbs were only true, as it were, on one side. They would not bear to be applied generally, or always, but only under special circumstances and times.. Indeed, it was pos- sible to find proverbs which appeared to distinctly con- tradict one another. Thus:— 11l weeds grow apace. Good rye grows high. A rolling stone gathers no moss. A prophet has no honour in his own country.

Proverbs, as they might naturally expect, were not only treasuries of wit and wisdom, but also frequently promul- gated rich lessons in morality and even in religion, and those present would, he was sure, acquit him of any desire to preach, in which employment he was already more than sufficiently engaged, when he said that he thought most excellent sermonettes might be made with some familiar proverb as the text. He proceeded to give illustrations, but said he felt he was detaining them too long. They wereall so full of proverbs that their thoughts and his could for the moment find expression in no other way. If his lecture was too short they would say, " A fool's bolt was soon shot." If it was too long and was beginning to con- fuse them," A little knowledge is a dangerous thing." If they were satisfied, Enough is as good as a feast," and if they were dissatisfied and thought be might have handled his subject better they might say, "Wise men make proverbs and fools repeat them." (Laughter and applause.) On the motion of Mr. •BROADBENT, seconded by Dr. Wirrrx, and supported by the Hey. R. PILCHER, a vote of thanks was accorded to the president, and the meeting con- chided.

div.head: LYMM LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: LYMM LOCAL BOARD.

Last evening, a special meeting of this Board was held at the offices Lymm, there being present—Masrs. Cameron (chairman), D. Rogers, Gibbon, Appleton, Forster, Dew- huist and Ridgway (clerk). The question of sewage works was first proceeded with. The Clerk read a letter from the Public Works Loan Commissioners, enclosing papers to be filled up for an additional advance of £1,586, which sum had been previously applied for, and there was also a proposi- tion before the Board to obtain the sanction of the Local Government Board to borrow £1,200 to complete the works. —The CLERK stated that he had prepared a statement showing how the monies had already been expended. On the Ist March, 1883, the sum of £3,000 was received from the Commissioners, and after everything had been paid, a balance was left on the Ist of May of £352 lie. 3d. On June Ist they received a further sum of £2,000 from the Commissioners, leaving a balance in hand at the present time of £303 183 Bd. The Clerk then deviled an estimate of the expenses to complete the works, and stated that after meeting these there would be a deficit of £1,187 17s 11d.— The Board approved of the Clerk's statement, and on the motion of Mr. DEWHURST, seconded by Mr. GIBBON, the Clerk was directed to write to the Local Ciovernment Boald, enclosing a copy of the same and asking for their sanction to borrow a further £1,200 for the completion of the works. —The CnAtitmax observed that no applications had been received for the renting of the sewage outfall field.—lt was decided to plant half with osiers and the other half dowa to grass.—The CLERK drew attentioa to the advisability of new bye-laws being framed by the Boarn, stating that the bye-laws at present in force were very old, and not under the Public Health Act. The Local Government Board had issued model bye-laws on sixteen different sub- jects, but only a portion of these would be required to be enforced by that Buard.—ln reply to the Chairman, the CLERK said that the principal expense would be the printing, which could be done by contract.—Mr. DEWHURST spoke in favour of a new set of bye-laws being adopted by the Board, and the clerk was eventually instructed to make the neces- sary arrangements.—lt being intimated that the footpath in Warrington-lane was in a dangerous state, an order for its repair was given.—There was no other business of interest before the Board.
RELIGIOUS INSTRUCTION. SERMON BY THE RECTOR OF WARRINGTON. _ _ _

The Rot. W. Quekett, M.A., rector of W-ar-ri-n-gt-on, preached in the Parish Church on Sunday morning. his epectai reference to religious instruction. The rector having made an allusion to Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, said: Behold the strength of religious prin- ciple, and see the force of its operation. Do you inquire, my brethren, what can be the cause of the holy fortitude which was displayed by these three men on this memorable occasion ?—a fortitude which may well put the generality of Christians to the blush. An answer to the question will he found in a single sentence of the Wise Man, "Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it." It was a religious education that pro- duced thr:se noble fruits. Their heroic conduct was the effec' of that love and fear of God which had been wrought into their souls when they were children. Let those who read this lessen to-day ponder in their heart whether they think they do right when they endeavour, by every means in their power, to prevent religious instruction being given in our public national schools, to the children of the rising generation. However, public opinion is daily growing against such wished-for proceed- ings, and if we are to keep pace with the requirements of the times we must raise and support schools to meet the in- creased population without an expensive school board. Crossley-street and Bank-street schools, in our own parish, wed our immediate attention. These schools have been in- spected this last week by two of Her Majesty's inspectors, and they have reported that they are not large enough for the present scholars, and must be greatly enlarged if the grants are to be continued for their support. It was my intention to have greatly enlarged Bank-street school this year, but circumstances have prevented this being carried into effect, and Crossley-street s.choer cannot be enlarged on its present site, and it is my wish and intention to remove it altogether to another locality on the other side of the Central Railway by the erection there of a large, commodious building for 400 children, to be used in the week dty as a schoel, and on the Sunday as a place of divine worship. Tee room will be of iron, and rented so -as to require less funds at first. Still great exertions will be required to accomplish it, and I trust and hope ready hearts and hands will Came forward at once and make a beginning. A dozen ladies and gentlemen, with an active secretary and treasurer, wculd do wonders, if they will only be in earnest in the work. Gad over works with His people. Tradesmen and fathers of familiee may do much. Those who worked before in the cause of this church and produced such liberal results, might do the same again. I should be glad to hear t )-day that volunteers have offered assistance, and if they only ray "I'll try" the victory is begun. And there is an Aber matter which is forcing itself on our notice, that is, the painful condition we hear of the young females con- nected with the factories and other employments in the town. They are left to wander in the streets, picking up the alphabet of vice at every turn and earner, who might by kind care and advice be taught to read and write in a night school, and be taught those duties and principles which will abide with them in after life, and may prove as it did with Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego—a shield of de- fence in the hour of trial and difficulty. I should be glad to open a night school at once and take these wanderers in —it is not asking too much of the members of the congrega- tion of all ages to come over and help us as teachers. Send us your names at once, and a day of meeting will be ap- pointed and the work will begin. And now, my young friends, let me remind you, in c.mclusion, that your al,es may be like Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, and may God enable you to feel the necessity and appreciate the value of a like firm and steady principle in the great concern of religion. You live not, it is true, in the court of Babylon, but you live in a sinful world. An .itnage is not sat up which you are commanded to worship, but there are other Jinares which will put your sincerity to the test, and will afford evidence of whem you serve. You are not in danger of the flames which were lighted by the rage of the idolatrous Nebuchadnezzar, nor has your lot fallen in the times of Popish persecution. The fires of Smithfield and Tower-hill are graciously extinguished, never, we trust, to be rekindled. Yet, though not liable to trials like these, you are still exposed to numerous tempta- tions from which nothing can effectually secure you but a religious training in the fear of God and the steadfast lie- lief of His truth. Therefore remember Shadrach, Meshach and Abeduego.

THE UNITED KINGDOM ALLIANCE MEETINGS AT MAN- CIIESTER.—About 36 temperance workers and friends of the temperance movement, resident in Earlestown, visited Man- chester, en Tuesday last, for the purpose of attending the annual meting, under the auspices of the United Kingdom Alliance. The party left Earlestown by the 6-45 a.m, train, and returned by the 10-45 p.m. train.

A BIRMINGHAM RUNAWAY HUSBAND APPREHENDED AT EARLESTOWN.—On Monday, P.C. Lloyd, of Earlestown, apprehended a man named David Hall, late of Aston, near Birmingham, who was wanted by the Birmingham police on a charge of deserting his wife and family since the 27th September last. The prisoner was handed over to P.C. Davies, of Birmingham, on Tuesday.
The Archbishop of Canterbury is seriously indisposed, and his medical advisers have ordered him complete rest for a time.

A telegram received laat evening from Marlboro states that the condition of the Earl of Craven grows increasingly serious, and the gravest apprehensions are felt. The Archbishop of Canterbury is not seriously indis- posed, but as he rtquires rest, his appointments at Birming- ham and elsewhere next week have been postponed. Comm* WINTER.—In Dumfriesshire wintry weather is being experienced, snow having fallen both on the hills and the low grounds. The Queensberry hills are covered with Mow.
The bulletin issued yesterday states that the condition of Sergeant Simon, M.P., continues to give cause for anxiety, but he is holding his ground well and shows signs of im- provement.

- A Conservative banquet is to be held at Watford early in December, at which it is stated the Marquis of Salisbury has consented to deliver an address. Preparations are being made to give his lordship a hearty reception. • The Skye Cotton Mill, near Haslingden, was totally destroyed by fire on Thursday night. The damage, which amounts to sevsral thousand pounds, is covered by insur- ance. It was at this mill Michael Davitt lost his arm some years ago.

TWELVE BRIGANDS SENTENCED TO DEATH.—A Central News telegram dated Palermo, Friday, states :—Twelve brigands have been tried and sentenced to death, eleven others being condemned to penal servitude. Fourteen murders were proved against them. OUTRAGE ON THE COMMANDER-IN-CHIEF : A CORPORAL AND His CLAY PIPE.—A lance—corporal of the transport service has been severely reprimanded at Chatham for ap— pearing on the parade ground, in the presence of the Duke of Camkidge, improperly dressed ani with a clay pipe in his mouth.

THE MANUFACTURE OF SPURIOUS SOVEREIGNS.—Ingram Belborough, of Appleton, near York, was at Birmingham yesterday remanded for a week for having in his possession discs for the manufacture of spurious sovereigns. The pri- soner im believed to be a member of a gang of comets, and the Yorkshire police expect to arrest the confederates.

Speaking at the annual meeting of the Royal Cornwall Geological Society at Penzance yesterday, Mr. Leonard Courtney, M P., said the study of geology convinced them of great changes which were going on in outward nature, and even as late as the Past year they had remarkable evi- dence of those changes, which showed that the earth was, in reality, subject to this perpetual mutation. HORRIBLE CRUELTY TO A STEP-SON.—At Macclesfield yesterday, William Mottram, labourer, Broken Cross, was charged with assaulting his step-son, aged three years. The evidence showed that the prisoner for some trifling fault the child had committed, took off his belt and beat its flesh almost into a pulp, and then placed it in a mug of cold water. The prisoner was committed to prison for six months with hard labour. OUTRAGE IN A WORKHOUSE.—At the Southwark Police Court, on Thursday, Mary Ann Pembroke (32), was brought before Mr. Slade for final examination, charged with wil— fully and maliciously throwing a quantity of boiling water over Margaret Lowy and her baby, scalding the latter in a severe manner. The outrage was committed in the St. George's London workhouse. The prisoner was sentenced to four months' hard labour.

MANSLAUGHTER AT GLASGOW -At Glasgow yesterday after- noon Archbald Dove and John Low were charged with the murder of John Anderson, a labourer, on September 14th. The case arose out of a drunken brawl on the highway be- tween Glasgow and Port Glasgow, during which the pri- soners, it was alleged, fatally stabbed the deceased. The Jury found a verdict of not proved against Dow, and con- victed Low of manslaughter. He was sentenced to five years' penal servitude. MR. MICHAEL DAVITT AND THE LoNDON BILL FOSTERS. —A novel paint has arisen in connection with the meeting to be addressed by Mr. Michael Davitt in London. The promoters applied to Messrs. Willing, the lessees of the ad- vertising hoardings in the metropolis, to post the bills announcing the meeting. This Messrs. Willing refuse to do, and the promoters intend bringing an action for damages against that firm to test the legality of their refusal. • THE FRACAS IN A LIVERPOOL CHURCH.—The Rev. Mr. Fitzroy, of St. Jude's Church, Liverpool, appeared in the Police Court yesterday to answer a summons charging him with assaulting the curate in charge, the Rev. Wasdale Watson, in church on Monday. The solicitor for Mr. Wat- son said they would not proceed with the charge in the interests of the church. Mr. Fitzroy's solicitor said they were astounded, and challenged Mr. Watson to go on with the case. A public scandal had been created, and his client denied that there was a word of truth in the charge. The case was dismissed. THE BALHAM MURDER. —At the Old Bailey, London, yesterday, before Mr. Justice Denman, Henry Powell, 24 years of age, was indicted for the wilful murder of John Dimry Bruton, at Balham, Surrey, on the 27th ult. De- ceased was the soil of a builder, by whom the prisoner had been employed; but the latter was discharged three days before the murder on account of the dissatisfaction of his employer. The prisoner conceived the idea that the deceased had caused his discharge, and he attacked Bruton with a chisel, causing fatal injuries. The case is proceeding. THE LIVERPOOL CANAL TRAGEDY: THE MURDERER IDENTIFIED.—Soon after midnight, on Thursday, Detective Marsh and a strong staff of Liverpool constables appre- hended Lewis Parry, aged thirty years, at the house of his parents, in Edmund-street, on suspicion of having mur- dered Susannah Hutton, on the canal bank, on Saturday night last. The prisoner fully answered the description of the supposed murderer. He is a married min, with three children, one of whom has been born since the murder was committed. He was known to have, been keeping company with the deceased for some time past, and was seen with her in a public-house, on Saturday night,•for about an hour and a half, drinking. They left together, and after the murder the prisoner was seen running down Leeds-street. The police are waiting to fully establish their suspicions as to the prisoner having been last in the deceased girl's company. COLLIERY EXPLOSION NEAR BARNSLEY: SUPPOSED Loss OF 20 LIVES.—Early yesterday morning a shocking explosion occurred at Wharncliffe Carlton Colliery, belonging to the Messrs. Craik„ about a mile from Barnsley. The colliery employs a large number of hands, but fortunately only 25 men were working the night shift when the explosion oc- curred. Soon after the explosion five men, working near the shaft, rushed to the pit bottom and were drawn out alive, although slightly injured. Information of the disaster was sent to Mr. Wardell, Government inspector; Joseph Mitchell, certificated manager; Superintendent Sykes, and others. As soon as possible an exploring party was organised, 54 volunteers promptly rendtring their services. Owing to the disordered state of the workings great cl•fileulty was experienced by the explorers, and only two bodies were recovered. Relays of explorers are working, but the after- damn being strong much cannot be done. It is believed that all the seventeen men in the workings are dead. Most of the miners are memb3-rs of the West Yorkshire Miners' Per- manent Relief Fund. The shaft is 130 yards deep. FRVIGD ON A CORNISH MINING COMPANY.

. 'Lie Central News Truro correspondent telegraphs that it having become known to the shareholders of the Wheel Jane Mine, Cornwall, that their Secretary, Mr. Granville Sharpe, late of Queen Victoria-street, London, had de- camped, the company's books have been investigated, and at a meeting of shareholders, held yesterday, the result of the enquiry was made known, and showed Mr. Sharpe had defrauded the company to the amount of £1,349. It seems that it was customary for .the shareholders to pay their calls direct. to Mr. Sharpe instead of to the cfflnpary's bankers, and in this way he had the opportunity, of which he availed himself, of appropriating money to his own use. Sharpe absconded after receiving the last call, and nothinc, has since been heard of him, although he is believed to have left England. His wife and six children remain in this country, and before absconding he settled his furniture upon Ins wife, and left £5O in a drawer for her use. Sharpe also held in his own name and in names of others, including his junior clerk, 1,047 shares, on which there are arrears of calls amounting to £661, most of which will also be lost to the company. This is the third large fraud perpetrated in connection with Cornish Mining Companies within a very short period.

A Grand Dramatic ENTEttTAINIIENT and CONCEIif will be given by the St. Edward's Catholi- Amateurs, in aid of the Irish National Brass Baud, Widnes, on lioNnAy EVEN', OcronEn 22nd. " Ireland as it Was ; or, The Eviction." to Conclude with a very langhable n&,,ro sketch entitled "The Troublesome Servant." Tickets 23, Is, and 6d, may be had from any of the members. DJors open at 7 p.m., to commence 4t 7-45 prompt.

PUBLIC HALL, RUN CORN. MR. BANTOCK PIERPOINT'S GRAND CONCERT, TUESDAY, NOVEMBER 13th, 1883. ARTISTES : Miss THUDIcHUM, Miss EMILIE LLOYD, Mr, CHARLES CHILLEY, Mr. BINTOCK PIERPOINT. SOLO VIOLIN; sir. BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON.—THE PUBLIC HEALTH ACT, 1875. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that the Mayor, Aldermen and Burgesses of the Borough of Warrington% in the counties of Lancaster and Chester. acting by the Council as the Urban Authority for the said borough, propose by virtue of the Public Health Act, 1875, to put in force and to present a Petition to the Local Government Board in pursuance of the said Act, praying that they may be allowed to put in force the powers of the Lands Clauses Consolidation Acts with respect to the purchase and taking of lands otherwise than by agreement for the purpose of widening, opening, and otherwise improving the West side of Bridge-street from Bridge Foot to Friar's Cate. And NOTICE IS HEREBY Furman GIVEN that a plan of the proposed undertaking is deposited at the office of the:Borough Surveyor, at the Town Hall. within the said borough, where the same may be inspected at all reasonable hours, and that, the total quantity of lands required by the said Mayor, Alder- men, and Burgesses for widening, opening, and otherwise im- proving the said street, and for the purpose of the said under- taking is 7.000 square yards or thereabouts. Dated this 13th day of October, 0383. WM. UT. BROOK. Town Clerk.

TO THE RATEPAYERS OF TIE TOWNSHIP OF WARRINGTON. Ladies an Gentlemen,—l beg to tender my sincere thanks for the honour which you have done me by electing me as Assistant-Overseer for your township. In so doing. children—all girls—were standing in a row, in the pasenge facing the judge, and they were all weeping and blowing their noses in their aprons while the trial was going on. And when the lawyer for the man who had travelled without ticket (here Wardle gave his wife a scared appealing look) was making his speech for the defence, you could see the tears as big as beans rolling down his honest cheeks. And the judge, in summing up, was so affected that he had to wipe his eyes and nose several times on his coat sleeve. He told the prisoner that he would like to let him off; but he said that duty was duty, and he mast do it; and though he had himself travelled many a time under the seat with- out ticket, he would be compelled to pass a sentence of four years with hard labour upon him." I did not expect that my nonsense would have had the effect it had upon Wardle. He turned pale, he gazed at the floor, and then across at his wife, and sed— " We'n bin wed aboon twenty yer, but we'n sever bin in a hobble like this afoor, hey we Alice?" "Aw think ther hevin thee on a bit, if aw may say wod aw think!" Just then the train began to slow for Lytham. Under t' seeat wi tha Wardle. T' trains stoppin !" Wardle dropped under the seat and the train stopped One of Wardle's friends then went to the window and shouted—" Gerd, gerd!" Wardle in a smothered voice said— .' Weal the hangment does ta want t' gerd for? Are ta beawn to tell him ?" Bat he still called for the guard, to Virardle's very evident trepidation, and when a porter came he simply asked him what time the train would get in and then he said to Wardle—" Tha con come (*left. Tiler nod collectin tickets here." "Aw couldn't like to stop under theer so long," said Wardle; "id is dusty," and his appearance proved it. Well, he had to bolt under the seat at Preston and &amber Bridge, and then he bethought himself that they would collect the tickets at Cherry Tree. But after he had been under the seat at Preston he offered a shilling if any of his friends would take his place and give him their ticket. Of course they declined. After we left Pleasingtoer, Wardle said he had better be getting ready, and, suiting the action to the word, he once more ensconced himself under the seat. The train was just stopping when he said, "Chaps, aw'm gooin to cough!" "If tha coughs tha'r done!" "I'd doesn't matter, aw man eyther cough or brast! Oh, dear! ough, ough, ough! Id's fair thick wi' dust under here !I and poor Wardle went on with his coughing. "Th hey to god done wi' thi coughin:or else tha mut as weel come eawt." "Aw wish some o yo as hasn't a bad cough wod come under here. Yo know varra weel as aw'm tekkin Kenyon's bottle! Aw's hey mi billy full o' dust if aw stop here mich longer." "Shut up; t' gerd's comm n for t' tickets." There never was such an object as Wardle was when he came from under the seat. With being afraid and making such efforts to stifle his desire to cough, he had begun to perspire, and when he went under the seat he naturally put his hands on the floor, which was very dirty. Well, after he had been under some time, to ease himself, he leaned his face on his dirty hands, and the result, as may be surmised, was ludicrous in the extreme. Come here, tha gred nasty-lookin thing, tan let's mek tha fit to be sin," said his wife. " Tha looks like an owd paysegger. Howd thi heyd up. Eh, tha ar an object! For God's sake, pat thi heyd eawt e'th' window an blow th nooas. Aw'm sure thi heyd's like a chimbly sweep's seci Aw wish thi mother could see thee neaw !" And she kept k. like this all the time she was wiping him; when we got on at Blackburn she was still grooming him down. I think that, on the whole, it is just about worth while making the journey, even though there is three and a half hour's riding out of the eight and a half. At any rate, I must admit that we enjoyed ourselves tolerably well.
